SDE-2 DSA Handbook

From complexity analysis to dynamic programming in 17 modules, practice first: every lesson opens with a problem to try, every drawing steps through, every worked example asks before it tells, and 407 free Medium and Hard LeetCode problems come with spaced review.

How this handbook teaches

The goal is not to remember 400 solutions. The goal is to look at a new problem, see its structure, and derive the algorithm. So the handbook asks you to do something before it explains anything.

  • Try before you read. Every lesson opens with one problem, or a two-minute question, to attempt before any explanation. Getting stuck first is what makes the explanation stick.
  • Short lessons, depth on request. Each lesson shows what the technique solves, an analogy, and its signal and required condition. Proofs, variants, comparison tables, and Java for each idea sit in folded "Go deeper" sections.
  • Step through every drawing. Figures start at step 1: predict the next state, then press Next. You should be able to redraw each one in under a minute; the drawing conventions show how.
  • Guided solves instead of finished solutions. Each worked example asks five questions and hides every answer until you have written your own.
  • One method, used everywhere. The decode method turns a statement into an algorithm in 8 steps. Its page starts with five drills, not an essay.
  • Java that runs. Every code block in this handbook comes from Java files that compile with javac --release 17 (so they work on Java 17 and 21) and pass a test harness with 321 checks, including the edge cases named in the text.
  • Practice that builds transfer. 407 LeetCode problems in 43 pattern banks, Medium and Hard only (357 Medium, 50 Hard), ordered from foundation to challenge, with one line on what each problem teaches.

About the problem links. Every problem was checked against two independent copies of LeetCode's problem catalog on October 14, 2026 (a daily export of LeetCode's own API and the doocs index). Both list all 407 as free, with the exact titles and difficulty shown here. The individual pages were not opened one by one. LeetCode occasionally moves a problem behind Premium; if a link shows a lock, skip it and take the next problem in the same bank.

How to study one module

Use this loop for every lesson. It works whether you have 30 minutes or 3 hours, because each step is a natural stopping point.

  1. Clear the revision queue first at the start of every session. Re-solve those problems from a blank editor.
  2. Attempt the "Try it first" problem for 15 minutes before reading. A brute force counts. Set its status honestly.
  3. Read the short part and step through the figure. Then close the page and say out loud: what signal points to this pattern, and when does it fail?
  4. Work the guided solve one question at a time. Write your answer, then reveal and compare the reasoning, not just the code.
  5. Open a "Go deeper" section only when you need it: your attempt failed for a reason the short part does not explain, or a bank problem needs a variant.
  6. Work the practice bank in order. The first two problems build the mechanism, the middle ones apply it, the last ones stretch it.
  7. Tick the mastery checklist only when an item is true with your notes closed.

Problem statuses and the revision queue

Each problem has a status. When you set one, the handbook schedules the next review. Problems whose date has arrived appear in the revision queue above and in the practice tracker.

Status Meaning Next review
Not started Not attempted Not scheduled
Not solved independently You needed the solution 2 days
Solved with hints You needed a hint, an editorial idea, or many failed submissions 4 days
Solved independently Clean solve, could explain the invariant 10 days
Needs revision Solved before, but a re-attempt went badly 1 day
Pattern mastered Solved twice, weeks apart, without help, and can explain why it works 30 days

When a problem comes up for review, re-solve it without looking at your old code. Then set the new status, or press "Reviewed, same status" to restart its timer.

Where your progress is saved

Statuses and checkboxes save automatically to your account, privately: nobody else who opens this page can see them, and they follow you to other devices. The indicator in the top bar shows where the latest change went. If the page cannot reach your account (for example in a private window), it saves in this browser instead, and the practice tracker has a backup and restore box for moving progress by hand.

Scope

This handbook covers the topics that general SDE-2 coding rounds actually test, in the depth they test them. Competitive-programming material (segment trees, suffix structures, flows, advanced string matching, heavy number theory) is excluded on purpose: it rarely appears in these rounds, and time spent there is better spent on pattern recognition and clean implementation.

Syllabus and prerequisite map

Seventeen modules in prerequisite order, with the reason each one comes where it does, and how much interview weight it carries.

On this page

The map

The order is not alphabetical and not by difficulty alone. Each module reuses ideas from the ones before it:

  • Complexity first, because every later decision ("is this fast enough?") is a complexity decision.
  • Arrays and hashing next, because nearly every other topic stores data in arrays or maps.
  • Two pointers, sliding window, sorting and binary search all exploit order in linear data. They are the highest-return patterns for Medium problems.
  • Linked lists and stacks teach pointer discipline and the "most recent item" idea that recursion and tree traversal depend on.
  • Recursion and backtracking before trees, because a tree problem is a recursion problem with a fixed shape.
  • Trees before graphs, because a tree is a graph without cycles; BFS and DFS on trees become BFS and DFS on graphs with a visited set.
  • Recursion and trees before DP, because a DP solution is a memoized recursion with a well-chosen state.

Priority overview

Priority reflects how often a topic decides general SDE-2 coding rounds at product companies, and how much other material depends on it.

How each module is organized

Every lesson follows the same practice-first order, so you always know what comes next:

  1. Try it first. One problem from the lesson's bank (or a two-minute question) to attempt for 15 minutes before any explanation.
  2. The short part. What the technique solves, an analogy, and the pattern card's two key fields: the signal, and the condition that must hold.
  3. A figure to step through. It starts at step 1; predict each next state, then press Next.
  4. A guided solve. Five questions (understand, brute force, key observation, build, check), each answer hidden until you reveal it.
  5. Go deeper sections, folded. Proofs, variants, comparison tables, and Java for each idea. Nothing was cut; open them when you need them.
  6. Common mistakes, the practice bank, and the module's mastery checklist.

Module 1: Complexity analysis

Complexity is how you decide, before writing code, whether an idea is fast enough. In an interview it is also the first follow-up question after every solution.

10 lessons0 guided solvesExercises, no problem bank

On this page

  1. 1.1What complexity measures
  2. 1.2Counting the cost of code
  3. 1.3Recursion: time from the call tree, space from the deepest path
  4. 1.4Space: auxiliary space and the recursion stack
  5. 1.5Amortized analysis
  6. 1.6Reading constraints: will it pass?
  7. 1.7Operation costs of common Java structures
  8. 1.8Comparing alternative approaches
  9. 1.9Common mistakes
  10. 1.10Self-check exercises
Try it firstWarm-up: five estimates

Before reading anything, write a complexity for each line. Then reveal and compare. Wrong answers are useful: they show which lesson to read closely.

  1. A loop over n that calls Arrays.sort on a copy of the array in every iteration.
    Reveal
    O(n^2 log n): n iterations, each copying (O(n)) and sorting (O(n log n)).
  2. For each of n words of length up to L, sort its characters and insert the result into a map.
    Reveal
    O(n * L log L): sorting each word dominates; hashing a key of length L is O(L).
  3. BFS over a grid with R rows and C columns.
    Reveal
    O(R * C) time and space: every cell enters the queue at most once.
  4. Generate all subsets of n items and copy each one into the result.
    Reveal
    O(2^n * n): there are 2^n subsets and each copy costs up to n.
  5. A while (lo < hi) binary search over the range 1 to 10^9 whose check loops over all n elements.
    Reveal
    O(n log 10^9), about 30n: 30 halvings, each with an O(n) check.

1.1What complexity measures

Try it first2 minutes, before you read on

Algorithm A does 100n steps and algorithm B does n^2 steps. Which is faster at n = 50? At n = 100,000?

Reveal the answer

At n = 50, B is faster: 2,500 steps against 5,000. At n = 100,000, A is faster by a factor of 1,000: 10^7 against 10^10. Constants decide small inputs; the growth rate decides large ones, and large inputs are what interviews test.

What it solves

Two solutions can both be correct and still differ by a factor of a million in running time. Complexity analysis predicts how the cost grows as the input grows, so you can reject a slow idea in seconds instead of after 20 minutes of coding.

Intuition

Think of estimating a commute. You do not count every traffic light; you say "about 2 minutes per kilometer". Complexity does the same with code: count the work per input element, ignore constants, and keep the part that dominates when the input is large.

What we count

Basic steps (comparisons, arithmetic, array reads, hash lookups) as a function of input size n. We drop constant factors and lower-order terms: 3n^2 + 10n + 7 is O(n^2), because for large n the n^2 term is all that matters.

Go deeper

Big-O, Big-Theta, Big-Omega at a practical level

Notation Plain meaning How interviewers use it
O(f(n)) Grows at most like f(n) (upper bound) "What is the complexity?" almost always means a tight O for the worst case
Omega(f(n)) Grows at least like f(n) (lower bound) "You cannot do better than reading the input": Omega(n)
Theta(f(n)) Grows exactly like f(n) (both bounds) Precise statements, e.g. merge sort is Theta(n log n) in every case

In practice, say "O(n log n) time and O(n) extra space", and make sure the bound is tight. Calling a linear algorithm O(n^2) is technically true and practically wrong.

Go deeper

Best, average, and worst case

The same algorithm can have different costs depending on the input arrangement.

Algorithm Best Average Worst What causes the worst case
Linear search O(1) O(n) O(n) Target absent or last
Quicksort O(n log n) O(n log n) O(n^2) Bad pivots, e.g. sorted input with first-element pivot
HashMap get O(1) O(1) O(n), or O(log n) once Java treeifies a crowded bucket Many keys in one bucket
Insertion sort O(n) O(n^2) O(n^2) Reverse-sorted input

Interviews default to the worst case, except for hashing, where O(1) average is the accepted convention. Say "O(1) average" when you rely on it.

1.2Counting the cost of code

Try it first2 minutes, before you read on

What does this cost in total?

for (int i = 1; i < n; i *= 2) for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) work();

Reveal the answer

O(n), not O(n log n). The inner loop runs 1 + 2 + 4 + ... up to n times, a geometric series that stays below 2n. Count the total work over the whole run, not (outer iterations) x (longest inner loop).

Most code can be analyzed with five rules:

  1. Sequential blocks add: O(a) + O(b), keep the larger.
  2. Nested loops multiply when the inner loop's length depends on n.
  3. A loop that halves (or doubles) its range runs log n times.
  4. Independent inputs keep their own variables: a loop over n items then over m items is O(n + m); nested is O(n * m). Do not merge them into O(n).
  5. Library calls have cost: Arrays.sort is O(n log n), list.contains is O(n), String.substring copies O(k) characters, s1 + s2 creates a new string.
Loops and their costs
// O(n): one pass, constant work per element
static long sum(int[] nums) {
    long total = 0;
    for (int x : nums) total += x;
    return total;
}

// O(n^2): the inner loop runs n-1, n-2, ..., 1 times -> about n^2 / 2
static int countPairsWithSum(int[] nums, int target) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++)
        for (int j = i + 1; j < nums.length; j++)
            if (nums[i] + nums[j] == target) count++;
    return count;
}

// O(log n): the remaining range halves every iteration
static int halvingSteps(int n) {
    int steps = 0;
    while (n > 1) { n /= 2; steps++; }
    return steps;
}

// O(n log n): n outer iterations, each doing O(log n) work
static int sumOfHalvingSteps(int n) {
    int total = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) total += halvingSteps(i);
    return total;
}

A useful mental table: log2(1000) ~ 10, log2(10^6) ~ 20, log2(10^9) ~ 30.

Go deeper

The trap of "two loops means O(n^2)"

Nested loops are not automatically quadratic. In a sliding window, the inner while loop moves left forward, and left never moves back. Across the whole run, left moves at most n times in total, so the algorithm is O(n). Count the total work over the entire run, not the worst case of one iteration multiplied by n.

1.3Recursion: time from the call tree, space from the deepest path

Try it first2 minutes, before you read on

int f(int n) { return n == 0 ? 1 : f(n - 1) + f(n - 1); }

What are the time and the space of f(n)?

Reveal the answer

Time O(2^n): every call makes two more, so the call tree has about 2^(n+1) nodes. Space O(n): only one chain of calls is open at a time, and it is n + 1 frames deep.

For a recursive function, draw the tree of calls.

  • Time = (number of calls) x (work per call, excluding the recursive calls).
  • Space = (deepest chain of calls that are open at the same time) x (memory per frame), plus any data you allocate.
Exponential vs linear recursion
// Time O(2^n): two calls per level, n levels. Space O(n): deepest call chain.
static long fibNaive(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return n;
    return fibNaive(n - 1) + fibNaive(n - 2);
}

// Time O(n), space O(n) for the memo plus O(n) stack depth.
static long fibMemo(int n, long[] memo) {
    if (n <= 1) return n;
    if (memo[n] != 0) return memo[n];
    return memo[n] = fibMemo(n - 1, memo) + fibMemo(n - 2, memo);
}

Common recurrences you should recognize on sight:

Recurrence Example Result
T(n) = T(n - 1) + O(1) Recursive sum, linked list traversal O(n)
T(n) = T(n / 2) + O(1) Binary search O(log n)
T(n) = 2T(n / 2) + O(n) Merge sort O(n log n)
T(n) = 2T(n / 2) + O(1) Tree traversal of a balanced tree O(n)
T(n) = 2T(n - 1) + O(1) Naive Fibonacci, subsets O(2^n)
T(n) = n * T(n - 1) Permutations O(n!)

For merge sort, the call tree has log n levels and each level does O(n) merging work in total, which is where n log n comes from. You rarely need the full Master Theorem in interviews; "levels times work per level" handles almost everything.

1.4Space: auxiliary space and the recursion stack

Try it first2 minutes, before you read on

A recursive DFS visits a tree of 10^5 nodes shaped like a linked list. It allocates no arrays. What is its space complexity, and what can go wrong in Java?

Reveal the answer

O(n), all of it call stack: the chain is 10^5 frames deep. That risks a StackOverflowError with Java's default stack, so switch to an explicit stack (or BFS) when the depth can reach about 10^4 or more.

  • Input space is the memory for the input itself. It is usually not counted.
  • Auxiliary space is what your algorithm adds: maps, copies, queues, the recursion stack.
  • Output space is sometimes excluded by convention (for example, the result list of all subsets), but say so explicitly.

The recursion stack is the most common hidden cost. A recursive DFS on a skewed tree of n nodes uses O(n) stack, even though it allocates nothing else. In Java the default thread stack handles roughly 10^4 frames of a small method safely; deeper recursion (10^5 nodes in a line, large grids) risks StackOverflowError. Convert to an explicit stack when depth can be that large.

1.5Amortized analysis

Try it first2 minutes, before you read on

An ArrayList starts with capacity 1 and doubles whenever it is full. About how many element copies happen in total while you add n elements?

Reveal the answer

Fewer than 2n. The resizes copy 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n elements, a geometric series. Spread over n adds, that is O(1) per add on average over the sequence (amortized), even though one unlucky add costs O(n).

Amortized cost is the average cost per operation over a whole sequence of operations, in the worst case. It matters when most operations are cheap and a few are expensive, and the expensive ones are rare by construction.

ArrayList growth
// ArrayList.add is amortized O(1): most adds are cheap, and a resize
// (copy of all elements) happens only when the backing array is full.
// Capacity grows geometrically (about 1.5x in the JDK), so total copies
// for n adds form a geometric series bounded by c * n: O(n) overall.
static List<Integer> buildList(int n) {
    List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) list.add(i);
    return list;
}

Three amortized arguments that show up again and again in this handbook:

Structure Expensive step Why the total stays linear
ArrayList.add Resize copies everything Capacity grows by a constant factor, so copies form a geometric series
Queue made of two stacks (Module 17) Moving all of in to out Each element moves at most once in its lifetime
Monotonic stack, sliding window A long run of pops or shrinks Each element is pushed once and popped at most once

Amortized O(1) is not the same as average-case O(1): hashing is O(1) on average over random inputs, while amortized bounds hold for every sequence.

1.6Reading constraints: will it pass?

Try it first2 minutes, before you read on

n is at most 10^5. In Java, which of these finish in about a second: O(n^2), O(n sqrt n), O(n log n)?

Reveal the answer

O(n log n) is about 1.7 * 10^6 operations: easily. O(n sqrt n) is about 3 * 10^7: usually fine. O(n^2) is 10^10: far too slow. A limit of 10^5 is the problem telling you to look for O(n log n) or O(n).

LeetCode and most interview judges allow roughly 10^7 to 10^8 simple operations per test in Java. Use the input limits to rule approaches in or out before you design anything:

Largest n Target complexity Typical techniques
n <= 10 to 12 O(n!) Permutations, brute-force search
n <= 20 to 25 O(2^n) or O(2^n * n) Subsets, bitmasks, backtracking
n <= 100 to 500 O(n^3) Interval DP, Floyd-Warshall
n <= 2,000 to 5,000 O(n^2) 2D DP, all pairs
n <= 10^5 to 10^6 O(n log n) or O(n) Sorting, heaps, binary search, two pointers, hashing, BFS
n up to 10^9 or more O(log n) or O(1) Binary search on the answer, math

Also read the value constraints. Values up to 10^9 summed over 10^5 elements exceed int (max about 2.1 x 10^9), so use long. Small values (lowercase letters, values <= 10^4) allow counting arrays instead of maps.

1.7Operation costs of common Java structures

Try it first2 minutes, before you read on

This drains a list of n items: while (!list.isEmpty()) { int x = list.remove(0); ... }. With an ArrayList, what does it cost, and what should it cost?

Reveal the answer

O(n^2): each remove(0) shifts every remaining element one place left. An ArrayDeque with pollFirst() removes from the front in O(1), so the loop becomes O(n).

Structure Access / search Insert Delete Notes
Array, ArrayList get(i) O(1), contains O(n) add at end O(1) amortized, at index O(n) O(n) (shifts) ArrayList.remove(int) vs remove(Object) overloads
HashMap, HashSet O(1) average O(1) average O(1) average No order; keys must have correct equals/hashCode
TreeMap, TreeSet O(log n) O(log n) O(log n) floorKey, ceilingKey, firstKey, subMap
ArrayDeque ends O(1) ends O(1) ends O(1) Use as stack or queue; no nulls
PriorityQueue peek O(1) O(log n) poll O(log n), remove(Object) O(n) Iteration is not sorted
LinkedList O(n) by index ends O(1) ends O(1) Rarely the best choice
String charAt O(1) concatenation O(n + m) substring O(k) copy Immutable: build with StringBuilder
Sorting Arrays.sort(int[]) dual-pivot quicksort, O(n log n) average; objects use TimSort, stable

1.8Comparing alternative approaches

Try it first2 minutes, before you read on

Two correct ways to detect a duplicate: sort and compare neighbors, or add values to a HashSet. Give the time and extra space of each, and one reason to pick the sort.

Reveal the answer

Sort: O(n log n) time, O(1) to O(log n) extra space, but it reorders the input. HashSet: O(n) average time, O(n) space. Pick the sort when memory is tight, when the input is already sorted, or when you need sorted order anyway.

Complexity is how you choose between correct ideas. Take "does any pair sum to target?":

Approach Time Extra space When to prefer it
Check every pair O(n^2) O(1) n is tiny, or as the first correct baseline
Sort, then two pointers O(n log n) O(1) to O(log n) Memory is tight, or the input is already sorted
Hash set of seen values O(n) average O(n) Default choice; also keeps original indices with a map

There is rarely one universally best answer. State the trade-off in one sentence: "Hashing is linear but uses O(n) memory; if memory matters, sorting gives O(1) extra space at O(n log n)."

1.9Common mistakes

Try it first2 minutes, before you read on

"One loop over n items, so it is O(n)." The loop body calls list.contains(x) on an ArrayList that grows to n items. What is the real cost?

Reveal the answer

O(n^2). contains scans the list, so each iteration costs up to O(n). A HashSet makes the whole loop O(n). Library calls inside loops are the most common hidden cost.

  • Ignoring hidden costs inside loops: list.contains, str.substring, s += c, list.remove(0) are each O(n) and turn an O(n) loop into O(n^2).
  • Merging different inputs: a grid is O(rows * cols), a graph is O(V + E), two strings are O(n * m) for a DP table. Do not call these O(n).
  • Forgetting the recursion stack in space complexity.
  • Calling a sliding window O(n^2) because of the nested loop. Count total pointer movement.
  • Quoting average case as worst case without saying so, outside of hashing.
  • Forgetting the sort: "two pointers is O(n)" is wrong if you had to sort first; the total is O(n log n).

1.10Self-check exercises

Try it firstFive more, after the lessons

Same drill, new code. If you miss one, the lesson it points to is worth a second look.

  1. for (i = 0; i < n; i++) for (j = i + 1; j < n; j++) with O(1) work inside.
    Reveal
    O(n^2): about n^2 / 2 pairs, and halving does not change the class.
  2. Building a string of n characters with s += c in a loop.
    Reveal
    O(n^2): each += copies the whole string built so far. A StringBuilder makes it O(n).
  3. A memoized recursion over states (i, j) with 0 <= i < n and 0 <= j < m, doing O(1) work per state.
    Reveal
    O(n * m) time and space: each state is computed once, plus up to O(n + m) recursion stack.
  4. Dijkstra with a binary heap on V vertices and E edges.
    Reveal
    O((V + E) log V): each edge can push one heap entry, and each heap operation is O(log V).
  5. Sort n values once, then answer q queries with binary search.
    Reveal
    O(n log n + q log n). Sorting once is what makes each query cheap.

Decode an unfamiliar problem

You learn this method by using it: one screen of steps, then five problems to decode with a reveal for every step. The detail behind each step is folded further down for when a drill surprises you.

On this page

  1. The method on one screen
  2. Practice: decode five problems
  3. The eight steps in detail
  4. Full walkthrough: two problems decoded from scratch
  5. Decision tables for commonly confused techniques

The method on one screen

Step Question you answer What you write down
1. Translate What exactly is asked, under which constraints? One plain sentence plus the task type
2. Input structure What properties does the input have? A list: sorted? contiguous? graph? stream?
3. Small example What happens when I solve it by hand? 2 to 4 tiny test cases and their answers
4. Brute force What is the simplest correct approach and its cost? The approach, its complexity, the repeated work
5. Key observation Which work is repeated, and which candidates can be discarded? One sentence: "because ..., we only need ..."
6. Map to a pattern Which technique exploits that observation? Pattern name, and why its required condition holds
7. Build it What variables, invariant, update rule, and stopping rule? A variable sheet
8. Validate Does it survive small, boundary, and adversarial cases? Pass or a counterexample

Spend most of the time on steps 3 to 5; steps 6 to 8 are quick once the observation is right. Keyword guessing ("it says substring, so sliding window") fails because a pattern is justified by a property of the problem, not a word in it.

Practice: decode five problems

Each drill has five steps. Write your answer to a step on paper, then reveal mine and compare. Give each problem about 15 minutes. You have not met every technique yet, and that is the point: the method should lead you to the right property of the problem before you know the technique's name. The module link on each drill is where that technique is taught.

Decode drill 1 of 5Pattern taught in Module 4
2300Successful Pairs of Spells and PotionsMedium

For each spell strength, count the potions whose product with it is at least success. Both lists have up to 10^5 values.

  1. 1Translate the statement
    Reveal my answer

    For each value s in spells, count the values p in potions with s * p >= success, and return the counts in spell order. Counting task. n and m up to 10^5; success up to 10^10, so the product needs long.

  2. 2Solve a tiny case by hand
    Reveal my answer

    spells = [5, 1, 3], potions = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], success = 7. Spell 5 works with potions 2 to 5: 4. Spell 1 needs 7 or more: 0. Spell 3 needs 3 or more: 3. Answer [4, 0, 3]. By hand you looked for the smallest potion that works and counted everything above it.

  3. 3Brute force and its repeated work
    Reveal my answer

    Check every pair: O(n * m), up to 10^10. The repeated work: every spell rescans all potions, although the potions never change.

  4. 4Key observation
    Reveal my answer

    The order of the potions does not matter, so sort them once. For a fixed spell, s * p >= success is false for small potions and true from some point on: a monotonic yes/no over sorted data.

  5. 5Pattern, build, validate
    Reveal my answer

    Sort plus binary search for the lower bound (Module 4). For each spell, find the first index with (long) s * potions[i] >= success; the count is m - index. O((n + m) log m). Check: when no potion works the index is m and the count is 0.

Write your answer to each step before revealing mine.
Decode drill 2 of 5Pattern taught in Module 5
1094Car PoolingMedium

A car with capacity seats only drives east. Each trip is (passengers, from, to). Can it serve every trip without ever exceeding capacity?

  1. 1Translate the statement
    Reveal my answer

    Each trip adds its passengers on the stretch [from, to). Is the total load at every point at most capacity? Existence task (true or false). Up to 1,000 trips, locations 0 to 1,000.

  2. 2Solve a tiny case by hand
    Reveal my answer

    trips = [[3, 2, 6], [2, 4, 8]], capacity = 4. Between 4 and 6 both groups ride: 5 > 4, so false. With capacity 5 it is true. By hand you only looked at the points where someone gets in or out.

  3. 3Brute force and its repeated work
    Reveal my answer

    For every location, add up the trips that cover it: O(trips * range). Here that passes, but the repeated work is clear: each trip adds the same amount to every point of its stretch, one point at a time.

  4. 4Key observation
    Reveal my answer

    The load only changes where someone boards or leaves. Record +p at from and -p at to; a running sum from left to right then gives the load at every point.

  5. 5Pattern, build, validate
    Reveal my answer

    Difference array, also called a sweep line (Modules 2 and 5). diff[from] += p; diff[to] -= p, then a running sum over 0 to 1,000 that fails as soon as it exceeds capacity. O(trips + range). Check: a drop-off and a pick-up at the same point land in the same cell, so they cancel correctly.

Write your answer to each step before revealing mine.
Decode drill 3 of 5Pattern taught in Module 7
739Daily TemperaturesMedium

For each day, how many days until a warmer temperature? Use 0 when there is none. Up to 10^5 days.

  1. 1Translate the statement
    Reveal my answer

    For each index i, find the nearest j > i with temps[j] > temps[i] and output j - i, or 0. n up to 10^5, so O(n^2) is too slow.

  2. 2Solve a tiny case by hand
    Reveal my answer

    [70, 71, 69, 68, 72, 70] gives [1, 3, 2, 1, 0, 0]. By hand, when 72 arrives it answers 68, 69, and 71 at once. The days still waiting were 71, 69, 68: always colder the more recent they are.

  3. 3Brute force and its repeated work
    Reveal my answer

    For each day, scan right until a warmer one: O(n^2) when temperatures keep falling. The repeated work: the same unanswered days are scanned past again and again.

  4. 4Key observation
    Reveal my answer

    Days still waiting form a decreasing sequence; a warmer day would already have answered the colder ones before it. A new day answers waiting days from the most recent backward and stops at the first one that is not colder.

  5. 5Pattern, build, validate
    Reveal my answer

    Monotonic stack of indices (Module 7). For each i: while the stack is not empty and temps[i] > temps[top], pop top and set ans[top] = i - top; then push i. Each index is pushed and popped at most once: O(n). Check: equal temperatures must not answer each other, which the strict > guarantees.

Write your answer to each step before revealing mine.
Decode drill 4 of 5Pattern taught in Module 12
207Course ScheduleMedium

There are n courses and prerequisite pairs [a, b] meaning b must come before a. Can you finish every course?

  1. 1Translate the statement
    Reveal my answer

    Given directed edges b -> a, is there an order of all n nodes that respects every edge? Existence task. n up to 2,000, up to 5,000 edges.

  2. 2Solve a tiny case by hand
    Reveal my answer

    n = 3 with [[1, 0], [2, 1]]: take 0, then 1, then 2: true. Add [0, 2] and 0 needs 2, 2 needs 1, 1 needs 0: a loop, nobody can start, false. By hand you began with courses that had no prerequisites and crossed them off.

  3. 3Brute force and its repeated work
    Reveal my answer

    Try every order of the courses: O(n!). The repeated work: orders that already broke a rule early are still extended and checked.

  4. 4Key observation
    Reveal my answer

    The prerequisites form a directed graph, and an order exists exactly when it has no cycle. A course with no remaining prerequisites can always be taken now, and taking it can only free other courses.

  5. 5Pattern, build, validate
    Reveal my answer

    Topological sort with Kahn's algorithm (Module 12). Count incoming edges per node, queue every node with none, then pop, count, and decrement each neighbor, queueing it when it reaches 0. Answer: processed count equals n. O(V + E). Check: a self-loop [a, a] never reaches 0, so the answer is false.

Write your answer to each step before revealing mine.
Decode drill 5 of 5Pattern taught in Module 14
322Coin ChangeMedium

Coins of several values, unlimited supply of each. Return the fewest coins that make amount exactly, or -1.

  1. 1Translate the statement
    Reveal my answer

    Minimize the number of items whose values sum to exactly amount, reusing any coin. Optimization task. Up to 12 coin values, amount up to 10^4.

  2. 2Solve a tiny case by hand
    Reveal my answer

    coins = [1, 3, 4], amount = 6. Largest first gives 4 + 1 + 1 = 3 coins, but 3 + 3 uses 2. By hand you compared "use a 4 and solve 2", "use a 3 and solve 3", "use a 1 and solve 5".

  3. 3Brute force and its repeated work
    Reveal my answer

    Try every combination recursively: exponential. The repeated work: "fewest coins for 2" is solved again on many different paths.

  4. 4Key observation
    Reveal my answer

    The best answer for an amount depends only on the amount, not on how you got there: best(a) = 1 + min(best(a - c)) over coins c. Overlapping subproblems with optimal substructure, and the greedy rule already failed.

  5. 5Pattern, build, validate
    Reveal my answer

    Dynamic programming, unbounded knapsack (Module 14). dp[0] = 0, everything else starts at amount + 1; for a from 1 to amount and each coin c <= a, dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a - c] + 1). Return -1 if dp[amount] is still amount + 1. O(amount * coins). Check: amount 0 returns 0.

The eight steps in detail

Open a step when a drill went wrong at that step. Each one lists the questions to ask and an example.

Go deeper

Why keyword guessing fails

"It says substring, so it is sliding window" works until it does not:

Statement Keyword guess What actually works Why the guess fails
Longest palindromic substring (LC 5) Sliding window Expand around each center Being a palindrome is not monotonic in window size: "aba" is one, "abab" is not, "ababa" is again
Count subarrays with sum exactly k, values can be negative (LC 560) Sliding window Prefix sums + hash map With negatives, growing a window can lower the sum, so you never know which side to move
Can this string be segmented into words (LC 139) Backtracking ("try every split") DP over prefixes Many split paths reach the same prefix; the question is yes/no, so you only need each prefix once
Fewest coins for an amount (LC 322) Greedy ("take the largest coin") DP Coins {1, 3, 4}, amount 6: greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1 = 3 coins, the optimum is 3 + 3 = 2 coins
Minimum capacity to ship within D days (LC 1011) Greedy or DP Binary search on the answer Computing the answer directly is hard, but checking a candidate capacity is easy and monotonic

A pattern is justified by a property of the problem: monotonicity, order, independence, overlapping subproblems. The method below finds those properties first and lets the pattern follow.

Go deeper

Step 1: Translate the statement into a simple problem

Strip the story, keep every constraint. Answer six questions:

  1. What is given? Types and shapes: an array of ints, a grid, a list of pairs, a stream of calls.
  2. What must be returned? A number, a boolean, an index, a list, a constructed object. "Return any" vs "return all" changes everything.
  3. What operations are allowed? Delete, swap, reorder, reuse elements, pick each once.
  4. What are the constraints? Sizes (they set the complexity budget, see Module 1), value ranges (negatives? overflow?), uniqueness.
  5. What type of task is it? See the table below.
  6. What special conditions hold? Sorted, contiguous, distinct, bounded, a guaranteed answer.
Task type Typical phrasing Families to consider first
Existence "Is it possible", "can you", "return true if" Search (BFS/DFS), DP over booleans, greedy with proof
Counting "How many", "number of ways" (often modulo 10^9 + 7) DP, prefix sums + hashing, combinatorics
Optimization "Minimum", "maximum", "longest", "fewest" DP, greedy, binary search on the answer, sliding window, Dijkstra
Search "Find the index", "return the element" Binary search, hashing
Ordering "Order of", "schedule", "sequence that satisfies" Sorting, topological sort, heaps
Connectivity "Connected", "reachable", "groups", "islands" BFS/DFS, Union-Find
Construction "Return all", "generate", "design a class" Backtracking, data structure design

Example of stripping a statement. LC 1011 reads: "A conveyor belt has packages that must be shipped from one port to another within days days. The i-th package on the conveyor belt has a weight of weights[i]. Each day, we load the ship with packages on the conveyor belt (in the order given by weights)..." Translated:

Split the array into at most D contiguous, in-order groups. Minimize the largest group sum. n up to 5 * 10^4, weights up to 500.

That translation already contains the key facts: contiguous, in order, "minimize the maximum". The story about ports and ships contains none.

Go deeper

Step 2: Identify the structure of the input

Each property removes approaches that cannot work, or enables ones that only work with it.

Property What it enables What it rules out or warns about
Sorted (or can be sorted without losing information) Binary search, two pointers, greedy by order If original indices matter, sorting loses them (keep index pairs)
Contiguous subarray or substring required Sliding window, prefix sums, Kadane, monotonic stack Subsequence techniques (DP over choices)
Order does not matter (sets, counts) Sorting, hashing, counting arrays Anything that relies on positions
Repeated values matter Frequency maps, duplicate skipping in backtracking Plain sets
Relationships or dependencies between items Graph modeling: BFS/DFS, topological sort, Union-Find Treating items independently
Stream or repeated updates and queries Heaps, two heaps, balanced trees, design with several structures Re-sorting after each update
Answer depends on earlier choices DP (if subproblems repeat), backtracking (if you need all answers) Greedy, unless a choice is provably safe
Small n (<= 20) Exponential search, bitmasks Nothing; exponential is allowed
Small value range Counting sort, bucket arrays, DP over values
Non-negative values Sliding window on sums, greedy accumulation With negatives, these usually break

Why this narrows the search: an interview problem is designed so that one property makes it solvable within the constraints. If n is 10^5, you need O(n log n) or better, and that means the problem must have order, monotonicity, or hashing-friendly structure somewhere. Your job is to find it.

Go deeper

Step 3: Start with a small example

Before choosing an algorithm, solve 2 to 4 tiny cases by hand. Make your own; the given examples are often chosen to hide edge cases.

Building useful test cases:

  • Minimal: empty input, one element, two elements.
  • Typical: 5 to 8 elements where the answer is not at either end.
  • Edge: all equal, all negative, already sorted, reverse sorted, answer is the whole input, no valid answer.
  • Adversarial for your idea: once you have an idea, build the case most likely to break it.

While solving by hand, watch yourself. Your hand solution is usually an inefficient version of the right algorithm. Ask:

  • What changes as I process each element?
  • What information do I keep in my head? (That becomes your state.)
  • What do I recompute? (That is what you will cache or maintain.)
  • What can I safely forget? (That is what lets you discard or shrink.)
  • What choice decides the next step? (That becomes a greedy rule or a DP transition.)
  • When is a partial answer valid? (That becomes the invariant.)

Example: longest substring with at most 2 distinct characters, s = "eceba". By hand, you scan and keep a stretch of text:

Notice what you kept in your head: the current stretch and how many of each letter it has. Notice what you never did: go back and restart from an earlier position. Those two observations are the sliding window pattern, discovered rather than guessed.

Go deeper

Step 4: Identify a brute-force approach

The brute force is the simplest approach you can prove correct. Write it in words (code it only if you are stuck or the interviewer asks). Then answer three questions:

  1. What does it try? All pairs, all subarrays, all subsets, all orders, every candidate answer.
  2. What work does it repeat? This is the most important question on the page.
  3. What does it cost, and how far is that from the budget? n = 10^5 with O(n^2) is 10^10 operations, far over budget.

Example: count subarrays with sum k. Brute force: for every start j, for every end i, sum the elements. O(n^3). The innermost work, "sum from j to i", is recomputed for every pair. Keeping a running sum per start makes it O(n^2). Now the repeated work is subtler: for each end i you check every start j, asking "does sum(j..i) equal k?" Since sum(j..i) = prefix(i) - prefix(j - 1), the question becomes "how many earlier prefixes equal prefix(i) - k?", which a hash map answers in O(1). The brute force pointed straight at the optimization.

The brute force is a tool for finding the optimization, not a box to tick. If you see the optimal idea immediately, say the brute force in one sentence and move on.

Go deeper

Step 5: Discover the key observation

Look at the brute force's innermost loop and ask these questions in order. Each "yes" points to a technique.

Question What it looks like in the brute force Technique Example
Am I recalculating the same information? A sum, count, or max over a range computed again for overlapping ranges Prefix sums, running aggregates LC 303, 238
Can I reuse previous results? The answer for i is built from answers for smaller inputs DP, memoization LC 70, 198
Can hashing replace repeated searching? An inner loop that searches for a value or complement HashMap / HashSet LC 1, 128
Can sorted order eliminate possibilities? Comparing every pair when order tells you which side to give up Two pointers, binary search LC 167, 15
Can two pointers avoid checking every pair? Pairs where moving one index monotonically changes the value Two pointers LC 11, 42
Can a window be maintained instead of recalculated? Re-scanning a contiguous range after adding one element Sliding window LC 3, 438
Can a greedy decision build the answer? Trying all choices when one choice is always at least as good Greedy with an exchange argument LC 435, 55
Can I keep only the best or most relevant elements? Scanning all previous elements to find the nearest greater, the max, the top k Monotonic stack/deque, heap LC 739, 239, 215
Can the problem split into smaller states? Same question on a prefix, suffix, subtree, or interval Recursion, DP, divide and conquer LC 1143, 124
Can relationships be a graph? Items that depend on, connect to, or transform into others BFS/DFS, topological sort, Union-Find LC 207, 127
Does an invariant make some elements irrelevant forever? Elements that, once beaten, can never be the answer again Monotonic structures, pruning LC 84, 402
Is checking easier than computing? You can verify a candidate answer quickly, and feasibility is monotonic Binary search on the answer LC 875, 410

How to discover the observation, not just recognize it. Three habits help:

  1. Name the inner loop's job in words. "This loop finds the previous index whose prefix equals X." Once named, you can ask "what data structure answers that in O(1) or O(log n)?"
  2. Look for monotonicity. When the right pointer moves forward, can the best left pointer only move forward too? When the capacity grows, does feasibility only go from false to true? Monotonic means you can discard instead of re-check.
  3. Look for dominance. If element A is worse than element B in every future comparison (older and smaller, for a window maximum), A can be deleted. Dominance is the idea behind monotonic stacks, deques, and many prunings.
Go deeper

Step 6: Map the observation to a pattern

Each pattern in this handbook has a pattern card with seven fields. Use them as a checklist, not a lookup table:

  • Signal: what in the problem suggests the pattern.
  • Required condition: what must be true for it to be correct. Verify this; it is where wrong guesses fail.
  • Mental model: how to think about it.
  • Core operation: what the algorithm repeatedly does.
  • Complexity benefit: what work it removes.
  • Limitations: when it breaks.
  • Alternative: what to use when the required condition fails.

Here is one card as an example. All cards are collected on the pattern cheat sheets page.

Pattern cardVariable-size sliding window
Signal
Longest or shortest contiguous subarray/substring satisfying a condition; 'at most k' distinct, zeros, or replacements.
Required condition
Monotonic validity: shrinking a valid window keeps it valid (or growing an invalid one keeps it invalid). Typically fails with negative numbers in sum conditions.
Mental model
An accordion: stretch right while it plays, squeeze from the left when it breaks.
Core operation
Expand right; while the window is invalid, shrink left; record the answer at the right moment.
Complexity benefit
Each index enters and leaves once: O(n) instead of O(n^2) over all windows.
Limitations
Breaks when adding an element can make the window either better or worse (sums with negatives).
Alternative
Prefix sums + hash map (exact sums with negatives); monotonic deque over prefix sums (shortest sum >= k with negatives); exactly(k) = atMost(k) - atMost(k-1).

The required condition is the field that saves you. Before committing, say it out loud and check it against your small examples: "Shrinking a valid window keeps it valid. Is that true here?" For "at most 2 distinct characters", yes. For "sum equals k with negatives", no, and the alternative row tells you where to go.

When two patterns seem to fit, use the decision tables at the bottom of this page.

Go deeper

Step 7: Build the solution incrementally

Before writing code, fill in a variable sheet. It turns a vague idea into a precise algorithm and gives you something to explain to the interviewer.

Item Question Example: minimum window substring (LC 76)
Variables What do I store? need[c] counts required, window[c] counts in window, left, formed
Meaning What does each variable mean, exactly? formed = number of distinct characters whose window count meets the requirement
State to maintain What must be updated on each step? Counts when a character enters or leaves, and formed when a count crosses its requirement
Invariant What is always true at a checkpoint? After the inner loop, the window [left, right] is the shortest valid window ending at right, or the window is invalid
Answer update When do I record a candidate? Inside the shrink loop, while the window is still valid
Discard rule When can an element or state be dropped? left advances when the window stays valid without s[left]
Termination When and why does it stop? right reaches the end; left never passes right + 1

If you cannot fill in the invariant, you do not understand the algorithm yet. Go back to the small example.

Go deeper

Step 8: Validate the reasoning

An observation that passes the given examples is not proven. Test it before coding:

  1. Run the small cases from Step 3 through your variable sheet by hand.
  2. Hit the boundaries: empty, single element, all equal, maximum values (overflow), no valid answer.
  3. Recheck the constraints: does the complexity fit? Does the memory fit? Are negatives allowed?
  4. Try to break it. Ask "what input would make this wrong?" and build it. For a greedy rule, look for a case where the locally best choice blocks a better global answer.
  5. Prove it in one sentence. "Each element enters and leaves the window once, and the window is valid exactly when ..." If you cannot say why it works, an interviewer will ask.

Attractive but wrong: greedy coin change. "Always take the largest coin that fits" passes every example with coins {1, 5, 10, 25}. Trying to break it with {1, 3, 4} and amount 6 gives 4 + 1 + 1 (3 coins) against the optimum 3 + 3 (2 coins). One counterexample is enough to move to DP.

Stress testing. When an idea is subtle, code the brute force too, run both on hundreds of random tiny inputs, and compare. It is the fastest way to find a wrong observation, and it is standard practice in real engineering.

Full walkthrough: two problems decoded from scratch

Guided decodeLC 1004. Max Consecutive Ones IIIThe decode method arrives at a sliding window without guessing

Problem: 1004Max Consecutive Ones IIIMedium. Answer each question on paper first, then reveal.

  1. 1
    Translate and read the input

    Strip the story: what is given, what is returned, and which properties does the input have?

    Reveal step 1
    Translate

    Given a binary array and k, return the length of the longest contiguous run of 1s if you may flip at most k zeros. n up to 10^5. Task type: optimization (longest).

    Input structure

    Contiguous subarray. Values are only 0 and 1. No sorting allowed (order matters).

  2. 2
    Small example and brute force

    Solve a tiny case by hand. Then name the simplest correct approach, its cost, and the work it repeats.

    Reveal step 2
    Small example

    [1,1,0,0,1,1,1,0,1], k = 1. By hand: I keep a stretch that contains at most one 0. When a second 0 arrives, I drop elements from the left until only one 0 remains. The answer is 5: indices 4 to 8 (1,1,1,0,1), flipping the zero at index 7.

    Brute force

    Every subarray, count zeros, keep the longest with zeros <= k. O(n^2) with a running count. Repeated work: after extending to right, I restart from every left again.

  3. 3
    Key observation

    Which property of the problem lets you skip the repeated work?

    Reveal step 3
    Key observation

    "Flipping at most k zeros" means "the subarray contains at most k zeros". If [left, right] is valid, every shorter window inside it is valid too; if it is invalid, every window that contains it is invalid. Validity is monotonic, so when right moves forward, the best left never needs to move back.

  4. 4
    Pattern and build

    Name the technique, check its required condition, and write the variables and the update rule.

    Reveal step 4
    Pattern

    Variable-size sliding window. Required condition (shrinking keeps validity) holds.

    Build it

    zeros = zeros in the window. Add nums[right]; while zeros > k, remove nums[left++]; then best = max(best, right - left + 1). Invariant: after the while loop, the window is the longest valid window ending at right.

  5. 5
    Validate

    Which boundary inputs could break it, and what does it cost?

    Reveal step 5
    Validate

    All ones: window grows to n. k = 0: longest run of ones. k >= number of zeros: answer n. Each index enters and leaves once: O(n) time, O(1) space.

Guided decodeLC 1011. Capacity To Ship Packages Within D DaysWhen computing the answer is hard but checking it is easy

Problem: 1011Capacity To Ship Packages Within D DaysMedium. Answer each question on paper first, then reveal.

  1. 1
    Translate and read the input

    Strip the story: what is given, what is returned, and which properties does the input have?

    Reveal step 1
    Translate

    Split weights into at most D contiguous groups in order; minimize the largest group sum. Optimization (minimum of a maximum).

    Input structure

    Order is fixed, groups are contiguous, weights are positive. n up to 5 * 10^4.

  2. 2
    Small example and brute force

    Solve a tiny case by hand. Then name the simplest correct approach, its cost, and the work it repeats.

    Reveal step 2
    Small example

    [1,2,3,4,5], D = 2. Try capacities: 7 needs [1,2,3] [4] [5] = 3 days, too many. 9 gives [1,2,3] [4,5] = 2 days, fine. 8 gives [1,2,3] [4] [5] = 3 days. So the answer is 9. Notice: checking one capacity was easy (greedy fill), and every capacity above 9 also works.

    Brute force

    Try every capacity from max(weights) up to sum(weights) and greedily check each. O(n * sum), up to 5 * 10^4 * 2.5 * 10^7: far too slow. Repeated work: checking capacities one by one when feasibility is monotonic.

  3. 3
    Key observation

    Which property of the problem lets you skip the repeated work?

    Reveal step 3
    Key observation

    feasible(cap) is false for small capacities and true from the answer onward. A monotonic yes/no function over a range is exactly what binary search finds.

  4. 4
    Pattern and build

    Name the technique, check its required condition, and write the variables and the update rule.

    Reveal step 4
    Pattern

    Binary search on the answer, with a greedy feasibility check. Required condition: monotonic feasibility (more capacity never needs more days). It holds.

    Build it

    lo = max(weights) (every package must fit), hi = sum(weights) (one day). Find the first capacity where daysNeeded(cap) <= D. daysNeeded fills the current day until the next package would overflow.

  5. 5
    Validate

    Which boundary inputs could break it, and what does it cost?

    Reveal step 5
    Validate

    D = n gives max(weights); D = 1 gives the sum. Cost: O(n log(sum)). The same skeleton solves LC 875 and LC 410; see Module 4.

Decision tables for commonly confused techniques

These tables are not rules. Each one names the property that decides between two techniques, so you can check the property instead of guessing.

Go deeper

Hashing vs sorting

Hashing Sorting
Use when You need membership, counts, or a complement lookup, and original positions matter You need order: neighbors, ranges, pairs via two pointers, grouping by adjacency
Cost O(n) average time, O(n) space O(n log n) time, O(1) to O(n) space
Breaks when You need the k-th smallest, ranges, or "closest" values You must return original indices (unless you sort index pairs)
Deciding question Do I need order, or only identity?
Go deeper

Two pointers vs sliding window

Two pointers (opposite ends) Sliding window (same direction)
Use when The answer is a pair of positions, and sorted order tells you which end to move The answer is a contiguous range with a running condition
What the pointers mean Two candidates being compared The two boundaries of one range
Example Two Sum II, 3Sum, Container With Most Water Longest substring without repeats, minimum size subarray sum
Deciding question Is the answer two separate elements, or everything between two indices?
Go deeper

Sliding window vs prefix sums

Sliding window Prefix sums (+ hash map)
Use when Validity is monotonic: all values non-negative, or the condition is about counts Exact sums, sums with negative numbers, many range queries
Finds Longest or shortest valid window, or counts under "at most" Number of subarrays with an exact sum, any range sum in O(1)
Breaks when Negatives make window sums non-monotonic You need the max or min of a range (not invertible)
Deciding question If I extend the window, can the condition get both better and worse? If yes, use prefix sums.
Go deeper

Prefix sums vs difference arrays

Prefix sums Difference array
Use when Many range queries on fixed data Many range updates, then read the final values once
Operation prefix[r+1] - prefix[l] diff[l] += x; diff[r+1] -= x, then take a prefix sum
Example Range Sum Query, Subarray Sum Equals K Corporate Flight Bookings, Car Pooling
Deciding question Am I asking about ranges, or adding to ranges?
Go deeper

Binary search on data vs binary search on an answer

On data On the answer
Search space Indices of a sorted or rotated array A range of possible answer values (speed, capacity, time, distance)
Predicate Compares nums[mid] with the target feasible(mid), computed by a greedy O(n) check
Signal "Sorted", "find the position" "Minimum X such that ...", "maximize the minimum", huge answer ranges
Deciding question Am I locating something in the input, or guessing a value and checking it?
Go deeper

BFS vs DFS

BFS DFS
Use when Shortest path in unweighted graphs, levels, nearest anything, spreading over time Reachability, components, cycle detection, topological order, backtracking, tree recursion
Memory O(width) queue O(depth) stack (recursion depth risk)
Breaks when Graph is huge and only one deep path matters You need shortest distances (DFS finds a path, not the shortest)
Deciding question Do I need the closest or fewest-step answer? Use BFS.
Go deeper

BFS vs Dijkstra

BFS Dijkstra
Edge weights All equal (or 0/1 with a deque) Non-negative, different
Cost O(V + E) O((V + E) log V)
First visit is final? Yes, because levels are distances Only when popped from the heap
Deciding question Do moves have different costs? If yes, Dijkstra.
Go deeper

Greedy vs DP

Greedy DP
Use when A local choice is provably safe (exchange argument) Choices interact; a locally good choice can hurt later
Cost Usually O(n log n) or O(n) States x transitions, often O(n^2) or O(n * W)
Proof Exchange argument or "stays ahead" Recurrence over subproblems
Deciding question Can I find a small counterexample to the greedy rule? If yes, DP.
Go deeper

Backtracking vs DP

Backtracking DP
Asked for All solutions, or a construction A count, a best value, or yes/no
Subproblems Partial paths differ (the path itself matters) Different paths reach the same state
Cost Exponential, prunable Polynomial in the number of states
Deciding question Do I need to list the answers, or just measure them?
Go deeper

Heap vs sorting

Heap Sorting
Use when Data arrives over time, or you need only the top k All data is known and you need full order
Cost O(n log k) for top k O(n log n)
Breaks when You need arbitrary access to the middle Data keeps changing (re-sort each time)
Deciding question Do I need all of the order, or just the current extreme?
Go deeper

Trie vs HashMap

Trie HashMap / HashSet
Use when Prefix queries, autocomplete, wildcard search, sharing work across many words Exact-match lookups
Cost O(L) per word, high memory O(L) to hash a string of length L, low overhead
Deciding question Will I ask about prefixes, or only whole keys?
Go deeper

Tree DP vs ordinary tree recursion

Ordinary recursion Tree DP
Return value One value (height, sum, found node) A small tuple of states per node (take/skip, covered/not covered)
Use when The parent needs one fact about each child The parent's choice depends on the child's choice (adjacent nodes cannot both be picked)
Example Max depth, diameter, LCA House Robber III, Binary Tree Cameras
Deciding question Does the parent need to know how the child decided, not just what it got?
Go deeper

Repeated computation vs memoization

Plain recursion Memoized recursion
Use when Every call has distinct arguments (tree traversal, backtracking) The same arguments recur (Fibonacci, grid paths, word break)
Detect it Draw the call tree for a small input: are there duplicate nodes?
Cost Number of calls in the tree Number of distinct states x work per state
Deciding question Does the function's result depend only on its arguments, and do arguments repeat?

2.1Arrays and in-place modification

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
189Rotate ArrayMedium

Any correct brute force counts. Note where you got stuck: the lesson below is about exactly that.

Show a hint
Three reversals rotate in O(1) extra space
What it solves

Many problems ask you to rearrange, filter, or transform an array without allocating another one ("in place", "O(1) extra space"). The difficulty is not the operation; it is overwriting values you still need.

Intuition

Picture tidying a bookshelf from left to right with two hands. One hand (the read pointer) looks at every book; the other (the write pointer) marks where the next book you keep should go. The write hand never gets ahead of the read hand, so you never overwrite a book you have not looked at yet.

How to recognize it

"In place", "O(1) extra memory", "return the new length", "do not allocate another array", or matrix rotation and spiral orders.

Go deeper

The read/write pointer technique

The invariant is what makes this safe: nums[0..write) holds exactly the kept elements seen so far, in their original order. Because write <= read always, writing at write only overwrites a position that has already been read.

Java
// LC 283. write = next position for a kept (non-zero) element.
static void moveZeroes(int[] nums) {
    int write = 0;
    for (int read = 0; read < nums.length; read++) {
        if (nums[read] != 0) {
            int tmp = nums[write]; nums[write] = nums[read]; nums[read] = tmp;
            write++;
        }
    }
}

The same skeleton solves "remove element" (LC 27), "remove duplicates from sorted array" (LC 26, keep nums[read] when it differs from nums[write - 1]), and string compression (LC 443).

Go deeper

Matrices and two-dimensional arrays

In Java, int[][] m is an array of row arrays: m.length is the number of rows, m[0].length the number of columns, and rows can even have different lengths. Iterate rows in the outer loop for cache-friendly access.

Three moves cover most matrix problems:

  1. Index mapping. Transpose maps (r, c) to (c, r). A flat index i in an R x C matrix maps to (i / C, i % C). That lets you binary search a sorted matrix as one array (LC 74).
  2. Layer or boundary walking. Spiral order walks four boundaries (top, bottom, left, right) and shrinks them after each side.
  3. Composition of simple transforms. A clockwise rotation is a transpose followed by reversing each row; counterclockwise is transpose then reverse each column.
Java
// LC 48. Clockwise rotation = transpose, then reverse each row.
static void rotate(int[][] m) {
    int n = m.length;
    for (int r = 0; r < n; r++)
        for (int c = r + 1; c < n; c++) {          // upper triangle only
            int tmp = m[r][c]; m[r][c] = m[c][r]; m[c][r] = tmp;
        }
    for (int[] row : m)
        for (int left = 0, right = n - 1; left < right; left++, right--) {
            int tmp = row[left]; row[left] = row[right]; row[right] = tmp;
        }
}
Java
// LC 54. Four boundaries shrink inward; re-check after the turn.
static List<Integer> spiralOrder(int[][] m) {
    List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
    int top = 0, bottom = m.length - 1, left = 0, right = m[0].length - 1;
    while (top <= bottom && left <= right) {
        for (int c = left; c <= right; c++) out.add(m[top][c]);
        top++;
        for (int r = top; r <= bottom; r++) out.add(m[r][right]);
        right--;
        if (top <= bottom) {
            for (int c = right; c >= left; c--) out.add(m[bottom][c]);
            bottom--;
        }
        if (left <= right) {
            for (int r = bottom; r >= top; r--) out.add(m[r][left]);
            left++;
        }
    }
    return out;
}

The spiral's two if checks matter: after walking the top row and right column, the remaining region may be a single row or a single column, and without the checks you would walk it twice.

Using the matrix as its own scratch space. When O(1) space is required, store markers inside the input: the first row and column in Set Matrix Zeroes (LC 73), or an extra bit per cell in Game of Life (LC 289, encode "was alive, now dead" as a state number).

Common mistakes

  • Advancing write for every element instead of only for kept ones.
  • Swapping m[r][c] and m[c][r] for every c instead of only c > r, which transposes twice and undoes the work.
  • Mixing up m.length and m[0].length on non-square matrices (LC 867).
  • Off-by-one in boundary walks: decide whether boundaries are inclusive and keep that everywhere.

2.2Hashing: HashMap and HashSet patterns

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
128Longest Consecutive SequenceMedium

Stuck after 15 minutes? The guided solve in this lesson walks through this exact problem, one question at a time.

Show a hint
Start counting only at sequence starts to stay O(n)
What it solves

The most common source of wasted work is an inner loop that searches for something: a complement, a duplicate, a previous occurrence. A hash map answers "have I seen X, and where, and how often?" in O(1) average time, turning O(n^2) into O(n).

Intuition

A coat check. Instead of searching every hook for your coat, you hand over a ticket number and get the coat back instantly. The key is the ticket; the value is what you stored.

Pattern cardHashing (lookup and counting)
Signal
You keep asking 'have I seen X?', 'how many X?', or 'where is X?' inside a loop. Pairs that must sum or match. Grouping by an equivalence (anagrams, same pattern).
Required condition
A key that identifies what you are looking for. Order of elements does not matter for the lookup itself.
Mental model, core operation, limits, and what to use instead
Mental model
A notebook keyed by value: before scanning again, check the notebook.
Core operation
For each element: query the map for its complement or key, then record the element.
Complexity benefit
Replaces an O(n) inner search with O(1) average lookup: O(n^2) to O(n).
Limitations
No ordering or range queries; O(n) extra memory; worst-case collisions; mutable keys break it.
Alternative
Sorting + two pointers (O(1) extra space), TreeMap for ordered or range queries, a counting array for small value ranges.
Go deeper

The four hashing moves

Move Question it answers Java idiom
Seen set Have I seen this value before? if (!seen.add(x)) duplicate (add returns false if present)
Complement map Is there an earlier element that pairs with this one? map.get(target - x) then map.put(x, i)
Frequency map How many times does each value appear? freq.merge(x, 1, Integer::sum)
Grouping map Which items share a canonical key? groups.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(item)

For lowercase letters or small value ranges, an int[26] or int[maxValue + 1] is a faster, simpler hash map. Two strings are anagrams exactly when their 26-count arrays are equal.

Go deeper

Brute force to optimal: Two Sum

The brute force checks every pair: O(n^2). The inner loop's job, in words, is "find an earlier index whose value is target - nums[i]". That is a lookup, so store earlier values in a map.

Java
// LC 1. For each x, ask "have I already seen target - x?"
static int[] twoSum(int[] nums, int target) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> indexOf = new HashMap<>();   // value -> index
    for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        int need = target - nums[i];
        Integer j = indexOf.get(need);                 // null if absent
        if (j != null) return new int[]{j, i};
        indexOf.put(nums[i], i);                       // insert AFTER the check
    }
    return new int[0];
}

Inserting after the check matters: it prevents pairing an element with itself ([3] with target 6), while still finding [3, 3] because the first 3 is in the map when the second arrives.

Go deeper

Canonical keys for grouping

Grouping problems need a key that is identical for items that belong together and different otherwise. For anagrams, the sorted letters ("eat" -> "aet") or the 26 counts joined into a string. For "same pattern" problems (LC 290, 205), map each item to the sequence of first-occurrence indices.

Java
// LC 49. Canonical key: the sorted letters of each word.
static List<List<String>> groupAnagrams(String[] strs) {
    Map<String, List<String>> groups = new HashMap<>();
    for (String s : strs) {
        char[] chars = s.toCharArray();
        Arrays.sort(chars);
        String key = new String(chars);
        groups.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(s);
    }
    return new ArrayList<>(groups.values());
}
Go deeper

Java hashing pitfalls

  • Arrays are not valid keys. int[] uses identity hashCode, so two equal arrays are different keys. Use Arrays.toString(arr), a String, or List<Integer>.
  • Never mutate a key after putting it in a map; it becomes unreachable.
  • Integer comparison with == works only for cached values in -128..127. Use .equals or unbox: map.get(a).intValue() == map.get(b).
  • map.get returns null for missing keys; unboxing null into int throws NullPointerException. Use getOrDefault.
  • Iteration order of HashMap is unspecified. Use LinkedHashMap for insertion order or TreeMap for sorted order.
Guided solveLC 128. Longest Consecutive SequenceFive questions, each with a reveal

Problem: 128Longest Consecutive SequenceMedium. Answer each question on paper first, then reveal.

  1. 1
    Understand the problem

    Say in one sentence what is asked. Which constraint sets the time budget?

    Reveal step 1
    Problem decoding

    Given an unsorted array, return the length of the longest set of values that form consecutive integers (x, x+1, x+2, ...), in any positions. Must run in O(n).

    Input analysis

    Unsorted, duplicates possible, negatives allowed, n up to 10^5. Order in the array does not matter: this is about the set of values.

  2. 2
    Brute force, then a pattern

    What is the simplest correct approach and what does it cost? Which pattern could beat it, and why does it apply?

    Reveal step 2
    Pattern discovery

    "Order does not matter" plus "O(n) required" rules out sorting (O(n log n)) and points at hashing. The repeated question is "is x + 1 present?"

    Brute force

    Sort and scan for runs: O(n log n), correct but over the stated budget. A naive hashing version, "for every x, count upward while x + 1 exists", is O(n^2) on [1, 2, ..., n] because every element re-walks the rest of the run.

  3. 3
    The key observation

    What single fact removes the repeated work? Trace a tiny input on paper until you see it.

    Reveal step 3

    Key idea. only start counting at the beginning of a run

    Key observation

    Each run should be counted once, from its smallest element. x is the start of a run exactly when x - 1 is not in the set. Skip every other element.

    Visualization
    set = {100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2}
x = 100: 99 absent  -> start; 101 absent         -> length 1
x = 4:   3 present  -> not a start, skip
x = 200: 199 absent -> start; length 1
x = 1:   0 absent   -> start; 2, 3, 4 present    -> length 4
x = 3:   2 present  -> skip
x = 2:   1 present  -> skip
best = 4
  4. 4
    Build it

    Write the algorithm in three or four lines, then code it. Reveal after you have run one small input by hand.

    Reveal step 4
    Algorithm

    Put all values in a set. For each value in the set: if x - 1 is present, skip. Otherwise count up while x + length is present and update the best.

    Java implementation
    Java
    // LC 128. O(n): only start counting at x when x - 1 is absent.
static int longestConsecutive(int[] nums) {
    Set<Integer> set = new HashSet<>();
    for (int x : nums) set.add(x);
    int best = 0;
    for (int x : set) {                    // iterate the set to skip duplicates
        if (set.contains(x - 1)) continue; // x is not a sequence start
        int length = 1;
        while (set.contains(x + length)) length++;
        best = Math.max(best, length);
    }
    return best;
}
    Dry run

    Shown in the visualization. Note that the inner while loop walked 1, 2, 3, 4 once in total, not once per element.

  5. 5
    Check it

    State time and space with a reason, name three inputs that could break the code, and say what this problem teaches beyond itself.

    Reveal step 5
    Complexity

    Time O(n): each value is inserted once, and each value is visited by an inner while loop at most once (only from its run's start). Space O(n) for the set.

    Edge cases

    Empty array (return 0, the loop never runs); duplicates (iterating the set, not the array, avoids re-counting); negatives (x - 1 works the same). Overflow: the constraints keep values within plus or minus 10^9, so x + length cannot overflow. If values could reach Integer.MAX_VALUE, x + length would wrap to Integer.MIN_VALUE and could falsely continue a run, so you would compute with long.

    Transfer lesson

    "Start work only at a canonical starting point" turns nested-looking loops into linear ones. The same counting argument appears in sliding windows and monotonic stacks: bound the total inner-loop work across the run.

Common mistakes

  • Using a list (contains is O(n)) where a set was needed.
  • Inserting before checking in complement problems, which pairs an element with itself.
  • Counting with map.put(x, map.get(x) + 1) on a missing key: NullPointerException.
  • Using char arithmetic on uppercase or non-letter input with c - 'a': check the character set in the constraints.
