2.3Prefix sums, suffix sums, and difference arrays

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
560Subarray Sum Equals KMedium

Stuck after 15 minutes? The guided solve in this lesson walks through this exact problem, one question at a time.

Show a hint
Count earlier prefixes equal to current - k (works with negatives)
What it solves

Sums over ranges, asked many times, or counting subarrays whose sum meets a condition. Recomputing each range is O(n) per query; prefix sums make it O(1).

Intuition

Mileposts on a highway. To know the distance from milepost 12 to milepost 47, you do not drive it again; you subtract the two readings.

Pattern cardPrefix sums
Signal
Sum (or count, XOR) over a contiguous range, asked many times. 'Subarray sum equals / divisible by k'. Negative numbers allowed.
Required condition
An invertible combine operation (sum, XOR, count): range = prefix[r+1] - prefix[l]. Max and min are NOT invertible.
Mental model, core operation, limits, and what to use instead
Mental model
An odometer: distance between two mileposts is the difference of their readings.
Core operation
Build cumulative totals once; answer a range with one subtraction. With a hash map: count earlier prefixes equal to current - k.
Complexity benefit
Each range query drops from O(n) to O(1); counting subarrays drops from O(n^2) to O(n).
Limitations
Static data (updates force a rebuild); does not answer max/min ranges; watch int overflow.
Alternative
Sliding window when all values are non-negative; difference array for many range updates; Fenwick or segment tree when the array changes.
Java
// prefix[i] = sum of nums[0..i-1]; prefix has length n + 1.
// Sum of nums[l..r] (inclusive) = prefix[r + 1] - prefix[l].
static long[] buildPrefix(int[] nums) {
    long[] prefix = new long[nums.length + 1];
    for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + nums[i];
    return prefix;
}

static long rangeSum(long[] prefix, int l, int r) {
    return prefix[r + 1] - prefix[l];
}

Why length n + 1? With prefix[0] = 0, the sum of nums[l..r] is always prefix[r + 1] - prefix[l], with no special case for l = 0. Use long when n * maxValue can exceed about 2.1 x 10^9.

Go deeper

Prefix sums with a hash map: counting subarrays

A subarray nums[j+1..i] has sum prefix(i) - prefix(j). Asking "does it equal k?" for every pair is O(n^2). Rearranged, the question for each i becomes "how many earlier prefixes equal prefix(i) - k?", which a frequency map answers in O(1). Variations change only what you store and look up:

Problem Transform Look up Store
Sum equals k (LC 560) none count of prefix - k count of each prefix
Divisible by k (LC 974) prefix mod k (fix negatives: ((p % k) + k) % k) count of the same remainder count of each remainder
Equal 0s and 1s (LC 525) 0 becomes -1, find sum 0 first index of the same prefix first index of each prefix (longest wants the earliest start)
Sum multiple of k, length >= 2 (LC 523) prefix mod k first index of the same remainder first index only
Go deeper

Suffix sums and prefix products

When an answer depends on everything to the left and everything to the right, compute both passes. Product of Array Except Self (LC 238) is the classic: the left products fill the output array, then a single running variable multiplies in the right products, giving O(1) extra space without division.

Java
// LC 238. answer[i] = (product left of i) * (product right of i).
static int[] productExceptSelf(int[] nums) {
    int n = nums.length;
    int[] answer = new int[n];
    answer[0] = 1;
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) answer[i] = answer[i - 1] * nums[i - 1]; // left products
    int right = 1;
    for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        answer[i] *= right;          // multiply in the product of everything to the right
        right *= nums[i];
    }
    return answer;
}
Go deeper

Difference arrays: many range updates

If you must add x to every element in [l, r] for many updates and read the result once, do not loop over the range. Record where the effect starts and stops, then take one prefix sum at the end.

n = 5, updates: +10 on [0,1], +20 on [1,2], +25 on [1,4]
diff after updates : [10, 45, -10, -20, 0, -25]   (index 5 is the extra slot)
running prefix     : [10, 55,  45,  25, 25]
Java
// LC 1109. Add seats to ranges, then read final totals.
// diff[l] += x starts the effect; diff[r + 1] -= x stops it.
static int[] corpFlightBookings(int[][] bookings, int n) {
    int[] diff = new int[n + 1];               // 1-based flights, extra slot for r + 1
    for (int[] b : bookings) {
        int first = b[0] - 1, last = b[1] - 1, seats = b[2];
        diff[first] += seats;
        diff[last + 1] -= seats;
    }
    int[] result = new int[n];
    int running = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        running += diff[i];
        result[i] = running;
    }
    return result;
}
Guided solveLC 560. Subarray Sum Equals KFive questions, each with a reveal

Problem: 560Subarray Sum Equals KMedium. Answer each question on paper first, then reveal.

  1. 1
    Understand the problem

    Say in one sentence what is asked. Which constraint sets the time budget?

    Reveal step 1
    Problem decoding

    Count contiguous subarrays whose elements sum to exactly k.

    Input analysis

    n up to 2 * 10^4, values between -1000 and 1000 (negatives allowed), k between -10^7 and 10^7.

  2. 2
    Brute force, then a pattern

    What is the simplest correct approach and what does it cost? Which pattern could beat it, and why does it apply?

    Reveal step 2
    Pattern discovery

    "Contiguous" and "sum" suggest a sliding window, but negatives break the window's monotonicity: adding an element can lower the sum. "Exact sum" with negatives is the signal for prefix sums plus hashing.

    Brute force

    For each start, extend the end with a running sum and count hits: O(n^2) time, O(1) space. 4 * 10^8 operations at the limits: too slow in the worst case, and it hides the repeated question.

  3. 3
    The key observation

    What single fact removes the repeated work? Trace a tiny input on paper until you see it.

    Reveal step 3

    Key idea. count earlier prefixes equal to prefix - k

    Key observation

    For a fixed end i, the brute force asks of every start "is prefix(i) - prefix(j) == k?" That is a single lookup: count how many earlier prefixes equal prefix(i) - k.

    Visualization

    nums = [1, 2, 1, -1, 2], k = 3. The map starts with {0: 1} for the empty prefix.

    i nums[i] prefix need = prefix - k count[need] total map after insert
    0 1 1 -2 0 0 {0:1, 1:1}
    1 2 3 0 1 1 {0:1, 1:1, 3:1}
    2 1 4 1 1 2 {..., 4:1}
    3 -1 3 0 1 3 {..., 3:2}
    4 2 5 2 0 3 {..., 5:1}

    The three subarrays: [1,2] (i=1), [2,1] (i=2, from the prefix 1), [1,2,1,-1] (i=3, from the empty prefix).

  4. 4
    Build it

    Write the algorithm in three or four lines, then code it. Reveal after you have run one small input by hand.

    Reveal step 4
    Algorithm

    Running prefix; for each element, add count[prefix - k] to the answer, then increment count[prefix]. Seed count[0] = 1.

    Java implementation
    Java
    // LC 560. Count subarrays with sum exactly k. Works with negative numbers.
// sum(j+1..i) = prefix(i) - prefix(j) = k  <=>  prefix(j) = prefix(i) - k
static int subarraySum(int[] nums, int k) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();   // prefix sum -> how many times
    seen.put(0, 1);                                 // empty prefix
    int prefix = 0, count = 0;
    for (int x : nums) {
        prefix += x;
        count += seen.getOrDefault(prefix - k, 0);  // look up BEFORE inserting
        seen.merge(prefix, 1, Integer::sum);
    }
    return count;
}
    Dry run

    The table above is the dry run. Check [1, -1, 0] with k = 0: prefixes 1, 0, 0 give hits 0, 1 (empty prefix), 2 (empty prefix and index 1): total 3, which matches [1,-1], [1,-1,0], [0].

  5. 5
    Check it

    State time and space with a reason, name three inputs that could break the code, and say what this problem teaches beyond itself.

    Reveal step 5
    Complexity

    O(n) time, O(n) space for the map.

    Edge cases

    Forgetting seen.put(0, 1) misses every subarray that starts at index 0. Inserting before looking up miscounts when k = 0 (a prefix would match itself, counting an empty subarray). Large sums: values here fit in int, but with bigger values use long keys.

    Transfer lesson

    "Count pairs (j, i) with a relationship between f(j) and f(i)" is a hash map over f. It reappears in LC 974 (remainders), LC 525 (balance), LC 1442 (prefix XOR), and LC 437 (prefix sums along a tree path).

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the leading zero (empty prefix).
  • Overflow in prefix arrays: use long.
  • Java's % returns negative results for negative numbers: -1 % 5 == -1. Use Math.floorMod or ((x % k) + k) % k.
  • Storing the latest index instead of the first when the question asks for the longest subarray.

2.4Maximum subarray: Kadane's algorithm

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
53Maximum SubarrayMedium

Stuck after 15 minutes? The guided solve in this lesson walks through this exact problem, one question at a time.

Show a hint
Extend the current run or restart at this element
What it solves

The best (maximum or minimum) sum of a contiguous subarray in one pass, and the family of "running best" problems like Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock.

Intuition

You are walking a path collecting coins, some negative. At each step you decide: keep the bag you have been filling, or empty it and start fresh here. You start fresh exactly when the bag's total has become a burden (negative).

Pattern cardKadane (best subarray ending here)
Signal
Maximum (or minimum) sum or product of a contiguous subarray. 'Best time to buy and sell once'.
Required condition
The best answer ending at i can be built from the best answer ending at i - 1 plus nums[i].
Mental model, core operation, limits, and what to use instead
Mental model
Walking with a running score: when the carried total hurts more than it helps, drop it and restart here.
Core operation
endingHere = max(x, endingHere + x); best = max(best, endingHere).
Complexity benefit
O(n^2) or O(n^3) subarray enumeration becomes one O(n) pass with O(1) memory.
Limitations
Needs contiguity. Products need both max and min. Length constraints break the simple form.
Alternative
Prefix sums with a running minimum prefix (same idea), DP with extra states for deletions or circular arrays.
Go deeper

From brute force to Kadane

  1. All subarrays with a fresh sum each: O(n^3).
  2. Running sum per start: O(n^2).
  3. Define best(i) = the best sum of a subarray ending exactly at i. Any such subarray either is just nums[i], or extends the best subarray ending at i - 1. So best(i) = max(nums[i], best(i - 1) + nums[i]). The answer is the maximum of best(i) over all i. O(n), and since best(i) only needs best(i - 1), O(1) space.

This is your first dynamic programming recurrence. Module 14 generalizes the same move: define the answer "ending here", then build it from the previous one.

Java
// LC 53. best ending here = max(start fresh at x, extend previous run with x).
static int maxSubArray(int[] nums) {
    int endingHere = nums[0], best = nums[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < nums.length; i++) {
        endingHere = Math.max(nums[i], endingHere + nums[i]);
        best = Math.max(best, endingHere);
    }
    return best;
}
Go deeper

Variations

Problem Change
Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock (LC 121) Track the minimum price so far; profit = price - min. Same running-best shape.
Maximum Product Subarray (LC 152) Keep both max and min ending here, because a negative flips them.
Circular array (LC 918) Answer = max(normal Kadane, total - minimum subarray), unless all numbers are negative.
One deletion allowed (LC 1186) Two states: best ending here with no deletion, and with one deletion used.
Java
// LC 152. A negative number turns the smallest product into the largest.
static int maxProduct(int[] nums) {
    int maxHere = nums[0], minHere = nums[0], best = nums[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < nums.length; i++) {
        int x = nums[i];
        int candMax = Math.max(x, Math.max(maxHere * x, minHere * x));
        int candMin = Math.min(x, Math.min(maxHere * x, minHere * x));
        maxHere = candMax;
        minHere = candMin;
        best = Math.max(best, maxHere);
    }
    return best;
}

Problem: 53Maximum SubarrayMedium. Answer each question on paper first, then reveal.

  1. 1
    Understand the problem

    Say in one sentence what is asked. Which constraint sets the time budget?

    Reveal step 1
    Problem decoding

    Return the largest sum of any non-empty contiguous subarray.

    Input analysis

    n up to 10^5, values from -10^4 to 10^4. Negatives allowed, so the answer can be negative. The maximum sum fits in int (10^5 * 10^4 = 10^9).

  2. 2
    Brute force, then a pattern

    What is the simplest correct approach and what does it cost? Which pattern could beat it, and why does it apply?

    Reveal step 2
    Pattern discovery

    Contiguous plus "maximum sum" plus negatives. A sliding window does not apply (no monotonic validity). The question "what is the best subarray ending here?" has a one-step recurrence.

    Brute force

    O(n^2) with running sums per start. The repeated work: for each end, we reconsider every start, although only the best start matters.

  3. 3
    The key observation

    What single fact removes the repeated work? Trace a tiny input on paper until you see it.

    Reveal step 3

    Key idea. best sum ending at i depends only on best sum ending at i - 1

    Key observation

    For a fixed end i, the best start is either i itself or the best start for i - 1. So the whole history collapses into one number: the best sum ending at i - 1.

    Visualization

    See the figure above: values on top, best-ending-here below each index.

  4. 4
    Build it

    Write the algorithm in three or four lines, then code it. Reveal after you have run one small input by hand.

    Reveal step 4
    Algorithm

    endingHere = nums[0], best = nums[0]. For each later element: endingHere = max(x, endingHere + x); best = max(best, endingHere).

    Java implementation

    The code above.

    Dry run

    [-3, -1, -2]: endingHere = -3, then max(-1, -4) = -1, then max(-2, -3) = -2. best = -1. Starting best at 0 instead of nums[0] would wrongly return 0.

  5. 5
    Check it

    State time and space with a reason, name three inputs that could break the code, and say what this problem teaches beyond itself.

    Reveal step 5
    Complexity

    O(n) time, O(1) space.

    Edge cases

    All negative (answer is the largest single element); single element; very long runs of zeros.

    Transfer lesson

    "Best answer ending exactly at i" is the most reusable DP state there is: LIS, longest valid parentheses, and many string problems use it. The follow-up "return the subarray itself" needs one extra variable: the start index, reset whenever you start fresh.

Common mistakes

  • Initializing best = 0, which fails for all-negative input.
  • Resetting the running sum to 0 when it goes negative before updating the best, which loses single negative answers.
  • Forgetting the min track in product problems.

2.5Strings and character processing

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
5Longest Palindromic SubstringMedium

Any correct brute force counts. Note where you got stuck: the lesson below is about exactly that.

Show a hint
Expand around 2n - 1 centers
What it solves

Strings add a few Java-specific costs and a few string-specific patterns: palindromes, parsing, and character counting.

Java essentials.

  • String is immutable. s += c inside a loop creates a new string each time: O(n^2) overall. Use StringBuilder (append, insert, reverse, setCharAt, deleteCharAt).
  • s.charAt(i) is O(1). s.toCharArray() copies once and is convenient for in-place work.
  • s.substring(a, b) copies b - a characters (since Java 7u6). Calling it inside a loop adds a factor of the substring length.
  • Character arithmetic: c - 'a' maps lowercase letters to 0..25; (char) ('a' + i) maps back; c - '0' turns a digit character into its value. Character.isLetterOrDigit, Character.toLowerCase handle the rest.
  • Compare strings with .equals, never ==.
Java
// Frequently used string idioms
static String stringIdioms(String s) {
    int[] freq = new int[26];
    for (char c : s.toCharArray()) freq[c - 'a']++;   // assumes lowercase a-z

    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();             // String is immutable: s + c in a loop is O(n^2)
    for (int i = 0; i < 26; i++)
        if (freq[i] > 0) sb.append((char) ('a' + i)).append(freq[i]);

    String[] words = "  the sky  is ".trim().split("\\s+"); // regex: one or more spaces
    return sb.toString() + ":" + String.join(",", words);
}
Go deeper

Palindromes: expand around the center

A palindrome mirrors around its center. There are 2n - 1 possible centers: each character (odd length) and each gap between characters (even length). From each center, expand while the two ends match. This is O(n^2) time and O(1) space, simpler than the O(n^2)-space DP and fast enough for n up to a few thousand.

Java
// LC 5. Expand around each of the 2n - 1 centers (characters and gaps).
static String longestPalindrome(String s) {
    int bestStart = 0, bestLen = 0;
    for (int center = 0; center < s.length(); center++) {
        int odd = expand(s, center, center);        // "aba"
        int even = expand(s, center, center + 1);   // "abba"
        int len = Math.max(odd, even);
        if (len > bestLen) {
            bestLen = len;
            bestStart = center - (len - 1) / 2;
        }
    }
    return s.substring(bestStart, bestStart + bestLen);
}

// Returns the length of the longest palindrome centered between left and right.
private static int expand(String s, int left, int right) {
    while (left >= 0 && right < s.length() && s.charAt(left) == s.charAt(right)) {
        left--;
        right++;
    }
    return right - left - 1;   // both pointers stopped one step past the palindrome
}

The returned length right - left - 1 is correct because both pointers stop one step outside the palindrome. Counting palindromic substrings (LC 647) uses the same loop and adds 1 for every successful expansion step.

Go deeper

Parsing step by step

Problems like String to Integer (LC 8) are about discipline, not algorithms. Process in phases (whitespace, sign, digits, stop), and check overflow before it happens: if (result > (Integer.MAX_VALUE - digit) / 10) then clamp.

Common mistakes

  • Building strings with + in loops.
  • Treating split(" ") as safe when there are repeated spaces: it produces empty strings. Use trim().split("\\s+").
  • Assuming lowercase input when the constraints allow any ASCII characters: use int[128] or a map.

2.6Choosing between arrays, sorting, and hashing

Try it first2 minutes, before you read on

Return true if any value in an array appears at least twice. Give three solutions with their time and extra space.

Reveal the answer

Check every pair: O(n^2) time, O(1) space. Sort, then compare neighbors: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra, and the input is reordered. A HashSet of seen values: O(n) average time, O(n) space. Which one wins depends on n, memory, and whether positions matter: that choice is this lesson.

When a problem can be solved several ways, compare them on the two resources and on what each preserves.

Need Counting array Hash map / set Sort first
Values in a small known range (letters, 0..10^4) Best: fastest, simplest Works Unnecessary
Arbitrary values, membership or counts Not possible Best: O(n) average O(n log n), O(1) extra
Original indices must be returned Works with index storage Best Must sort (value, index) pairs
Neighbors in value order, ranges, closest pairs No No Best
Memory is tight O(range) O(n) O(1) to O(log n)
Deterministic worst-case time Yes Average only Yes

A good interview answer names the trade-off: "A hash set gives O(n) time and O(n) space. If we cannot afford the memory, sorting gives O(n log n) time with O(1) extra space, but we lose the original order."

Module 3: Two pointers and sliding window

Both techniques replace "check every pair" or "check every subarray" with two indices that only move forward (or toward each other). Each index moves at most n times, so O(n^2) becomes O(n).

3.1Two pointers

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
153SumMedium

Stuck after 15 minutes? The guided solve in this lesson walks through this exact problem, one question at a time.

Show a hint
Fix one element, two-pointer the rest, skip duplicates
What it solves

Finding pairs or triplets that meet a target, partitioning an array in place, comparing a sequence with its reverse. The brute force checks all O(n^2) pairs; two pointers checks O(n) pairs and proves the rest cannot matter.

Intuition

Two people search a sorted bookshelf for two books whose page counts add up to exactly 500. One starts at the thinnest book, the other at the thickest. If their sum is too small, only making the left book thicker can help; if too big, only making the right book thinner can help. Each step permanently rules out one book.

Pattern cardTwo pointers
Signal
Sorted array or string; pairs or triplets meeting a target; palindromes; in-place removal or partitioning.
Required condition
Moving one pointer must safely discard candidates. Usually needs sorted order or a symmetric structure.
Mental model, core operation, limits, and what to use instead
Mental model
Two fingers on a ruler: the comparison tells you which finger can move without missing the answer.
Core operation
Compare the elements at the pointers, move the pointer that cannot be part of a better answer.
Complexity benefit
Checks all useful pairs in O(n) instead of O(n^2), with O(1) extra space.
Limitations
Unsorted input needs an O(n log n) sort first (and loses original indices). No safe discard rule, no pattern.
Alternative
Hash map for unsorted pair search; sliding window when the pair bounds a contiguous range with a running condition.
Go deeper

Opposite-direction pointers: why moving is safe

At positions (L, R) on sorted data with sum < target: for every k <= R, nums[L] + nums[k] <= nums[L] + nums[R] < target. So nums[L] cannot pair with anything still in range, and L can move. The symmetric argument handles sum > target. This "eliminate one candidate entirely" argument is the correctness proof; say it in the interview.

The same reasoning drives Container With Most Water (LC 11): the area is limited by the shorter wall, so keeping the shorter wall and moving the taller one inward can only shrink the width without raising the limit. Move the shorter one.

Java
// LC 11. Area is limited by the shorter wall, so moving the taller wall
// inward can only shrink width without raising the limit.
static int maxArea(int[] height) {
    int left = 0, right = height.length - 1, best = 0;
    while (left < right) {
        int h = Math.min(height[left], height[right]);
        best = Math.max(best, h * (right - left));
        if (height[left] < height[right]) left++;
        else right--;
    }
    return best;
}
Go deeper

Three-way partitioning

When elements fall into three classes (less than, equal to, greater than a pivot; or colors 0, 1, 2), keep three regions and one unknown region in the middle. Each step shrinks the unknown region by one.

[0, low)      all 0s
[low, mid)    all 1s
[mid, high]   unknown
(high, n-1]   all 2s
Java
// LC 75. Invariant: [0, low) = 0s, [low, mid) = 1s, (high, n-1] = 2s, [mid, high] unknown.
static void sortColors(int[] nums) {
    int low = 0, mid = 0, high = nums.length - 1;
    while (mid <= high) {
        if (nums[mid] == 0) swap(nums, low++, mid++);
        else if (nums[mid] == 1) mid++;
        else swap(nums, mid, high--);     // do NOT advance mid: the swapped-in value is unknown
    }
}

private static void swap(int[] a, int i, int j) { int t = a[i]; a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = t; }

When nums[mid] == 2 is swapped with nums[high], the value that arrives at mid has not been examined yet, so mid stays. When nums[mid] == 0 is swapped with nums[low], the arriving value is a known 1 (or low == mid), so both advance.

Go deeper

Same-direction pointers

When both pointers move left to right at different speeds, the slow one usually marks the end of a "kept" or "processed" region and the fast one scans. You met this as read/write pointers in Module 2. Two other forms:

  • Merging two sorted sequences: one pointer per sequence, always advance the one with the smaller current value.
  • Fast and slow pointers on linked lists and implicit sequences (cycle detection, middle element): covered in Module 6.
Guided solveLC 15. 3SumFive questions, each with a reveal

Problem: 153SumMedium. Answer each question on paper first, then reveal.

  1. 1
    Understand the problem

    Say in one sentence what is asked. Which constraint sets the time budget?

    Reveal step 1
    Problem decoding

    Return all unique triplets [a, b, c] from the array with a + b + c = 0. Triplets are sets of values; the same values in a different order count once.

    Input analysis

    n up to 3000, values from -10^5 to 10^5, duplicates allowed. O(n^2) = 9 * 10^6 is fine; O(n^3) = 2.7 * 10^10 is not.

  2. 2
    Brute force, then a pattern

    What is the simplest correct approach and what does it cost? Which pattern could beat it, and why does it apply?

    Reveal step 2
    Pattern discovery

    "Pairs/triplets summing to a target" plus "order of output does not matter" means we may sort. Once sorted, for a fixed first element the rest is Two Sum II, which two pointers solve in O(n).

    Brute force

    Three nested loops plus a set of sorted triplets to remove duplicates: O(n^3).

  3. 3
    The key observation

    What single fact removes the repeated work? Trace a tiny input on paper until you see it.

    Reveal step 3

    Key idea. fix one element, two-pointer the rest, skip duplicates at every level

    Key observation

    Fix the smallest element nums[i]. The remaining two must sum to -nums[i] within nums[i+1..], which is sorted: two pointers. Duplicates come from equal values at the same "role", so skip equal values for i, and after a hit skip equal values for left.

    Visualization
    sorted: [-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2]
i=0 (-4): need 4.  L=-1,R=2 -> 1 <4 L++ ... no pair
i=1 (-1): need 1.  L=-1(idx2),R=2 -> sum 0: hit [-1,-1,2]; L->0,R->1: sum 0: hit [-1,0,1]
i=2 (-1): same value as i=1 -> skip
i=3 (0):  need 0.  L=1,R=2 -> 3 > 0, R-- -> L==R stop
  4. 4
    Build it

    Write the algorithm in three or four lines, then code it. Reveal after you have run one small input by hand.

    Reveal step 4
    Algorithm

    Sort. For each i (skip if equal to nums[i-1], stop if nums[i] > 0): two pointers on [i+1, n-1]; on a hit, record, move both pointers, and skip duplicate left values.

    Java implementation
    Java
    // LC 15. Sort, fix nums[i], then find pairs in nums[i+1..] that sum to -nums[i].
static List<List<Integer>> threeSum(int[] nums) {
    Arrays.sort(nums);
    List<List<Integer>> result = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < nums.length - 2; i++) {
        if (i > 0 && nums[i] == nums[i - 1]) continue;   // same first value -> same triplets
        if (nums[i] > 0) break;                          // smallest is positive: no zero sum
        int left = i + 1, right = nums.length - 1;
        while (left < right) {
            int sum = nums[i] + nums[left] + nums[right];
            if (sum < 0) left++;                          // need a bigger sum
            else if (sum > 0) right--;                    // need a smaller sum
            else {
                result.add(List.of(nums[i], nums[left], nums[right]));
                left++;
                right--;
                while (left < right && nums[left] == nums[left - 1]) left++;   // skip duplicate
            }
        }
    }
    return result;
}
    Dry run

    The visualization is the dry run. Check [0, 0, 0, 0]: i = 0, hit [0,0,0], then left skips the remaining zeros; i = 1 is skipped as a duplicate. One triplet.

  5. 5
    Check it

    State time and space with a reason, name three inputs that could break the code, and say what this problem teaches beyond itself.

    Reveal step 5
    Complexity

    Sorting O(n log n) plus O(n) per i: O(n^2) time. Extra space O(1) beyond the output (sorting uses O(log n) stack).

    Edge cases

    Fewer than 3 elements (loop does not run). All zeros. No solution. Many duplicates (the skips keep it O(n^2) and the output unique).

    Transfer lesson

    "k-sum = fix one element + (k-1)-sum" generalizes to 4Sum. The duplicate-skipping rule "skip equal values in the same role" is exactly the rule you will use in backtracking (Subsets II, Combination Sum II).

Common mistakes

  • Two pointers on unsorted data for a sum problem: the elimination argument needs order.
  • Sorting when the problem asks for original indices (LC 1): sort index pairs or use a map.
  • Skipping duplicates with while (nums[left] == nums[left + 1]) before recording, which can skip valid answers and overrun the array.
  • Using left <= right when the two pointers must be different elements.

3.2Fixed-size sliding window

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
438Find All Anagrams in a StringMedium

Any correct brute force counts. Note where you got stuck: the lesson below is about exactly that.

Show a hint
Window frequency array compared against the target
What it solves

Questions about every contiguous block of exactly k elements: maximum sum, average, number of vowels, whether a block is a permutation of a pattern. Recomputing each block costs O(k), for O(n * k) total; sliding costs O(1) per step.

Intuition

A camera frame of fixed width panning across a long photograph. Each step, one column enters on the right and one leaves on the left; everything in between is unchanged.

Pattern cardFixed-size sliding window
Signal
'Every subarray/substring of length k', anagram or permutation of a pattern, averages over k items.
Required condition
Window state can be updated in O(1) when one element enters and one leaves.
Mental model, core operation, limits, and what to use instead
Mental model
A frame of width k sliding over a film strip: one frame enters on the right, one leaves on the left.
Core operation
Add nums[right]; once right >= k, remove nums[right - k]; evaluate when the window is full.
Complexity benefit
O(n * k) recomputation becomes O(n).
Limitations
The state must support removal. Max/min of a window needs a monotonic deque, not a single variable.
Alternative
Monotonic deque for window max/min; prefix sums for window sums with random access.
Go deeper

The template

for right in 0..n-1:
    add nums[right] to the state
    if right >= k: remove nums[right - k] from the state
    if right >= k - 1: the window [right - k + 1, right] is full -> evaluate

The state can be a sum, a count, or a frequency array. Comparing two int[26] arrays is O(26) = O(1), so anagram-style windows stay linear.

Java
// LC 438. Fixed window of length p.length(); compare counts as it slides.
static List<Integer> findAnagrams(String s, String p) {
    List<Integer> result = new ArrayList<>();
    int k = p.length();
    if (s.length() < k) return result;
    int[] need = new int[26], window = new int[26];
    for (char c : p.toCharArray()) need[c - 'a']++;
    for (int right = 0; right < s.length(); right++) {
        window[s.charAt(right) - 'a']++;                 // element enters
        if (right >= k) window[s.charAt(right - k) - 'a']--;   // element leaves
        if (right >= k - 1 && Arrays.equals(window, need)) result.add(right - k + 1);
    }
    return result;
}

A useful reframing. "Take k cards from either end" (LC 1423) looks like a choice problem, but taking k from the ends means leaving a contiguous block of n - k in the middle. Minimize that block's sum with a fixed window. When a choice problem fixes how many items you take from the ends, look for the complementary window.

Common mistakes

  • Evaluating before the first window is full.
  • Removing nums[right - k + 1] instead of nums[right - k] (the element that just left).
  • Window maximum with a single variable: when the maximum leaves, you cannot recover the next one. Use a monotonic deque (Module 7).

3.3Variable-size sliding window

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
3Longest Substring Without Repeating CharactersMedium

Stuck after 15 minutes? The guided solve in this lesson walks through this exact problem, one question at a time.

Show a hint
Grow right, shrink left until the window is valid again
What it solves

The longest or shortest contiguous subarray or substring that satisfies a condition, and the number of subarrays that satisfy an "at most" condition.

Intuition

An accordion: stretch it to the right while the condition holds, squeeze from the left when it breaks. You never move the left hand back, because a window that was invalid stays invalid when you only add to it.

Pattern cardVariable-size sliding window
Signal
Longest or shortest contiguous subarray/substring satisfying a condition; 'at most k' distinct, zeros, or replacements.
Required condition
Monotonic validity: shrinking a valid window keeps it valid (or growing an invalid one keeps it invalid). Typically fails with negative numbers in sum conditions.
Mental model, core operation, limits, and what to use instead
Mental model
An accordion: stretch right while it plays, squeeze from the left when it breaks.
Core operation
Expand right; while the window is invalid, shrink left; record the answer at the right moment.
Complexity benefit
Each index enters and leaves once: O(n) instead of O(n^2) over all windows.
Limitations
Breaks when adding an element can make the window either better or worse (sums with negatives).
Alternative
Prefix sums + hash map (exact sums with negatives); monotonic deque over prefix sums (shortest sum >= k with negatives); exactly(k) = atMost(k) - atMost(k-1).
Go deeper

Three flavors and where the answer is updated

Goal Shrink while Update the answer Example
Longest valid window the window is invalid after the while loop (window is valid again) LC 3, 424, 1004, 904
Shortest valid window the window is valid inside the while loop, before removing nums[left] LC 209, 76
Count subarrays (at most) the window is invalid add right - left + 1 after the loop: every subarray ending at right with start in [left, right] is valid LC 713

"Exactly k" is rarely monotonic, but "at most k" is. Use exactly(k) = atMost(k) - atMost(k - 1) (LC 992, 930, 1248).

Java
// LC 3. Longest window with all-distinct characters.
static int lengthOfLongestSubstring(String s) {
    Map<Character, Integer> count = new HashMap<>();
    int left = 0, best = 0;
    for (int right = 0; right < s.length(); right++) {
        char in = s.charAt(right);
        count.merge(in, 1, Integer::sum);
        while (count.get(in) > 1) {                     // window became invalid
            char out = s.charAt(left++);
            count.merge(out, -1, Integer::sum);
        }
        best = Math.max(best, right - left + 1);        // window is valid here
    }
    return best;
}
Java
// LC 209. Shortest window with sum >= target (all numbers positive).
static int minSubArrayLen(int target, int[] nums) {
    int left = 0, sum = 0, best = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
    for (int right = 0; right < nums.length; right++) {
        sum += nums[right];
        while (sum >= target) {                         // valid: record, then try smaller
            best = Math.min(best, right - left + 1);
            sum -= nums[left++];
        }
    }
    return best == Integer.MAX_VALUE ? 0 : best;
}
Java
// LC 992. Exactly K distinct = atMost(K) - atMost(K - 1).
static int subarraysWithKDistinct(int[] nums, int k) {
    return atMostKDistinct(nums, k) - atMostKDistinct(nums, k - 1);
}

private static int atMostKDistinct(int[] nums, int k) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> count = new HashMap<>();
    int left = 0, total = 0;
    for (int right = 0; right < nums.length; right++) {
        count.merge(nums[right], 1, Integer::sum);
        while (count.size() > k) {
            int out = nums[left++];
            if (count.merge(out, -1, Integer::sum) == 0) count.remove(out);
        }
        total += right - left + 1;   // every subarray ending at right, starting in [left, right]
    }
    return total;
}
Go deeper

When sliding window does not work

The window's correctness rests on one property: if a window is valid, every window inside it is valid (for longest), or if a window is valid, every window containing it is valid (for shortest). Negative numbers in sum conditions break this.

When values can be negative:

  • Exact sum count (LC 560): prefix sums plus a hash map (Module 2).
  • Shortest subarray with sum at least k (LC 862): prefix sums plus a monotonic deque (Module 7).
  • Maximum sum (LC 53): Kadane.
Go deeper

Two pointers vs sliding window vs prefix sums

Clue in the problem Technique
A pair of elements; sorted data; "two values that sum to" Two pointers (opposite ends)
A contiguous range; a condition that stays true when you shrink a valid window (non-negative sums, counts, distinct characters) Sliding window
A contiguous range; exact sums; negative values; many range queries Prefix sums (with a hash map for counting)
A contiguous range; max/min inside each window Monotonic deque
Guided solveLC 3. Longest Substring Without Repeating CharactersFive questions, each with a reveal

Problem: 3Longest Substring Without Repeating CharactersMedium. Answer each question on paper first, then reveal.

  1. 1
    Understand the problem

    Say in one sentence what is asked. Which constraint sets the time budget?

    Reveal step 1
    Problem decoding

    Length of the longest contiguous substring with all distinct characters.

    Input analysis

    Length up to 5 * 10^4, characters are English letters, digits, symbols, and spaces (so not just a to z).

  2. 2
    Brute force, then a pattern

    What is the simplest correct approach and what does it cost? Which pattern could beat it, and why does it apply?

    Reveal step 2
    Pattern discovery

    "Longest contiguous" with a condition ("all distinct"). Check the required condition: if a substring has no repeats, every substring inside it has none. Monotonic, so a variable window works.

    Brute force

    All substrings with a set check: O(n^3), or O(n^2) by extending each start until a repeat. Repeated work: after a repeat, the brute force restarts from start + 1 and re-scans characters it already knows are distinct.

  3. 3
    The key observation

    What single fact removes the repeated work? Trace a tiny input on paper until you see it.

    Reveal step 3

    Key idea. a duplicate inside the window can only be fixed by moving left past its earlier copy

    Key observation

    When s[right] duplicates a character in the window, every window that still contains the earlier copy is invalid. So left must move past that copy, and it never needs to come back.

    Visualization

    See the figure above.

  4. 4
    Build it

    Write the algorithm in three or four lines, then code it. Reveal after you have run one small input by hand.

    Reveal step 4
    Algorithm

    Count characters in the window. Add s[right]; while its count exceeds 1, remove s[left++]; update the best with the window length.

    Java implementation

    The lengthOfLongestSubstring code above. A faster variant stores each character's last index and jumps left = max(left, last[c] + 1) directly.

    Dry run

    "pwwkew": p (len 1), w (2), w duplicates: drop p, drop w, window "w" (1); k (2); e (3: "wke"); w duplicates: drop w, window "kew" (3). Answer 3.

  5. 5
    Check it

    State time and space with a reason, name three inputs that could break the code, and say what this problem teaches beyond itself.

    Reveal step 5
    Complexity

    O(n) time: each index enters once and leaves at most once. O(min(n, alphabet)) space.

    Edge cases

    Empty string (0), all identical characters (1), all distinct (n), spaces and symbols (use a map or int[128], not int[26]).

    Transfer lesson

    "Longest window where every element appears at most once" generalizes to "at most k distinct" (LC 904), "at most k replacements" (LC 424), "at most k zeros" (LC 1004). Only the validity check changes.

Guided solveLC 76. Minimum Window SubstringFive questions, each with a reveal

Problem: 76Minimum Window SubstringHard. Answer each question on paper first, then reveal.

  1. 1
    Understand the problem

    Say in one sentence what is asked. Which constraint sets the time budget?

    Reveal step 1
    Problem decoding

    Shortest substring of s that contains every character of t with multiplicity.

    Input analysis

    Up to 10^5 characters, upper and lower case letters.

  2. 2
    Brute force, then a pattern

    What is the simplest correct approach and what does it cost? Which pattern could beat it, and why does it apply?

    Reveal step 2
    Pattern discovery

    Shortest contiguous window satisfying a coverage condition. If a window covers t, every larger window covers it too: the shortest-window flavor.

    Brute force

    Every substring with a count comparison: O(n^2 * alphabet).

  3. 3
    The key observation

    What single fact removes the repeated work? Trace a tiny input on paper until you see it.

    Reveal step 3

    Key idea. track how many required characters are fully satisfied

    Key observation

    Comparing full count arrays at every step costs O(alphabet). Instead keep formed = number of distinct characters whose requirement is met. The window is valid exactly when formed == required. Update formed only when a count crosses its requirement.

    Visualization
    s = "ADOBECODEBANC", t = "ABC"   (need A:1, B:1, C:1, required = 3)
R=5  'C': ADOBEC valid (formed 3) -> record length 6; drop A -> formed 2
R=10 'A': DOBECODEBA valid -> shrink while valid down to CODEBA (6, not shorter); drop C -> formed 2
R=12 'C': ODEBANC valid -> shrink: EBANC (record 5), BANC (record 4); drop B -> formed 2
answer "BANC"
  4. 4
    Build it

    Write the algorithm in three or four lines, then code it. Reveal after you have run one small input by hand.

    Reveal step 4
    Algorithm

    Expand right; when the count of s[right] reaches its requirement, formed++. While formed == required: record the window if shorter, remove s[left]; if its count drops below the requirement, formed--; left++.

    Java implementation
    Java
    // LC 76. formed = how many distinct required characters currently meet their count.
static String minWindow(String s, String t) {
    int[] need = new int[128], window = new int[128];
    int required = 0;
    for (char c : t.toCharArray()) if (need[c]++ == 0) required++;
    int formed = 0, left = 0, bestLen = Integer.MAX_VALUE, bestStart = 0;
    for (int right = 0; right < s.length(); right++) {
        char c = s.charAt(right);
        if (++window[c] == need[c]) formed++;          // c just became satisfied
        while (formed == required) {                    // valid: record, then shrink
            if (right - left + 1 < bestLen) { bestLen = right - left + 1; bestStart = left; }
            char out = s.charAt(left++);
            if (window[out]-- == need[out]) formed--;   // out drops below its need
        }
    }
    return bestLen == Integer.MAX_VALUE ? "" : s.substring(bestStart, bestStart + bestLen);
}

    The check ++window[c] == need[c] fires only for required characters: for a character with need[c] == 0, the window count becomes at least 1 and never equals 0.

    Dry run

    Shown above. Note that formed only changes at the moments a count crosses its requirement, which keeps each step O(1).

  5. 5
    Check it

    State time and space with a reason, name three inputs that could break the code, and say what this problem teaches beyond itself.

    Reveal step 5
    Complexity

    O(|s| + |t|) time, O(alphabet) space.

    Edge cases

    t longer than s (empty result), t has repeated characters (multiplicity counts), no valid window.

    Transfer lesson

    "Count how many constraints are satisfied" turns an O(alphabet) validity check into O(1). The same trick appears in LC 438 and LC 567 if you want them faster than comparing arrays.

Common mistakes

  • Using if instead of while to shrink: one removal may not restore validity.
  • Updating the answer at the wrong place for the flavor (see the table).
  • Applying a sum window to arrays with negative numbers.
  • Recomputing the window's validity from scratch each step, which hides an O(alphabet) or O(k) factor.

Module 4: Sorting and binary search

Sorting creates order; binary search exploits it. The most valuable idea in this module is that binary search works on any monotonic yes/no question, including questions about the answer itself.

4.1Sorting in practice

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
179Largest NumberMedium

Any correct brute force counts. Note where you got stuck: the lesson below is about exactly that.

Show a hint
Comparator on concatenation a+b vs b+a
What it solves

Sorting turns a problem about arbitrary positions into a problem about neighbors. Duplicates become adjacent, pairs can be found with two pointers, intervals can be swept in order, and greedy choices become "take the next one". It costs O(n log n), which is within budget for n up to about 10^6.

Intuition

Sorting a pile of exam papers by student ID makes finding duplicates trivial: they end up next to each other.

Go deeper

What you need to know about sorting algorithms

Algorithm Time Extra space Stable Where you meet it
Merge sort O(n log n) always O(n) Yes Counting inversions (LC 315, 493), linked list sort (LC 148)
Quicksort O(n log n) average, O(n^2) worst O(log n) stack No Quickselect for the kth element (LC 215)
Heap sort O(n log n) O(1) No Rarely written; the idea behind priority queues
Counting / bucket sort O(n + range) O(range) Yes (counting) Small value ranges, frequencies (LC 451, 347)
TimSort O(n log n), O(n) on nearly sorted O(n) Yes Java's Arrays.sort(Object[]) and List.sort
Dual-pivot quicksort O(n log n) O(log n) No (primitives, so it does not matter) Java's Arrays.sort(int[])

Interviews rarely ask you to implement a sort from scratch, but merge sort comes up because its merge step can count things (inversions, smaller elements to the right) while it sorts. Know it cold:

Java
// LC 912. Merge sort: O(n log n) always, stable, O(n) extra space.
static int[] sortArray(int[] nums) {
    mergeSort(nums, new int[nums.length], 0, nums.length - 1);
    return nums;
}

private static void mergeSort(int[] a, int[] buf, int lo, int hi) {
    if (lo >= hi) return;
    int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
    mergeSort(a, buf, lo, mid);
    mergeSort(a, buf, mid + 1, hi);
    int i = lo, j = mid + 1, k = lo;
    while (i <= mid && j <= hi) buf[k++] = (a[i] <= a[j]) ? a[i++] : a[j++];   // <= keeps it stable
    while (i <= mid) buf[k++] = a[i++];
    while (j <= hi) buf[k++] = a[j++];
    System.arraycopy(buf, lo, a, lo, hi - lo + 1);
}

Stability means equal elements keep their original relative order. It matters when you sort by one key after another: sort by name, then stably by department, and each department stays sorted by name.

Go deeper

Custom sorting and comparators in Java

Java
static void comparatorExamples() {
    int[][] intervals = {{5, 6}, {1, 3}, {1, 2}};
    // Sort by start, then by end. Integer.compare avoids overflow from a[0] - b[0].
    Arrays.sort(intervals, (a, b) -> a[0] != b[0] ? Integer.compare(a[0], b[0])
                                                  : Integer.compare(a[1], b[1]));

    String[] words = {"banana", "kiwi", "apple", "fig"};
    // Length ascending, then alphabetical. Comparator chaining reads clearly.
    Arrays.sort(words, Comparator.comparingInt(String::length)
                                 .thenComparing(Comparator.naturalOrder()));

    // Primitive int[] cannot take a comparator. Box it (Integer[]) or sort indices.
    Integer[] boxed = {3, 1, 2};
    Arrays.sort(boxed, Collections.reverseOrder());

    List<int[]> people = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new int[]{170, 0}, new int[]{160, 1}));
    people.sort((a, b) -> Integer.compare(b[0], a[0]));   // descending by height
}

A comparator returns a negative number when a should come first, positive when b should, zero when they tie. Three rules prevent most bugs:

  1. Never subtract for comparison: a[0] - b[0] overflows for values near Integer.MIN_VALUE or MAX_VALUE. Use Integer.compare, Long.compare, Comparator.comparingInt.
  2. Primitive arrays cannot take a comparator. Arrays.sort(int[], comparator) does not exist. Use Integer[], int[][] (each row is an object), or sort an array of indices.
  3. Be consistent. A comparator that says a < b and b < a (for example, a random tie-break) can throw "Comparison method violates its general contract".

Sorting by a derived key is a common trick: Largest Number (LC 179) sorts strings by comparing a + b with b + a; Car Fleet (LC 853) sorts by position and then compares arrival times.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting that sorting destroys original indices (store {value, index} pairs).
  • Claiming O(n) for "sort then two pointers".
  • Sorting inside a loop.

4.2Binary search fundamentals

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
34Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted ArrayMedium

Any correct brute force counts. Note where you got stuck: the lesson below is about exactly that.

Show a hint
Lower bound and upper bound as two searches
What it solves

Finding a position in sorted data in O(log n): an exact value, the first element at least x, the insertion point, the boundary between two kinds of elements.

Intuition

Looking up a word in a paper dictionary. Open in the middle; the word you see tells you which half to keep. Every look discards half of what remains, so a million pages need about 20 looks.

Pattern cardBinary search on data
Signal
Sorted or rotated-sorted input, 'first/last position', insertion point, peak, or any O(log n) requirement.
Required condition
A predicate over indices that is false...false true...true (monotonic). Sorting gives one for free.
Mental model, core operation, limits, and what to use instead
Mental model
Guessing a number between 1 and 100 with 'higher/lower' hints: every guess discards half.
Core operation
Test mid; keep the half that still contains the answer; stop when the range has one candidate.
Complexity benefit
O(n) scan becomes O(log n).
Limitations
Needs a monotonic predicate. Duplicates can break rotated-array reasoning (worst case O(n)).
Alternative
Linear scan when unsorted and queried once; hash set for membership only; TreeMap floor/ceiling for dynamic data.
Go deeper

One template for every boundary search

The most reliable way to write binary search is to stop thinking about "find the target" and start thinking about a predicate that is false for a prefix of the range and true for the rest:

index:      0      1      2      3      4      5      6
nums:       1      3      3      3      5      8      9
nums >= 3:  false  true   true   true   true   true   true
                   ^ first true = lower bound

Find the first true. Everything else is a choice of predicate.

Java
// First index i with nums[i] >= target (nums.length if none).
// Half-open search space [lo, hi). Invariant: answer is always inside [lo, hi].
static int lowerBound(int[] nums, int target) {
    int lo = 0, hi = nums.length;
    while (lo < hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;      // avoids (lo + hi) overflow
        if (nums[mid] >= target) hi = mid; // mid could be the answer: keep it
        else lo = mid + 1;                 // mid is too small: discard it
    }
    return lo;                             // lo == hi
}

// First index i with nums[i] > target. Same loop, strict comparison.
static int upperBound(int[] nums, int target) {
    int lo = 0, hi = nums.length;
    while (lo < hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (nums[mid] > target) hi = mid;
        else lo = mid + 1;
    }
    return lo;
}

// LC 34. First and last position = [lowerBound, upperBound - 1].
static int[] searchRange(int[] nums, int target) {
    int first = lowerBound(nums, target);
    if (first == nums.length || nums[first] != target) return new int[]{-1, -1};
    return new int[]{first, upperBound(nums, target) - 1};
}
Go deeper

Deriving the boundaries and update rules

Write these four decisions down before coding:

Decision Choice used here Why
Search space [lo, hi) with lo = 0, hi = n hi = n represents "no element qualifies" naturally
Loop condition while (lo < hi) Stop when one candidate remains
Midpoint lo + (hi - lo) / 2 (rounds down) Never equals hi, so nums[mid] is always valid; no overflow
Updates true: hi = mid; false: lo = mid + 1 Each branch strictly shrinks the range, so the loop terminates

Why this never loops forever: when hi - lo >= 1, mid is in [lo, hi - 1]. hi = mid makes hi smaller; lo = mid + 1 makes lo larger. The classic infinite loop comes from writing lo = mid with a rounded-down mid: when hi = lo + 1, mid = lo and nothing changes. If you ever need lo = mid, round the midpoint up: mid = lo + (hi - lo + 1) / 2.

Go deeper

The variants, all from one template

Question Predicate Result
First index with value >= x (lower bound, insertion position) nums[i] >= x first true
First index with value > x (upper bound) nums[i] > x first true
First occurrence of x lower bound, then check nums[i] == x first true if it matches
Last occurrence of x upper bound - 1, then check
Largest value <= x (floor) upper bound - 1
Count of x upper bound - lower bound

The classic "closed interval" version (while (lo <= hi), hi = mid - 1, return mid on equality) is fine for finding an exact value. For boundaries, the predicate version above is far less error prone. Pick one style and use it everywhere.

Common mistakes

  • (lo + hi) / 2 overflowing when indices or values are near 2^31 (use lo + (hi - lo) / 2, or (lo + hi) >>> 1).
  • Mixing interval conventions: hi = n with while (lo <= hi) reads nums[n].
  • Returning lo without checking that it is in range and actually matches when the target may be absent.
  • Writing lo = mid with a rounded-down midpoint (infinite loop).

4.3Rotated and modified sorted arrays

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
33Search in Rotated Sorted ArrayMedium

Stuck after 15 minutes? The guided solve in this lesson walks through this exact problem, one question at a time.

Show a hint
One half is always sorted; decide which side holds the target
What it solves

Searching arrays that are not fully sorted but keep enough order: rotated sorted arrays, arrays with a single peak, sorted arrays with one odd element out.

Key insight

Binary search does not need the array to be sorted. It needs a test at mid that tells you which half cannot contain the answer.

Java
// LC 33. At least one half of [lo, hi] is sorted. Check whether target lies in it.
static int searchRotated(int[] nums, int target) {
    int lo = 0, hi = nums.length - 1;               // closed interval [lo, hi]
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (nums[mid] == target) return mid;
        if (nums[lo] <= nums[mid]) {                 // left half [lo, mid] is sorted
            if (nums[lo] <= target && target < nums[mid]) hi = mid - 1;
            else lo = mid + 1;
        } else {                                     // right half [mid, hi] is sorted
            if (nums[mid] < target && target <= nums[hi]) lo = mid + 1;
            else hi = mid - 1;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}
Java
// LC 153. Compare with the right end: if nums[mid] > nums[hi], the drop is right of mid.
static int findMin(int[] nums) {
    int lo = 0, hi = nums.length - 1;
    while (lo < hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (nums[mid] > nums[hi]) lo = mid + 1;
        else hi = mid;                       // mid may be the minimum
    }
    return nums[lo];
}

Why compare with nums[hi] for the minimum? If nums[mid] > nums[hi], the drop (the minimum) is strictly to the right of mid. Otherwise the segment [mid, hi] is sorted, so the minimum is at mid or to its left. Comparing with nums[lo] instead fails on an unrotated array.

Peaks without sorting. In LC 162, if nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1] the values rise to the right, and since the array "falls off" to negative infinity past the end, a peak must exist on the right. Otherwise one exists at mid or to its left.

Java
// LC 162. If nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1], a peak exists to the right (the slope must come down).
static int findPeakElement(int[] nums) {
    int lo = 0, hi = nums.length - 1;
    while (lo < hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;          // mid < hi, so mid + 1 is valid
        if (nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1]) lo = mid + 1;
        else hi = mid;
    }
    return lo;
}

Duplicates (LC 81, 154) break the "which half is sorted" test when nums[lo] == nums[mid] == nums[hi]. The fix is to shrink by one (lo++ or hi--), which makes the worst case O(n). Mention this if asked about duplicates.

Guided solveLC 33. Search in Rotated Sorted ArrayFive questions, each with a reveal

Problem: 33Search in Rotated Sorted ArrayMedium. Answer each question on paper first, then reveal.

  1. 1
    Understand the problem

    Say in one sentence what is asked. Which constraint sets the time budget?

    Reveal step 1
    Problem decoding

    A sorted array of distinct values was rotated at an unknown pivot. Return the index of target or -1, in O(log n).

    Input analysis

    Distinct values (important: it makes the sorted-half test unambiguous), n up to 5000, O(log n) required.

  2. 2
    Brute force, then a pattern

    What is the simplest correct approach and what does it cost? Which pattern could beat it, and why does it apply?

    Reveal step 2
    Pattern discovery

    "O(log n)" plus "sorted, but modified" means binary search with a modified decision rule.

    Brute force

    Linear scan: O(n). Or find the pivot first, then binary search the correct side: also O(log n), but two searches and more edge cases.

  3. 3
    The key observation

    What single fact removes the repeated work? Trace a tiny input on paper until you see it.

    Reveal step 3

    Key idea. one half is always sorted; test the target against that half only

    Key observation

    For any mid, either [lo, mid] or [mid, hi] is sorted (the rotation point can only be in one of them). In a sorted range, "is the target inside?" is a simple range check.

    Visualization

    See the figure above.

  4. 4
    Build it

    Write the algorithm in three or four lines, then code it. Reveal after you have run one small input by hand.

    Reveal step 4
    Algorithm

    Closed interval [lo, hi]. If nums[mid] == target, return. If nums[lo] <= nums[mid], the left half is sorted: go left iff nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid]. Otherwise the right half is sorted: go right iff nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi].

    Java implementation

    searchRotated above.

    Dry run

    [3, 1], target 1: lo = 0, hi = 1, mid = 0. nums[0] = 3 != 1. nums[lo] <= nums[mid] (3 <= 3): left half [3] is "sorted"; is 3 <= 1 < 3? No, so lo = 1. Next mid = 1, found. The <= in nums[lo] <= nums[mid] is what handles the case lo == mid.

  5. 5
    Check it

    State time and space with a reason, name three inputs that could break the code, and say what this problem teaches beyond itself.

    Reveal step 5
    Complexity

    O(log n) time, O(1) space.

    Edge cases

    Not rotated at all; rotated by n - 1; single element; target smaller than everything; two elements (the <= case above).

    Transfer lesson

    Ask "what does mid tell me about which side cannot contain the answer?" rather than "is the array sorted?". The same question solves peaks (LC 162), the single non-duplicate (LC 540: pairs before the single element start at even indices), and the minimum of a rotated array (LC 153).

4.4Binary search on the answer

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
875Koko Eating BananasMedium

Stuck after 15 minutes? The guided solve in this lesson walks through this exact problem, one question at a time.

Show a hint
Feasibility(speed) is monotonic; find the minimum feasible
What it solves

Optimization problems of the form "find the minimum X such that the task is possible" or "the maximum X such that ...", where X ranges over a large space (speeds, capacities, days, distances) and checking a single X is easy.

Intuition

Adjusting a shower's temperature. You cannot compute the perfect setting, but for any setting you can tell "too cold" or "warm enough", and anything warmer than warm enough is also warm enough. Halve the range each time.

Pattern cardBinary search on the answer
Signal
'Minimum largest', 'maximum smallest', 'least capacity/speed/time so that...'. You can check a candidate answer easily but cannot compute it directly.
Required condition
feasible(x) is monotonic: if x works, every larger (or smaller) x also works.
Mental model, core operation, limits, and what to use instead
Mental model
Adjusting a thermostat: too cold, go up; warm enough, try a little lower.
Core operation
Pick bounds that surely contain the answer, binary search for the first feasible value, check feasibility greedily in O(n).
Complexity benefit
Searching a huge answer range costs only log(range) feasibility checks: O(n log range).
Limitations
Feasibility must be monotonic and cheap. Off-by-one bounds and overflow in the check are the usual bugs.
Alternative
Direct formula, greedy, or DP when the answer can be constructed; heap-based simulation for some scheduling problems.
Go deeper

The recipe

  1. Name the answer variable and what "feasible" means for a candidate value.
  2. Prove monotonicity in one sentence. "If Koko can finish at speed k, she can finish at any speed above k."
  3. Pick bounds that surely contain the answer. Low: the smallest value that could possibly work (often the max single item). High: a value that always works (often the total).
  4. Write the feasibility check, usually a greedy O(n) pass.
  5. Binary search for the first feasible value (or the last feasible, for "maximize the minimum": search for the first infeasible and subtract one).
Phrase Shape Search for
"Minimum speed / capacity / time such that ..." false ... false true ... true First true
"Minimize the maximum ..." (split array, distribute) Same First true of "max part <= cap"
"Maximize the minimum ..." (magnetic force, aggressive cows) true ... true false ... false Last true
Guided solveLC 875. Koko Eating BananasFive questions, each with a reveal

Problem: 875Koko Eating BananasMedium. Answer each question on paper first, then reveal.

  1. 1
    Understand the problem

    Say in one sentence what is asked. Which constraint sets the time budget?

    Reveal step 1
    Problem decoding

    Piles of bananas; per hour Koko eats up to k bananas from one pile. Find the minimum integer k that lets her finish all piles within h hours.

    Input analysis

    Up to 10^4 piles, each up to 10^9 bananas, h up to 10^9. The answer lies in [1, max(piles)], a range of up to 10^9 values.

  2. 2
    Brute force, then a pattern

    What is the simplest correct approach and what does it cost? Which pattern could beat it, and why does it apply?

    Reveal step 2
    Pattern discovery

    "Minimum k such that ..." with a huge range for k, and a quick way to compute hours for a given k: binary search on the answer.

    Brute force

    Try k = 1, 2, 3, ... until feasible: up to 10^9 checks of O(n) each. Far too slow.

  3. 3
    The key observation

    What single fact removes the repeated work? Trace a tiny input on paper until you see it.

    Reveal step 3

    Key idea. the answer is hard to compute but easy to check

    Key observation

    hours(k) = sum of ceil(pile / k) never increases as k grows, so hours(k) <= h is false then true. Binary search finds the boundary with about 30 checks.

    Visualization

    See the figure: speeds 1 to 11 for piles [3, 6, 7, 11], h = 8.

  4. 4
    Build it

    Write the algorithm in three or four lines, then code it. Reveal after you have run one small input by hand.

    Reveal step 4
    Algorithm

    lo = 1, hi = max(piles). While lo < hi: if canFinish(mid), hi = mid; else lo = mid + 1. Return lo.

    Java implementation
    Java
    // LC 875. canFinish(speed) is false...false true...true as speed grows.
// Find the first true.
static int minEatingSpeed(int[] piles, int h) {
    int lo = 1, hi = 0;
    for (int p : piles) hi = Math.max(hi, p);   // speed = max pile always works
    while (lo < hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (canFinish(piles, h, mid)) hi = mid; // feasible: try slower
        else lo = mid + 1;                       // infeasible: must go faster
    }
    return lo;
}

private static boolean canFinish(int[] piles, int h, int speed) {
    long hours = 0;                              // long: sum can exceed int
    for (int p : piles) hours += (p + (long) speed - 1) / speed;   // ceil(p / speed); long avoids overflow
    return hours <= h;
}
    Dry run

    [3, 6, 7, 11], h = 8: lo = 1, hi = 11. mid 6: 6 hours, feasible, hi = 6. mid 3: 10 hours, lo = 4. mid 5: 8 hours, hi = 5. mid 4: 8 hours, hi = 4. Return 4.

  5. 5
    Check it

    State time and space with a reason, name three inputs that could break the code, and say what this problem teaches beyond itself.

    Reveal step 5
    Complexity

    O(n log(max pile)) time, O(1) space.

    Edge cases

    Overflow, twice. The hour total can exceed int (10^4 piles x 10^9 hours), so it is a long. And p + speed - 1 can exceed int when both are near 10^9, so the ceiling is computed in long too. Also: h == piles.length forces k = max(piles).

    Transfer lesson

    Ship within D days (LC 1011), split array largest sum (LC 410), and m bouquets (LC 1482) all use this exact skeleton. Only the feasibility function and the bounds change.

Second example, minimize the maximum. In Split Array Largest Sum (LC 410), the candidate is a cap on part sums; the greedy check counts how many parts you need if you never exceed the cap. More cap means fewer parts, so feasibility is monotonic.

Java
// LC 410. Minimize the largest part sum when splitting into k parts.
static int splitArray(int[] nums, int k) {
    long lo = 0, hi = 0;
    for (int x : nums) { lo = Math.max(lo, x); hi += x; }
    while (lo < hi) {
        long mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (partsNeeded(nums, mid) <= k) hi = mid;   // cap 'mid' is achievable
        else lo = mid + 1;
    }
    return (int) lo;
}

// Greedy: extend the current part until adding the next number would exceed cap.
private static int partsNeeded(int[] nums, long cap) {
    int parts = 1;
    long current = 0;
    for (int x : nums) {
        if (current + x > cap) { parts++; current = 0; }
        current += x;
    }
    return parts;
}
Go deeper

When binary search applies, and when it does not

Applies Does not apply
Sorted (or rotated sorted) data, searching a position Unsorted data searched once: a linear scan is O(n) and sorting costs more
A monotonic predicate over indices or answers Feasibility that is not monotonic (more capacity sometimes worse)
A cheap check for a candidate answer When the check is as hard as the original problem
Integer answers, or real answers to a fixed precision When the answer is a structure, not a number on a line

Common mistakes

  • Bounds that exclude the answer: lo = 0 when 0 is not valid and the check divides by it; hi too small.
  • A feasibility check with int overflow.
  • Searching for the first true when the problem needs the last true ("maximize the minimum").
  • Forgetting to prove monotonicity. If you cannot say why more of X never hurts, the method may be wrong.
