9.1Tree fundamentals

Try it first2 minutes, before you read on

A binary tree has n nodes. What are its smallest and largest possible heights, and why does that matter for recursive code?

Reveal the answer

Smallest: about log2(n) levels, when every level is full. Largest: n levels, when every node has one child (a chain). Recursion depth equals the height, so balanced trees cost O(log n) stack and a chain costs O(n), which can overflow Java's stack near 10^5.

What it solves

Trees represent hierarchy (file systems, org charts, the DOM), sorted data with fast updates (BSTs), and the call structure of recursion itself.

The node class LeetCode uses
class TreeNode {
    int val;
    TreeNode left, right;
    TreeNode(int val) { this.val = val; }
    TreeNode(int val, TreeNode left, TreeNode right) {
        this.val = val; this.left = left; this.right = right;
    }
}
Term Meaning
Depth of a node Edges from the root down to it (root has depth 0)
Height of a node Edges on the longest path from it down to a leaf (some problems count nodes; read carefully)
Balanced For every node, left and right heights differ by at most 1 (one common definition)
Complete Every level full except possibly the last, which fills left to right (heaps)
Full Every node has 0 or 2 children
BST Left subtree values < node < right subtree values, for every node

Complexity vocabulary. Visiting every node is O(n). Recursion depth is O(h), where h is the height: O(log n) for balanced trees, O(n) for skewed ones. Say "O(h) space, which is O(n) in the worst case".

9.2Traversals: DFS orders and BFS levels

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
102Binary Tree Level Order TraversalMedium

Any correct brute force counts. Note where you got stuck: the lesson below is about exactly that.

Show a hint
Snapshot queue size to separate levels
What it solves

Every tree algorithm visits nodes in some order. Choosing the order is choosing when a node's information is available: before its children (preorder), between them (inorder), after them (postorder), or level by level (BFS).

Java
// Recursive DFS: the only difference between orders is WHERE you visit the node.
static void preorder(TreeNode node, List<Integer> out) {
    if (node == null) return;
    out.add(node.val);            // visit BEFORE children
    preorder(node.left, out);
    preorder(node.right, out);
}

static void inorder(TreeNode node, List<Integer> out) {
    if (node == null) return;
    inorder(node.left, out);
    out.add(node.val);            // visit BETWEEN children (sorted order for a BST)
    inorder(node.right, out);
}

static void postorder(TreeNode node, List<Integer> out) {
    if (node == null) return;
    postorder(node.left, out);
    postorder(node.right, out);
    out.add(node.val);            // visit AFTER children (children's answers are ready)
}
Order Node processed Use it when
Preorder Before children Copying or serializing a tree, passing info down (path from root)
Inorder Between children BSTs: produces sorted order
Postorder After children The node needs its children's answers (height, diameter, deleting a tree)
Level order (BFS) By depth Anything per level, minimum depth, nearest node
Go deeper

Iterative DFS

Recursion uses the call stack; an explicit stack does the same job without the depth limit. Iterative inorder pushes the whole left spine, pops the leftmost node, visits it, then moves to its right subtree.

Java
// LC 94. Simulate the call stack: go left as far as possible, visit, then go right.
static List<Integer> inorderIterative(TreeNode root) {
    List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
    Deque<TreeNode> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    TreeNode curr = root;
    while (curr != null || !stack.isEmpty()) {
        while (curr != null) {          // push the whole left spine
            stack.push(curr);
            curr = curr.left;
        }
        curr = stack.pop();             // leftmost unvisited node
        out.add(curr.val);
        curr = curr.right;              // then its right subtree
    }
    return out;
}

Iterative preorder is simpler: pop a node, visit it, push right then left (so left is processed first). Postorder can be produced as reversed "node, right, left" preorder.

Go deeper

BFS with level separation

Java
// LC 102. Queue size at the start of a round = number of nodes on this level.
static List<List<Integer>> levelOrder(TreeNode root) {
    List<List<Integer>> levels = new ArrayList<>();
    if (root == null) return levels;
    Deque<TreeNode> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
    queue.offer(root);
    while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
        int size = queue.size();                 // snapshot BEFORE adding children
        List<Integer> level = new ArrayList<>(size);
        for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
            TreeNode node = queue.poll();
            level.add(node.val);
            if (node.left != null) queue.offer(node.left);
            if (node.right != null) queue.offer(node.right);
        }
        levels.add(level);
    }
    return levels;
}

Snapshotting queue.size() before the inner loop is what separates levels: exactly that many nodes belong to the current level, and everything added during the loop belongs to the next.

DFS can also answer level questions. Pass the depth down and use it as an index. The right side view (LC 199) visits the right child first, so the first node seen at each depth is the visible one:

Java
// LC 199. DFS right child first; the first node seen at each depth is the visible one.
static List<Integer> rightSideView(TreeNode root) {
    List<Integer> view = new ArrayList<>();
    see(root, 0, view);
    return view;
}

private static void see(TreeNode node, int depth, List<Integer> view) {
    if (node == null) return;
    if (depth == view.size()) view.add(node.val);   // first visit to this depth
    see(node.right, depth + 1, view);
    see(node.left, depth + 1, view);
}

Common mistakes

  • Reading queue.size() inside the loop condition, which changes as children are added.
  • Null checks: either check before recursing or start each call with if (node == null) return ...; mixing both leads to missed cases.
  • Width problems with heap indices (LC 662): indices double per level and overflow; subtract the level's first index.

9.3Tree recursion with return values

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
2265Count Nodes Equal to Average of SubtreeMedium

Any correct brute force counts. Note where you got stuck: the lesson below is about exactly that.

Show a hint
Return (sum, count) pairs from each subtree
What it solves

Height, diameter, balance, maximum path sum, lowest common ancestor, tree DP: anything where a node's answer is built from its children's answers.

Intuition

A company report going up the org chart. Each manager receives a summary from each direct report, combines them, and passes a single summary up. The CEO's answer emerges without anyone seeing the whole company.

Pattern cardTree recursion (bottom-up return values)
Signal
Height, diameter, balance, path sums through a node, LCA, subtree properties, 'information from children'.
Required condition
A node's answer can be computed from its children's answers plus its own value.
Mental model, core operation, limits, and what to use instead
Mental model
A company report: each manager summarizes their team's numbers for their own boss.
Core operation
Recurse left and right, combine their return values, optionally update a global best, return what the parent needs.
Complexity benefit
Every node visited once: O(n). Avoids recomputing subtree facts (naive balance check is O(n^2)).
Limitations
The return value must be what the PARENT needs, which is often different from the final answer.
Alternative
Top-down parameters for ancestor information; BFS for level-based questions; parent pointers + BFS for distance-k.
Go deeper

The framework: return what the parent needs

Before writing code, answer two questions:

  1. What does this function return to its parent? Often not the final answer. For diameter, the parent needs the child's height, not its diameter.
  2. What global answer is updated along the way? The best path that bends at a node uses both children, so it cannot be passed up; it is recorded in a variable outside the recursion.

The smallest example of the framework is the diameter of a tree (the longest path between any two nodes). Each node returns its height; the best path that bends at a node is left + right, recorded on the side:

Java
// LC 543. Each call RETURNS height; the answer is collected on the side.
static int diameterOfBinaryTree(TreeNode root) {
    int[] best = {0};                 // array as a mutable holder for the recursion
    height(root, best);
    return best[0];
}

// Returns the number of NODES on the longest downward path (null -> 0, leaf -> 1).
// So left + right = number of EDGES on the longest path that bends at this node.
private static int height(TreeNode node, int[] best) {
    if (node == null) return 0;
    int left = height(node.left, best);
    int right = height(node.right, best);
    best[0] = Math.max(best[0], left + right);   // best path that bends here
    return 1 + Math.max(left, right);            // what the parent needs
}
Guided solveLC 124. Binary Tree Maximum Path SumFive questions, each with a reveal

Problem: 124Binary Tree Maximum Path SumHard. Answer each question on paper first, then reveal.

  1. 1
    Understand the problem

    Say in one sentence what is asked. Which constraint sets the time budget?

    Reveal step 1
    Problem decoding

    A path is any sequence of connected nodes, each used at most once, and it need not pass through the root. Return the largest sum of node values on any non-empty path.

    Input analysis

    Up to 3 * 10^4 nodes, values from -1000 to 1000. Negative values mean a path should sometimes stop early, and the answer itself can be negative.

  2. 2
    Brute force, then a pattern

    What is the simplest correct approach and what does it cost? Which pattern could beat it, and why does it apply?

    Reveal step 2
    Pattern discovery

    Every path has one highest node where it bends. At that node the path is (best downward chain on the left) + node + (best downward chain on the right). That needs information from children: postorder, the same shape as the diameter above.

    Brute force

    For every node, compute the best downward chain on each side from scratch: O(n) per node, O(n^2) on skewed trees.

  3. 3
    The key observation

    What single fact removes the repeated work? Trace a tiny input on paper until you see it.

    Reveal step 3

    Key idea. return a one-sided gain, record the two-sided path

    Key observation

    A parent can extend only one side of a child's path (a path cannot fork), so each call returns the best one-sided gain node.val + max(leftGain, rightGain). A negative gain helps nobody, so clamp it to 0, which means "do not extend into that subtree".

    Visualization
    tree: [-10, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7]

node   left gain  right gain  path through node        best   returns (one side)
9      0          0           9                        9      9
15     0          0           15                       15     15
7      0          0           7                        15     7
20     15         7           15 + 20 + 7 = 42         42     20 + 15 = 35
-10    9          35          9 - 10 + 35 = 34         42     -10 + 35 = 25
answer 42 (path 15 -> 20 -> 7)
  4. 4
    Build it

    Write the algorithm in three or four lines, then code it. Reveal after you have run one small input by hand.

    Reveal step 4
    Algorithm

    gain(node): null returns 0. left = max(0, gain(node.left)), right = max(0, gain(node.right)). Update best = max(best, node.val + left + right). Return node.val + max(left, right).

    Java implementation
    Java
    // LC 124. Each call returns the best DOWNWARD path starting at node (one side only).
// The best path THROUGH node may use both sides; that goes into the global answer.
static int maxPathSum(TreeNode root) {
    int[] best = {Integer.MIN_VALUE};
    gain(root, best);
    return best[0];
}

private static int gain(TreeNode node, int[] best) {
    if (node == null) return 0;
    int left = Math.max(0, gain(node.left, best));    // a negative branch is better skipped
    int right = Math.max(0, gain(node.right, best));
    best[0] = Math.max(best[0], node.val + left + right);
    return node.val + Math.max(left, right);           // a parent can extend only one side
}
    Dry run

    The table above. For the single node [-3]: both gains are 0, best = -3, which is the answer. Initializing best to 0 instead of Integer.MIN_VALUE would wrongly return 0 here.

  5. 5
    Check it

    State time and space with a reason, name three inputs that could break the code, and say what this problem teaches beyond itself.

    Reveal step 5
    Complexity

    O(n) time, O(h) space for the recursion.

    Edge cases

    All values negative (the answer is the largest single value), a single node, a chain (recursion depth n), the best path entirely inside one subtree (the global variable catches it).

    Transfer lesson

    "Return the one-sided value, record the two-sided value" also solves Longest Univalue Path (LC 687), Longest ZigZag Path (LC 1372, return one value per direction), and Diameter of N-ary Tree problems. When the parent needs more than one fact, return a pair or a small array, as in tree DP below.

Go deeper

Using a sentinel return value

To check balance in O(n), the recursion must return a height and a "failed" signal. Returning -1 for "unbalanced" lets one integer carry both:

Java
// LC 110. Return the height, or -1 as a "not balanced" signal so each node is visited once.
static boolean isBalanced(TreeNode root) {
    return checkHeight(root) != -1;
}

private static int checkHeight(TreeNode node) {
    if (node == null) return 0;
    int left = checkHeight(node.left);
    if (left == -1) return -1;                       // stop early: already unbalanced
    int right = checkHeight(node.right);
    if (right == -1 || Math.abs(left - right) > 1) return -1;
    return 1 + Math.max(left, right);
}
Go deeper

Lowest common ancestor

Java
// LC 236. Return p or q if found in this subtree, else null.
// The first node where both sides return non-null is the LCA.
static TreeNode lowestCommonAncestor(TreeNode root, TreeNode p, TreeNode q) {
    if (root == null || root == p || root == q) return root;
    TreeNode left = lowestCommonAncestor(root.left, p, q);
    TreeNode right = lowestCommonAncestor(root.right, p, q);
    if (left != null && right != null) return root;   // p and q split here
    return (left != null) ? left : right;             // pass up whatever was found
}

This works because the problem guarantees both nodes exist. If one might be missing, count how many were found instead of returning early.

Go deeper

Tree DP: return several states

When the parent's choice depends on the child's choice (not just the child's best value), return one value per possible state. In House Robber III (LC 337), robbing a node forbids robbing its children, so each node returns the best total if robbed and if skipped.

Java
// LC 337. Tree DP: each node returns {best if robbed, best if skipped}.
static int rob(TreeNode root) {
    int[] r = robPair(root);
    return Math.max(r[0], r[1]);
}

private static int[] robPair(TreeNode node) {
    if (node == null) return new int[]{0, 0};
    int[] l = robPair(node.left), r = robPair(node.right);
    int robThis = node.val + l[1] + r[1];                          // children must be skipped
    int skipThis = Math.max(l[0], l[1]) + Math.max(r[0], r[1]);    // children are free to choose
    return new int[]{robThis, skipThis};
}
Ordinary tree recursion Tree DP
One return value per node A small tuple of states per node
"Tell me your best result" "Tell me your best result for each way you might decide"
Height, diameter, LCA House Robber III, Binary Tree Cameras (3 states), Distribute Coins (excess)

Common mistakes

  • Returning the final answer instead of what the parent needs (diameter instead of height).
  • Recomputing subtree facts in a loop over nodes (O(n^2) balance checks).
  • Forgetting that negative values exist in path sums: clamp gains at 0, but initialize the global answer to Integer.MIN_VALUE, not 0.

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on

Show a hint
Add on the way down, remove on the way up
What it solves

Problems where a node's answer depends on its ancestors: the path sum so far, the maximum on the path, the current number formed by digits, which values appear along the path.

The pattern

Pass the ancestor information down as a parameter. Return results up (or collect them in a list). When the parameter is a mutable structure (a path list, a count map), undo your change before returning, exactly as in backtracking.

Problem Passed down Collected
Path Sum (LC 112) remaining target true if any leaf hits 0
Sum Root to Leaf Numbers (LC 129) value * 10 + digit sum at leaves

Guided solveLC 437. Path Sum IIIFive questions, each with a reveal

Problem: 437Path Sum IIIMedium. Answer each question on paper first, then reveal.

  1. 1
    Understand the problem

    Say in one sentence what is asked. Which constraint sets the time budget?

    Reveal step 1
    Problem decoding

    Count downward paths (from any node to any descendant) whose values sum to target.

    Input analysis

    Up to 1000 nodes, values up to 10^9 in magnitude (sums need long).

  2. 2
    Brute force, then a pattern

    What is the simplest correct approach and what does it cost? Which pattern could beat it, and why does it apply?

    Reveal step 2
    Pattern discovery

    A downward path is a contiguous segment of a root-to-node path. "Count segments with a given sum" on a sequence is LC 560: prefix sums plus a frequency map. Here the sequence is the current root-to-node path.

    Brute force

    From every node, DFS downward and count sums: O(n * h), up to O(n^2).

  3. 3
    The key observation

    What single fact removes the repeated work? Trace a tiny input on paper until you see it.

    Reveal step 3

    Key idea. prefix sums along the current root-to-node path

    Key observation

    Keep the counts of prefix sums for the nodes on the current path only. Entering a node adds its prefix; leaving removes it (backtracking), so sibling subtrees never see each other's prefixes.

    Visualization
                10            prefix at 10 = 10
           /  \
          5   -3          prefix at 5 = 15
         / \    \
        3   2    11       prefix at 3 = 18: need 18 - 8 = 10 -> one path (5, 3)
       / \   \            prefix at 2 = 17: need 9  -> none
      3  -2   1           prefix at 1 = 18: need 10 -> one path (5, 2, 1)
                          prefix at 11 = 18 (via -3): need 10 -> one path (-3, 11)
target 8: total 3
  4. 4
    Build it

    Write the algorithm in three or four lines, then code it. Reveal after you have run one small input by hand.

    Reveal step 4
    Algorithm

    DFS with the running sum. At each node: count += prefixCount[sum - target], then add sum to the map, recurse on both children, then remove sum.

    Java implementation
    Java
    // LC 437. Count downward paths summing to target.
// Same idea as LC 560, applied to the root-to-current path.
static int pathSum(TreeNode root, int targetSum) {
    Map<Long, Integer> prefixCount = new HashMap<>();
    prefixCount.put(0L, 1);
    return countPaths(root, 0L, targetSum, prefixCount);
}

private static int countPaths(TreeNode node, long sum, int target, Map<Long, Integer> prefixCount) {
    if (node == null) return 0;
    sum += node.val;                                         // long: values can overflow int
    int count = prefixCount.getOrDefault(sum - target, 0);
    prefixCount.merge(sum, 1, Integer::sum);                 // enter: this prefix is on the path
    count += countPaths(node.left, sum, target, prefixCount);
    count += countPaths(node.right, sum, target, prefixCount);
    prefixCount.merge(sum, -1, Integer::sum);                // leave: backtrack
    return count;
}
    Dry run

    As above. The removal step matters: after finishing the subtree under 5, the prefix 15 is removed, so the right subtree (under -3) does not count paths that would jump from the left subtree.

  5. 5
    Check it

    State time and space with a reason, name three inputs that could break the code, and say what this problem teaches beyond itself.

    Reveal step 5
    Complexity

    O(n) time, O(h) for the map entries on the path plus recursion.

    Edge cases

    Overflow (use long), negative values, target 0 with zero-valued nodes, the empty-prefix seed 0 -> 1 for paths that start at the root.

    Transfer lesson

    Top-down state plus backtracking turns any "segment of a root-to-node path" question into the corresponding array technique. When ancestor information must reach nodes outside the downward path (All Nodes Distance K, LC 863), add parent pointers and treat the tree as a graph (Module 12).

9.5Constructing trees and serialization

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
105Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder TraversalMedium

Stuck after 15 minutes? The guided solve in this lesson walks through this exact problem, one question at a time.

Show a hint
Preorder gives root; inorder index splits left/right
What it solves

Rebuilding a tree from traversal sequences, converting between trees and strings, and building balanced trees from sorted data.

Go deeper

Which traversals determine a tree?

Given Unique binary tree? How
Preorder + inorder (distinct values) Yes Preorder gives the root; inorder splits left and right
Postorder + inorder Yes Same, reading postorder from the end
Preorder + postorder Only for full binary trees Left subtree root is pre[1]; find it in postorder to size the left subtree
Preorder with null markers Yes Read tokens in the same order they were written
Preorder of a BST Yes Values bound the subtrees (LC 1008)
Guided solveLC 105. Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder TraversalFive questions, each with a reveal

Problem: 105Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder TraversalMedium. Answer each question on paper first, then reveal.

  1. 1
    Understand the problem

    Say in one sentence what is asked. Which constraint sets the time budget?

    Reveal step 1
    Problem decoding

    Rebuild the tree from its preorder and inorder sequences (values are unique).

    Input analysis

    Up to 3000 nodes. Unique values make "position in inorder" well defined.

  2. 2
    Brute force, then a pattern

    What is the simplest correct approach and what does it cost? Which pattern could beat it, and why does it apply?

    Reveal step 2
    Pattern discovery

    Recursive structure: the tree is a root plus two subtrees, and both sequences decompose the same way.

    Brute force

    For each root, scan inorder to find it (O(n)) and copy subarrays: O(n^2) time and space.

  3. 3
    The key observation

    What single fact removes the repeated work? Trace a tiny input on paper until you see it.

    Reveal step 3

    Key idea. preorder supplies roots in order; inorder index ranges define subtrees

    Key observation

    A hash map from value to inorder index finds the split in O(1). And preorder is consumed strictly left to right if we build the left subtree before the right one, so a single shared index replaces array copies.

    Visualization

    The figure above: root 3, left [9], right [15, 20, 7] in inorder; then root 20 splits [15] and [7].

  4. 4
    Build it

    Write the algorithm in three or four lines, then code it. Reveal after you have run one small input by hand.

    Reveal step 4
    Algorithm

    build(inLo, inHi): if empty, null. Take pre[next++] as the root, find its inorder index mid, build left from (inLo, mid - 1), then right from (mid + 1, inHi).

    Java implementation
    Java
    // LC 105. preorder[0] is the root; its position in inorder splits left and right.
static TreeNode buildTree(int[] preorder, int[] inorder) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> inIndex = new HashMap<>();          // values are unique
    for (int i = 0; i < inorder.length; i++) inIndex.put(inorder[i], i);
    int[] next = {0};                                         // next root in preorder
    return build(preorder, next, 0, inorder.length - 1, inIndex);
}

private static TreeNode build(int[] pre, int[] next, int inLo, int inHi, Map<Integer, Integer> inIndex) {
    if (inLo > inHi) return null;
    int rootVal = pre[next[0]++];
    TreeNode root = new TreeNode(rootVal);
    int mid = inIndex.get(rootVal);
    root.left = build(pre, next, inLo, mid - 1, inIndex);    // left FIRST: preorder order
    root.right = build(pre, next, mid + 1, inHi, inIndex);
    return root;
}
    Dry run

    next = 0: root 3, mid = 1. Left (0, 0): root 9, children empty. Right (2, 4): root 20 (next = 2), mid = 3; left (2, 2): 15; right (4, 4): 7.

  5. 5
    Check it

    State time and space with a reason, name three inputs that could break the code, and say what this problem teaches beyond itself.

    Reveal step 5
    Complexity

    O(n) time and O(n) space (map plus recursion).

    Edge cases

    Single node; skewed trees (recursion depth n); building right before left (breaks the preorder index).

    Transfer lesson

    "One sequence supplies the order of construction, the other supplies boundaries" also builds from postorder (consume from the end, right subtree first) and builds BSTs from preorder with value bounds instead of a map.

Go deeper

Serialization and deserialization

Java
// LC 297. Preorder with "#" for null. The null markers make the shape unambiguous.
static String serialize(TreeNode root) {
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
    writeNode(root, sb);
    return sb.toString();
}

private static void writeNode(TreeNode node, StringBuilder sb) {
    if (node == null) { sb.append("#,"); return; }
    sb.append(node.val).append(',');
    writeNode(node.left, sb);
    writeNode(node.right, sb);
}

static TreeNode deserialize(String data) {
    Deque<String> tokens = new ArrayDeque<>(Arrays.asList(data.split(",")));
    return readNode(tokens);
}

private static TreeNode readNode(Deque<String> tokens) {
    String t = tokens.poll();
    if (t.equals("#")) return null;
    TreeNode node = new TreeNode(Integer.parseInt(t));
    node.left = readNode(tokens);     // consume tokens in the same order they were written
    node.right = readNode(tokens);
    return node;
}

Preorder with explicit null markers is self-describing: the reader consumes tokens in exactly the order the writer produced them, so no sizes or indices are needed. A level-order format (LeetCode's own) also works. Serializing subtrees as strings is also a hashing tool: Find Duplicate Subtrees (LC 652) maps each subtree's serialization to a count.

9.6Binary search trees

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
98Validate Binary Search TreeMedium

Stuck after 15 minutes? The guided solve in this lesson walks through this exact problem, one question at a time.

Show a hint
Pass (low, high) bounds; checking only children is wrong
What it solves

Ordered data with fast search, insert, and delete in O(h). In interviews BSTs appear as a structure to exploit (sorted inorder, one-sided search) more than as one to implement.

Pattern cardBinary search tree
Signal
'BST' in the statement, sorted order, kth smallest, floor/ceiling, validate, range sum.
Required condition
Every left-subtree value < node < every right-subtree value (strict, unless stated).
Mental model, core operation, limits, and what to use instead
Mental model
A decision tree of 'smaller go left, larger go right' questions.
Core operation
Choose one side by comparison (O(h)); inorder traversal visits values in sorted order.
Complexity benefit
Search, insert, delete in O(h): O(log n) when balanced, O(n) when skewed.
Limitations
Unbalanced trees degrade to lists; interview BSTs are usually not self-balancing.
Alternative
TreeMap / TreeSet in Java (red-black tree, guaranteed O(log n)); sorted array + binary search for static data.
Java
// LC 700 and 701. One comparison per level chooses the side: O(h).
static TreeNode searchBST(TreeNode node, int val) {
    while (node != null && node.val != val) node = (val < node.val) ? node.left : node.right;
    return node;
}

static TreeNode insertIntoBST(TreeNode root, int val) {
    if (root == null) return new TreeNode(val);
    if (val < root.val) root.left = insertIntoBST(root.left, val);
    else root.right = insertIntoBST(root.right, val);
    return root;
}

// LC 230. Inorder visits a BST in sorted order; stop at the k-th node.
static int kthSmallest(TreeNode root, int k) {
    Deque<TreeNode> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    TreeNode curr = root;
    while (true) {
        while (curr != null) { stack.push(curr); curr = curr.left; }
        curr = stack.pop();
        if (--k == 0) return curr.val;
        curr = curr.right;
    }
}
Go deeper

Deletion

Three cases: a leaf is removed; a node with one child is replaced by that child; a node with two children takes the value of its inorder successor (smallest value in the right subtree), and the successor is deleted from the right subtree.

Java
// LC 450. Cases: leaf, one child, two children (replace with inorder successor).
static TreeNode deleteNode(TreeNode root, int key) {
    if (root == null) return null;
    if (key < root.val) root.left = deleteNode(root.left, key);
    else if (key > root.val) root.right = deleteNode(root.right, key);
    else {
        if (root.left == null) return root.right;      // covers the leaf case too
        if (root.right == null) return root.left;
        TreeNode succ = root.right;                     // smallest value in the right subtree
        while (succ.left != null) succ = succ.left;
        root.val = succ.val;
        root.right = deleteNode(root.right, succ.val);  // remove the duplicate successor
    }
    return root;
}

Problem: 98Validate Binary Search TreeMedium. Answer each question on paper first, then reveal.

  1. 1
    Understand the problem

    Say in one sentence what is asked. Which constraint sets the time budget?

    Reveal step 1
    Problem decoding

    Is the tree a valid BST (strictly smaller on the left, strictly larger on the right, for every subtree)?

    Input analysis

    Up to 10^4 nodes, values span the full int range, including Integer.MIN_VALUE and MAX_VALUE.

  2. 2
    Brute force, then a pattern

    What is the simplest correct approach and what does it cost? Which pattern could beat it, and why does it apply?

    Reveal step 2
    Pattern discovery

    The BST rule is about whole subtrees, which means information from ancestors: pass allowed ranges down.

    Brute force

    For each node, check that the max of its left subtree is smaller and the min of its right subtree is larger: O(n^2) if recomputed, O(n) if returned bottom-up. The common wrong answer checks only left.val < node.val < right.val.

  3. 3
    The key observation

    What single fact removes the repeated work? Trace a tiny input on paper until you see it.

    Reveal step 3

    Key idea. every node must respect bounds from all its ancestors

    Key observation

    Going left tightens the upper bound to the current value; going right tightens the lower bound. A node is valid if it lies in its range and both children are valid in their tightened ranges.

    Visualization
  4. 4
    Build it

    Write the algorithm in three or four lines, then code it. Reveal after you have run one small input by hand.

    Reveal step 4
    Algorithm

    inRange(node, low, high): null is valid; the node must satisfy low < val < high; recurse with (low, val) on the left and (val, high) on the right.

    Java implementation
    Java
    // LC 98. Every node must lie in (low, high) set by ALL ancestors, not just its parent.
static boolean isValidBST(TreeNode root) {
    return inRange(root, Long.MIN_VALUE, Long.MAX_VALUE);   // long: values can equal int limits
}

private static boolean inRange(TreeNode node, long low, long high) {
    if (node == null) return true;
    if (node.val <= low || node.val >= high) return false;
    return inRange(node.left, low, node.val) && inRange(node.right, node.val, high);
}
    Dry run

    On the invalid tree: root 5 in (-inf, inf); right child 6 in (5, inf); its left child 3 in (5, 6): 3 <= 5, invalid.

  5. 5
    Check it

    State time and space with a reason, name three inputs that could break the code, and say what this problem teaches beyond itself.

    Reveal step 5
    Complexity

    O(n) time, O(h) space.

    Edge cases

    A single node with value Integer.MAX_VALUE (int bounds would wrongly reject it; long bounds or nullable bounds fix it), duplicates (invalid under the strict definition).

    Transfer lesson

    The alternative proof is "inorder traversal is strictly increasing", checked with a prev variable. Both views (bounds from ancestors, sorted inorder) solve most BST problems: kth smallest (inorder count), recover BST (find the two inversions in inorder), convert to greater tree (reverse inorder with a running sum).

Go deeper

BSTs in Java practice

Interview BSTs are not balanced; their height can be n. When you need a sorted structure in your own solution, use TreeMap / TreeSet (red-black trees): floorKey, ceilingKey, firstKey, lastKey, headMap, tailMap, all O(log n).

Module 10: Heaps and priority queues

A heap gives you the smallest (or largest) element in O(1) and lets you insert or remove in O(log n). Use it whenever you repeatedly need the current extreme while data keeps arriving.

5 lessons2 guided solves18 practice problems

On this page

  1. 10.1Heap fundamentals
  2. 10.2Top-K and the kth element
  3. 10.3K-way merge and frontier expansion
  4. 10.4Two heaps: the running median
  5. 10.5Heap vs sorting vs other structures

10.1Heap fundamentals

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
1962Remove Stones to Minimize the TotalMedium

Any correct brute force counts. Note where you got stuck: the lesson below is about exactly that.

Show a hint
Max-heap simulation: always halve the largest pile
What it solves

"Repeatedly take the most urgent item": the next meeting to end, the closest unvisited node, the k largest so far, the smallest head among k sorted lists. Sorting answers this once; a heap keeps answering it as items are added and removed.

Intuition

An emergency room. Patients arrive in any order, but the doctor always sees the most urgent one next. The nurse does not re-sort the whole waiting room on each arrival; she only checks where the new patient fits relative to a few others.

Pattern cardHeap / priority queue
Signal
Top k, kth largest/smallest, 'repeatedly take the smallest/largest', merging sorted sources, scheduling by time or priority.
Required condition
You need fast access to the current extreme while elements keep arriving or changing.
Mental model, core operation, limits, and what to use instead
Mental model
An emergency room queue: the most urgent patient is always seen next, whatever the arrival order.
Core operation
offer and poll in O(log n), peek in O(1). Keep the heap at size k for top-k.
Complexity benefit
Top k in O(n log k) instead of O(n log n) sorting; streaming answers without re-sorting.
Limitations
No fast search or removal of arbitrary elements (O(n)); iteration order is not sorted.
Alternative
Sorting when all data is known up front; quickselect for one kth element (O(n) average); TreeMap when you need removal by key.
Go deeper

Structure: a complete binary tree stored in an array

Operation How it works Cost
peek Read index 0 O(1)
offer (insert) Append at the end, sift up: swap with the parent while smaller O(log n)
poll (remove top) Move the last element to index 0, sift down: swap with the smaller child while larger O(log n)
heapify n elements Sift down from the last parent to the root O(n), not O(n log n)
remove arbitrary / contains Linear search, then fix O(n)

You rarely implement a heap in an interview, but you should be able to explain sift up and sift down, and why the height is log n (the tree is complete).

Go deeper

PriorityQueue in Java

Java
static void priorityQueueApi() {
    PriorityQueue<Integer> minHeap = new PriorityQueue<>();                        // smallest on top
    PriorityQueue<Integer> maxHeap = new PriorityQueue<>(Collections.reverseOrder()); // largest on top
    PriorityQueue<int[]> byDist = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]));
    minHeap.offer(5); minHeap.offer(1); maxHeap.offer(5); maxHeap.offer(1);
    byDist.offer(new int[]{3, 0});
    // offer/poll: O(log n). peek: O(1). size: O(1).
    // remove(Object) and contains(Object): O(n) - avoid them in hot loops.
    // Iterating a PriorityQueue does NOT give sorted order; only repeated poll() does.
    if (minHeap.peek() != 1 || maxHeap.peek() != 5 || byDist.peek()[0] != 3) throw new AssertionError();
}

Pitfalls specific to PriorityQueue:

  • Iteration order is not sorted. for (int x : pq) or new ArrayList<>(pq) gives heap order. Only repeated poll() produces sorted output.
  • remove(Object) is O(n). For "delete this element" use lazy deletion (mark it invalid and skip it when it reaches the top) or a TreeMap with counts.
  • Mutating an element inside the heap breaks it. Remove, change, and re-insert.
  • Comparator overflow. (a, b) -> a - b fails for large or negative values; use Integer.compare.

10.2Top-K and the kth element

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
215Kth Largest Element in an ArrayMedium

Stuck after 15 minutes? The guided solve in this lesson walks through this exact problem, one question at a time.

Show a hint
Size-k heap vs quickselect trade-offs

The size-k heap trick. To keep the k largest elements of a stream, use a min-heap of size k: its top is the smallest of the k largest, which is exactly the kth largest. Every new element either beats the top (replace it) or is ignored. It sounds backward until you see why: the top is the element most likely to be evicted.

Want Heap type Size Top is
k largest / kth largest min-heap k kth largest
k smallest / kth smallest max-heap k kth smallest
k closest points max-heap by distance k the farthest of the k closest
Java
// LC 215. Keep the k largest seen so far in a MIN-heap; its top is the kth largest.
static int findKthLargest(int[] nums, int k) {
    PriorityQueue<Integer> heap = new PriorityQueue<>();
    for (int x : nums) {
        heap.offer(x);
        if (heap.size() > k) heap.poll();     // evict the smallest of the k + 1
    }
    return heap.peek();
}
Guided solveLC 215. Kth Largest Element in an ArrayFive questions, each with a reveal

Problem: 215Kth Largest Element in an ArrayMedium. Answer each question on paper first, then reveal.

  1. 1
    Understand the problem

    Say in one sentence what is asked. Which constraint sets the time budget?

    Reveal step 1
    Problem decoding

    Return the kth largest value (by sorted order, duplicates count separately).

    Input analysis

    n up to 10^5, values from -10^4 to 10^4. The follow-up asks for better than sorting.

  2. 2
    Brute force, then a pattern

    What is the simplest correct approach and what does it cost? Which pattern could beat it, and why does it apply?

    Reveal step 2
    Pattern discovery

    "kth largest" with k possibly much smaller than n: a size-k heap. Values in a small range also allow counting sort.

    Brute force

    Sort descending and take index k - 1: O(n log n).

  3. 3
    The key observation

    What single fact removes the repeated work? Trace a tiny input on paper until you see it.

    Reveal step 3

    Key idea. a min-heap of size k holds the k largest; its top is the answer

    Key observation

    We never need the order among elements outside the top k, nor among elements inside it except for the smallest. A min-heap of size k tracks exactly that.

    Visualization
    nums = [3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4], k = 2      heap (min at the left)
3  -> [3]
2  -> [2, 3]
1  -> [1, 2, 3] -> poll 1 -> [2, 3]
5  -> [2, 3, 5] -> poll 2 -> [3, 5]
6  -> [3, 5, 6] -> poll 3 -> [5, 6]
4  -> [4, 5, 6] -> poll 4 -> [5, 6]
top = 5
  4. 4
    Build it

    Write the algorithm in three or four lines, then code it. Reveal after you have run one small input by hand.

    Reveal step 4
    Algorithm

    Offer each element; if the size exceeds k, poll. Return the top.

    Java implementation

    findKthLargest above.

    Dry run

    The trace above returns 5.

  5. 5
    Check it

    State time and space with a reason, name three inputs that could break the code, and say what this problem teaches beyond itself.

    Reveal step 5
    Complexity

    O(n log k) time, O(k) space. With k close to n, it approaches O(n log n).

    Edge cases

    k = 1 (the max), k = n (the min), duplicates (they occupy separate slots, which is what "kth largest by sorted order" means).

    Transfer lesson

    Alternatives worth naming: quickselect partitions around a pivot and recurses into one side, O(n) average and O(n^2) worst (randomize the pivot); counting works when the value range is small. For top-k by frequency (LC 347), count first, then apply the same heap to (value, count) pairs, or bucket by frequency in O(n).

Java
// LC 347. Count with a map, then keep the k most frequent in a size-k min-heap.
static int[] topKFrequent(int[] nums, int k) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();
    for (int x : nums) freq.merge(x, 1, Integer::sum);
    PriorityQueue<Map.Entry<Integer, Integer>> heap =
        new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Integer.compare(a.getValue(), b.getValue()));
    for (Map.Entry<Integer, Integer> e : freq.entrySet()) {
        heap.offer(e);
        if (heap.size() > k) heap.poll();
    }
    int[] result = new int[k];
    for (int i = k - 1; i >= 0; i--) result[i] = heap.poll().getKey();   // most frequent first
    return result;
}
Go deeper

Heaps for scheduling and simulation

When the next event to process is "the one with the smallest time" or "the most valuable available option", a heap drives the simulation:

  • Single-Threaded CPU (LC 1834): sort tasks by arrival; whenever the CPU is free, add every arrived task to a heap ordered by (duration, index) and run the top.
  • IPO (LC 502): sort projects by required capital; unlock all affordable ones into a max-heap of profits; take the best k times.
  • Furthest Building (LC 1642): use ladders on the largest climbs. Keep a min-heap of the climbs assigned to ladders; when it exceeds the number of ladders, the smallest climb switches to bricks.
  • Meeting rooms with room ids (LC 2402): one heap of free room ids, one heap of (end time, room) for busy rooms.

The pattern is "sort the inputs by when they become available, and keep the available ones in a heap ordered by priority".

10.3K-way merge and frontier expansion

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
23Merge k Sorted ListsHard

Any correct brute force counts. Note where you got stuck: the lesson below is about exactly that.

Show a hint
Heap holds the current head of each list
What it solves

Merging k sorted sequences, or exploring candidates in increasing order when each candidate generates a few "next" candidates (pairs from two sorted arrays, cells of a sorted matrix, ugly numbers).

The idea

The next smallest element overall must be the smallest among the current fronts of the sources. Keep one front per source in a heap; when you take a front, push its successor.

Java
// LC 23. The heap holds one candidate (the current head) from each list.
static ListNode mergeKLists(ListNode[] lists) {
    PriorityQueue<ListNode> heap = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Integer.compare(a.val, b.val));
    for (ListNode head : lists) if (head != null) heap.offer(head);
    ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0), tail = dummy;
    while (!heap.isEmpty()) {
        ListNode smallest = heap.poll();
        tail.next = smallest;
        tail = smallest;
        if (smallest.next != null) heap.offer(smallest.next);   // its successor becomes a candidate
    }
    return dummy.next;
}

Merging N total elements from k lists costs O(N log k): each element enters and leaves a heap of size at most k.

Frontier expansion. For K Pairs with Smallest Sums (LC 373), the "sources" are rows i paired with columns j. Start with (i, 0) for each i (or just (0, 0) and expand both directions with a visited set), and when (i, j) is taken, push (i, j + 1). The heap never holds more than k + rows entries, and you never generate pairs you will not need.

10.4Two heaps: the running median

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
295Find Median from Data StreamHard

Stuck after 15 minutes? The guided solve in this lesson walks through this exact problem, one question at a time.

Show a hint
Max-heap low half, min-heap high half, rebalance
The idea

Split the numbers into a lower half and an upper half. The lower half is a max-heap (its top is the largest small number); the upper half is a min-heap (its top is the smallest large number). The median lives at the tops.

Pattern cardTwo heaps and k-way merge
Signal
Running median, balancing two halves, merging k sorted lists, smallest pairs from sorted arrays.
Required condition
The answer is defined by a boundary between two halves, or by the next smallest among k sorted frontiers.
Mental model, core operation, limits, and what to use instead
Mental model
Median: two piles, small values on the left pile (top = largest), large on the right (top = smallest).
Core operation
Median: push, move tops across to keep order and sizes. K-way: heap holds one frontier element per source.
Complexity benefit
Median in O(log n) per insert; merging N elements from k lists in O(N log k).
Limitations
Deletion of arbitrary elements needs lazy deletion bookkeeping.
Alternative
TreeMap multiset; divide-and-conquer pairwise merging for k-way merge.
Guided solveLC 295. Find Median from Data StreamFive questions, each with a reveal

Problem: 295Find Median from Data StreamHard. Answer each question on paper first, then reveal.

  1. 1
    Understand the problem

    Say in one sentence what is asked. Which constraint sets the time budget?

    Reveal step 1
    Problem decoding

    Support addNum(x) and findMedian() over a growing stream.

    Input analysis

    Up to 5 * 10^4 calls, values within int. The median of an even count is the mean of the middle two.

  2. 2
    Brute force, then a pattern

    What is the simplest correct approach and what does it cost? Which pattern could beat it, and why does it apply?

    Reveal step 2
    Pattern discovery

    We need the middle of a changing multiset. Sorting after each insert is O(n log n) per call. A heap gives one extreme; two heaps give the two middle values.

    Brute force

    Keep a sorted ArrayList and insert with binary search: O(log n) to find the spot, O(n) to shift.

  3. 3
    The key observation

    What single fact removes the repeated work? Trace a tiny input on paper until you see it.

    Reveal step 3

    Key idea. two heaps meeting in the middle, kept balanced

    Key observation

    Only the boundary between the halves matters. Maintain two invariants: every element of low is <= every element of high, and low has the same size as high or one more.

    Visualization
    add 5:  low [5]          high []        median 5
add 2:  low [2]          high [5]       median (2 + 5) / 2 = 3.5
add 8:  low [5, 2]       high [8]       median 5
add 1:  low [2, 1]       high [5, 8]    median (2 + 5) / 2 = 3.5
(low is a max-heap: its top is listed first)
  4. 4
    Build it

    Write the algorithm in three or four lines, then code it. Reveal after you have run one small input by hand.

    Reveal step 4
    Algorithm

    Push the new number into low, then move low's top to high (this restores the ordering invariant whatever the number was). If high is now larger than low, move high's top back. Median: low.peek() if sizes differ, else the mean of both tops.

    Java implementation
    Java
    // LC 295. low = max-heap of the smaller half, high = min-heap of the larger half.
// Invariants: every value in low <= every value in high; low.size() is high.size() or +1.
static class MedianFinder {
    private final PriorityQueue<Integer> low = new PriorityQueue<>(Collections.reverseOrder());
    private final PriorityQueue<Integer> high = new PriorityQueue<>();

    void addNum(int num) {
        low.offer(num);
        high.offer(low.poll());          // move low's max across: keeps the ordering invariant
        if (high.size() > low.size()) low.offer(high.poll());   // rebalance sizes
    }

    double findMedian() {
        if (low.size() > high.size()) return low.peek();
        return ((long) low.peek() + high.peek()) / 2.0;          // long avoids overflow
    }
}
    Dry run

    The trace above. Note that "push into low, move top to high" means a large number travels to high immediately and a small number pushes low's largest up.

  5. 5
    Check it

    State time and space with a reason, name three inputs that could break the code, and say what this problem teaches beyond itself.

    Reveal step 5
    Complexity

    addNum O(log n), findMedian O(1). Space O(n).

    Edge cases

    Two Integer.MAX_VALUE values: their sum overflows int, hence the cast to long. Negative numbers and duplicates need no special handling.

    Transfer lesson

    Two heaps solve any "balance two halves" problem. For a sliding window median (LC 480), add lazy deletion: record outgoing values in a map and discard them when they surface at a heap top, adjusting the size accounting.

10.5Heap vs sorting vs other structures

Try it first2 minutes, before you read on

You need the 10 largest values from a stream of 10^9 numbers and cannot store them all. Sort, a heap of size 10, or quickselect?

Reveal the answer

A min-heap of size 10: push each value, pop the smallest whenever the size exceeds 10. O(n log 10) time, O(10) memory, and it works on a stream. Sorting and quickselect both need every value in memory at once.

Situation Best choice
All data known, need full order Sort, O(n log n)
All data known, need the kth element once Quickselect O(n) average, or size-k heap O(n log k)
Data arrives over time, need the current extreme repeatedly Heap
Need the extreme and also delete arbitrary elements TreeMap<value, count> or heap + lazy deletion
Need the median or another fixed rank repeatedly Two heaps
Values in a small range Counting / bucket arrays

Common mistakes

  • Using a max-heap of all n elements for top-k (O(n log n) instead of O(n log k)).
  • Expecting a heap to be sorted when iterated or printed.
  • Forgetting ties in the comparator when the problem specifies a tie-break (Top K Frequent Words: higher frequency first, then lexicographic).
  • Pushing duplicates of a frontier state without a visited set.

Module 11: Greedy algorithms

A greedy algorithm makes the locally best choice at each step and never reconsiders it. It is often the shortest code in the interview and the hardest to justify. The skill is not finding a greedy rule; it is proving it or breaking it.

3 lessons1 guided solves10 practice problems

On this page

  1. 11.1What greedy means and when it works
  2. 11.2Greedy patterns you will meet
  3. 11.3Greedy vs dynamic programming

11.1What greedy means and when it works

Try it first2 minutes, before you read on

Coins are {1, 3, 4} and the amount is 6. Does "always take the largest coin that fits" give the fewest coins?

Reveal the answer

No. Greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1 = 3 coins; the optimum is 3 + 3 = 2 coins. One small counterexample is enough to reject a greedy rule. This lesson is about telling the rules that are safe from the ones that only look safe.

What it solves

Optimization problems where one natural choice is always safe: the interval that ends first, the furthest reachable index, the cheapest option per unit, the largest coin in some (not all) coin systems.

Intuition

Packing a car trunk by always placing the largest remaining bag that fits. Sometimes this is optimal; sometimes a cleverer arrangement fits more. Greedy is correct only when you can show that no cleverer arrangement exists.

Pattern cardGreedy
Signal
Optimize one quantity with a natural order (earliest end, largest value per unit, furthest reach); local decision seems obviously safe.
Required condition
Greedy-choice property: some optimal solution starts with the greedy choice. Prove it (exchange argument) or find a counterexample.
Mental model, core operation, limits, and what to use instead
Mental model
Packing a suitcase by a rule you can defend: if a better packing existed, you could swap it into yours without loss.
Core operation
Sort or scan by the key, take or reject each item once, never revisit.
Complexity benefit
Usually O(n log n) or O(n), far below DP or search.
Limitations
Fails silently when the choice is not safe (coin change with arbitrary coins). Always test small counterexamples.
Alternative
DP when choices interact; heap-based greedy when the best choice changes as you go.
Go deeper

Local vs global optimum

A greedy rule optimizes the next step. It is correct when the problem has the greedy-choice property (some optimal solution begins with the greedy choice) and optimal substructure (after making it, the rest is the same kind of problem). DP needs only the second property; that is why DP is more general and slower.

Go deeper

Three ways to test a greedy idea

  1. Hunt for a counterexample first. Try 3 to 5 tiny inputs, especially ones where the "obvious" choice blocks a better later option. One counterexample ends the idea. Coin change with coins {1, 3, 4} and amount 6: largest-first gives 4 + 1 + 1 (3 coins), but 3 + 3 uses 2.
  2. Exchange argument. Take any optimal solution that differs from the greedy one. Show you can swap one of its choices for the greedy choice without making it worse. Repeating the swap turns the optimal solution into the greedy one, so greedy is optimal.
  3. Stays ahead. Show that after every step, the greedy solution is at least as good as any other solution measured by some quantity (reach, count, finish time). Then it is also at least as good at the end.
Go deeper

An exchange argument, written out

Two City Scheduling (LC 1029): send exactly n of 2n people to city A, the rest to B, minimizing cost. For each person, sending them to A instead of B changes the total by a - b. Claim: send to A the n people with the smallest a - b.

Proof. Suppose an optimal assignment sends person x to A and person y to B, with a_x - b_x > a_y - b_y. Swapping them (y to A, x to B) changes the cost by (a_y - b_y) - (a_x - b_x) < 0, which is an improvement: contradiction. So in an optimal assignment, everyone sent to A has a smaller a - b than everyone sent to B. That is the sorted split.

Java
// LC 1029. Exchange argument: sending person p to A instead of B changes cost by a - b.
// Sort by (a - b) and send the first half to A.
static int twoCitySchedCost(int[][] costs) {
    Arrays.sort(costs, (x, y) -> Integer.compare(x[0] - x[1], y[0] - y[1]));
    int n = costs.length / 2, total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < costs.length; i++) total += (i < n) ? costs[i][0] : costs[i][1];
    return total;
}

11.2Greedy patterns you will meet

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
55Jump GameMedium

Any correct brute force counts. Note where you got stuck: the lesson below is about exactly that.

Show a hint
Track the furthest reachable index
Go deeper

Reachability: track the furthest point

Java
// LC 55. Track the furthest index reachable from everything seen so far.
static boolean canJump(int[] nums) {
    int furthest = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        if (i > furthest) return false;            // i itself is unreachable
        furthest = Math.max(furthest, i + nums[i]);
    }
    return true;
}

Stays-ahead argument: furthest is the maximum index reachable using only indices <= i; if i exceeds it, no path can reach i, and therefore nothing beyond it.

For the minimum number of jumps, think of BFS layers without a queue: all indices reachable with j jumps form a contiguous range, and the next range ends at the furthest point reachable from the current one.

Java
// LC 45. Layers like BFS: [start, currentEnd] is reachable in 'jumps' jumps.
static int jump(int[] nums) {
    int jumps = 0, currentEnd = 0, furthest = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < nums.length - 1; i++) {    // no jump needed from the last index
        furthest = Math.max(furthest, i + nums[i]);
        if (i == currentEnd) {                      // layer exhausted: must jump
            jumps++;
            currentEnd = furthest;
        }
    }
    return jumps;
}

Reset when a segment fails

Guided solveLC 134. Gas StationFive questions, each with a reveal

Problem: 134Gas StationMedium. Answer each question on paper first, then reveal.

  1. 1
    Understand the problem

    Say in one sentence what is asked. Which constraint sets the time budget?

    Reveal step 1
    Problem decoding

    Stations in a circle; gas[i] is added at station i, cost[i] is needed to reach the next. Find the unique start index from which you can complete the circle, or -1.

    Input analysis

    n up to 10^5. O(n^2) (try every start) is too slow.

  2. 2
    Brute force, then a pattern

    What is the simplest correct approach and what does it cost? Which pattern could beat it, and why does it apply?

    Reveal step 2
    Pattern discovery

    A single pass with a running total, where a failure tells you something about many starts at once: greedy with a reset.

    Brute force

    Simulate from each start: O(n^2).

  3. 3
    The key observation

    What single fact removes the repeated work? Trace a tiny input on paper until you see it.

    Reveal step 3

    Key idea. a failing segment rules out every start inside it

    Key observation

    Two facts. (a) If the total gain sum(gas - cost) is negative, no start works. (b) If you start at s and first run dry going from i to i + 1, then no start between s and i works either. The run from s reached each such k with a non-negative tank; starting fresh at k means arriving there with an empty tank, so from k onward you never have more gas than the run from s had, and you also run dry before i + 1. So the next candidate is i + 1.

    Visualization
  4. 4
    Build it

    Write the algorithm in three or four lines, then code it. Reveal after you have run one small input by hand.

    Reveal step 4
    Algorithm

    One pass: accumulate total and tank; when tank < 0, set start = i + 1 and tank = 0. At the end, return start if total >= 0, else -1.

    Java implementation
    Java
    // LC 134. If the tank goes negative at i, no start in [start, i] can work,
// because each of them arrives at i with no more gas than 'start' did.
static int canCompleteCircuit(int[] gas, int[] cost) {
    int total = 0, tank = 0, start = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < gas.length; i++) {
        int gain = gas[i] - cost[i];
        total += gain;
        tank += gain;
        if (tank < 0) {          // cannot reach i + 1 from 'start'
            start = i + 1;
            tank = 0;
        }
    }
    return total >= 0 ? start : -1;   // total >= 0 guarantees the remaining start works
}
    Dry run

    Gains -2, -2, -2, 3, 3: tank fails at 0, 1, 2 (start becomes 3), then 3, 6. Total 0, so start 3.

  5. 5
    Check it

    State time and space with a reason, name three inputs that could break the code, and say what this problem teaches beyond itself.

    Reveal step 5
    Complexity

    O(n) time, O(1) space.

    Edge cases

    One station; total exactly 0 (still feasible); the answer at index 0 (no resets).

    Transfer lesson

    "When a prefix fails, the whole prefix is ruled out as a starting point" is Kadane's restart rule in disguise (Module 2). Proving that the skipped starts are all hopeless is what makes it correct.

Go deeper

Extend a segment to cover its constraints

Partition Labels (LC 763): a part must reach the last occurrence of every character inside it. Scan, extending the current part's end to last[c]; when the scan reaches the end, the part is closed. Each cut is as early as possible, so the number of parts is maximal.

Java
// LC 763. A part must extend at least to the last occurrence of every char inside it.
static List<Integer> partitionLabels(String s) {
    int[] last = new int[26];
    for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) last[s.charAt(i) - 'a'] = i;
    List<Integer> sizes = new ArrayList<>();
    int start = 0, end = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
        end = Math.max(end, last[s.charAt(i) - 'a']);
        if (i == end) {                     // nothing inside reaches further
            sizes.add(end - start + 1);
            start = i + 1;
        }
    }
    return sizes;
}
Go deeper

Sort first, then take greedily

Many greedy solutions are "sort by the right key, then scan once":

Problem Sort by Then
Assign Cookies (LC 455) children's greed and cookie sizes give the smallest sufficient cookie to the least greedy child
Maximum Units on a Truck (LC 1710) units per box, descending take boxes until the truck is full
Non-overlapping Intervals (LC 435) end time keep each interval that starts after the last kept end (Module 5)
Two City Scheduling (LC 1029) cost difference first half to A
Hand of Straights (LC 846) card value (TreeMap) always start a group at the smallest remaining card

Choosing the key is the whole problem. Test the key against small cases where a different key would choose differently.

Go deeper

Satisfy constraints in two passes

Candy (LC 135): each child with a higher rating than a neighbor needs more candy than that neighbor. A left-to-right pass satisfies the left-neighbor constraints; a right-to-left pass satisfies the right-neighbor constraints while keeping the larger of the two values. Each pass is greedy for one direction; the max combines them.

Go deeper

Track a range of possibilities

Valid Parenthesis String (LC 678): with * able to be (, ), or empty, keep the range [low, high] of possible open counts. ( raises both, ) lowers both, * lowers low and raises high. If high < 0 the string is invalid; clamp low at 0. Valid if low == 0 at the end. Tracking a range instead of one value avoids branching.

11.3Greedy vs dynamic programming

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
45Jump Game IIMedium

Any correct brute force counts. Note where you got stuck: the lesson below is about exactly that.

Show a hint
BFS-like layers: jump when you reach the current layer end
Greedy DP
Decision Commit to the locally best choice Evaluate every choice, reuse subresults
Needs Greedy-choice property + optimal substructure Optimal substructure + overlapping subproblems
Typical cost O(n log n) or O(n) O(states x transitions)
Proof Exchange or stays-ahead argument The recurrence is the proof
Failure mode Silently wrong answers Too slow or too much memory

Same story, different answer. Activity selection (maximize the number of intervals) is greedy; weighted interval scheduling (maximize total weight) is DP, because a short low-value interval can block a long high-value one. Fractional knapsack is greedy by value density; 0/1 knapsack is DP. Coin change is greedy for canonical coin systems like {1, 5, 10, 25} and DP in general. When the interviewer adds weights or values to a greedy problem, re-check the property.

Common mistakes

  • Trusting a greedy rule because it passes the examples. Spend two minutes hunting for a counterexample.
  • Sorting by the wrong key (start instead of end for interval selection).
  • Not explaining why it works. "It seems right" is not an answer; give the exchange argument in two sentences.

Module 13: Tries

A trie stores strings by their characters, one level per position, so that all words with a common prefix share a path. It turns "which words start with this?" from a scan of every word into a walk of the prefix length.

3 lessons1 guided solves10 practice problems

On this page

  2. 13.2Tries inside other searches

13.1Trie structure and operations

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
208Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)Medium

Any correct brute force counts. Note where you got stuck: the lesson below is about exactly that.

Show a hint
Node = children array + end-of-word flag
What it solves

Many words, many prefix questions: autocomplete, "does any word start with ...", dictionary lookups with wildcards, replacing words by their shortest root, searching a grid for many words at once.

Intuition

A phone menu. Pressing 1 narrows the options to one branch, pressing 3 next narrows further. Two callers who both start with "1, 3" share the first two steps.

Pattern cardTrie (prefix tree)
Signal
Many prefix queries, autocomplete, 'words starting with', dictionary with wildcards, word search with many words, max XOR.
Required condition
Keys are sequences (strings, bits) and queries share prefixes.
Mental model, core operation, limits, and what to use instead
Mental model
A phone tree menu: each key press narrows the choices.
Core operation
Walk one character at a time, creating or following child links; mark word ends.
Complexity benefit
Prefix lookup in O(L) independent of the number of words; prunes searches that share prefixes.
Limitations
Memory heavy (26 references per node); overkill for exact-match lookups.
Alternative
HashSet for exact matches; sorted list + binary search for prefix ranges; HashSet of all prefixes for small inputs.
Java
// LC 208. Each node has up to 26 children; a path from the root spells a prefix.
static class Trie {
    private static class Node {
        Node[] children = new Node[26];
        boolean isEnd;                    // a word ends exactly here
    }

    private final Node root = new Node();

    void insert(String word) {
        Node node = root;
        for (char ch : word.toCharArray()) {
            int i = ch - 'a';
            if (node.children[i] == null) node.children[i] = new Node();
            node = node.children[i];
        }
        node.isEnd = true;
    }

    boolean search(String word) {
        Node node = walk(word);
        return node != null && node.isEnd;    // the full word, not just a prefix
    }

    boolean startsWith(String prefix) {
        return walk(prefix) != null;
    }

    private Node walk(String s) {             // follow s; null if the path breaks
        Node node = root;
        for (char ch : s.toCharArray()) {
            node = node.children[ch - 'a'];
            if (node == null) return null;
        }
        return node;
    }
}
Operation Time Notes
insert(word) O(L) Creates at most L nodes
search(word) O(L) Must also check isEnd
startsWith(prefix) O(L) Only checks the path exists
Space O(total characters x alphabet) 26 references per node with arrays; a HashMap per node uses less for sparse alphabets

Array or map children? TrieNode[26] is fastest and simplest for lowercase letters. For large or unknown alphabets (Unicode, mixed case, digits), use Map<Character, TrieNode>.

Go deeper

Putting data on nodes

The isEnd flag is the minimum. Many problems store more:

Store on each node Solves
The word itself at its end node Word Search II: no need to rebuild the word from the path
Count of words passing through Sum of Prefix Scores (LC 2416), counting words with a prefix
Sum of values below Map Sum Pairs (LC 677)
Up to 3 best words below Search Suggestions System (LC 1268)
Go deeper

Wildcards: branch where the pattern is unknown

With . matching any letter (LC 211), the search follows the single matching child for a normal character and every existing child for .. The trie prunes all branches that do not exist, so the search is fast unless the pattern is mostly dots.

Java
// LC 211. '.' matches any letter: branch into every existing child.
static class WordDictionary {
    private final WordDictionary[] children = new WordDictionary[26];
    private boolean isEnd;

    void addWord(String word) {
        WordDictionary node = this;
        for (char ch : word.toCharArray()) {
            if (node.children[ch - 'a'] == null) node.children[ch - 'a'] = new WordDictionary();
            node = node.children[ch - 'a'];
        }
        node.isEnd = true;
    }

    boolean search(String word) { return match(word, 0, this); }

    private static boolean match(String w, int i, WordDictionary node) {
        if (i == w.length()) return node.isEnd;
        char ch = w.charAt(i);
        if (ch != '.') {
            WordDictionary next = node.children[ch - 'a'];
            return next != null && match(w, i + 1, next);
        }
        for (WordDictionary child : node.children)
            if (child != null && match(w, i + 1, child)) return true;
        return false;
    }
}

13.2Tries inside other searches

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
212Word Search IIHard

Stuck after 15 minutes? The guided solve in this lesson walks through this exact problem, one question at a time.

Show a hint
Trie-guided grid backtracking with pruning
Guided solveLC 212. Word Search IIFive questions, each with a reveal

Problem: 212Word Search IIHard. Answer each question on paper first, then reveal.

  1. 1
    Understand the problem

    Say in one sentence what is asked. Which constraint sets the time budget?

    Reveal step 1
    Problem decoding

    Return every word from a list that can be traced in the grid (adjacent cells, each cell used once per word).

    Input analysis

    Grid up to 12 x 12, up to 3 * 10^4 words of length up to 10.

  2. 2
    Brute force, then a pattern

    What is the simplest correct approach and what does it cost? Which pattern could beat it, and why does it apply?

    Reveal step 2
    Pattern discovery

    Word Search I (Module 8) per word would repeat the grid search 3 * 10^4 times. The words share prefixes, so a structure that searches all of them at once is needed: a trie.

    Brute force

    Run Word Search for each word: O(W * R * C * 3^L). Too slow.

  3. 3
    The key observation

    What single fact removes the repeated work? Trace a tiny input on paper until you see it.

    Reveal step 3

    Key idea. walk the grid and the trie together; stop when the path leaves the trie

    Key observation

    A single DFS from each cell can follow the trie: moving to a neighbor cell is allowed only if the trie has a child for that letter. Any grid path that is not a prefix of some word is cut immediately, and every word is found during the same walk.

    Visualization
    board          words: oath, pea, eat, rain
o a a n        from (0,0) 'o': trie has o -> a -> t -> h
e t a e        path o(0,0) a(0,1) t(1,1) h(2,1): "oath" found
i h k r        from (1,0) 'e': the trie needs 'a' next; neighbors are o, i, t: stop
i f l v        from (1,3) 'e': e(1,3) a(1,2) t(1,1): "eat" found
  4. 4
    Build it

    Write the algorithm in three or four lines, then code it. Reveal after you have run one small input by hand.

    Reveal step 4
    Algorithm

    Build a trie storing each word at its end node. For each cell, DFS with the current trie node: stop if out of bounds, already used, or no child for this letter. If the child holds a word, record it and clear it (so it is reported once). Mark the cell, recurse into four neighbors, restore.

    Java implementation
    Java
    // LC 212. Insert all words into a trie, then DFS the grid once, following trie edges.
// A path that is not a prefix of any word is abandoned immediately.
static List<String> findWords(char[][] board, String[] words) {
    TNode root = new TNode();
    for (String w : words) {
        TNode n = root;
        for (char ch : w.toCharArray()) {
            if (n.next[ch - 'a'] == null) n.next[ch - 'a'] = new TNode();
            n = n.next[ch - 'a'];
        }
        n.word = w;                                     // store the word at its end node
    }
    List<String> found = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int r = 0; r < board.length; r++)
        for (int c = 0; c < board[0].length; c++)
            explore(board, r, c, root, found);
    return found;
}

private static class TNode {
    TNode[] next = new TNode[26];
    String word;                                        // non-null if a word ends here
}

private static void explore(char[][] b, int r, int c, TNode parent, List<String> found) {
    if (r < 0 || c < 0 || r >= b.length || c >= b[0].length) return;
    char ch = b[r][c];
    if (ch == '#' || parent.next[ch - 'a'] == null) return;   // visited, or not a prefix
    TNode node = parent.next[ch - 'a'];
    if (node.word != null) {
        found.add(node.word);
        node.word = null;                               // report each word once
    }
    b[r][c] = '#';
    explore(b, r + 1, c, node, found); explore(b, r - 1, c, node, found);
    explore(b, r, c + 1, node, found); explore(b, r, c - 1, node, found);
    b[r][c] = ch;
}
    Dry run

    The trace above finds "oath" and "eat"; "pea" fails because no 'p' exists, "rain" because no path continues r -> a.

  5. 5
    Check it

    State time and space with a reason, name three inputs that could break the code, and say what this problem teaches beyond itself.

    Reveal step 5
    Complexity

    O(R * C * 4 * 3^(L-1)) in the worst case, but the trie prunes most paths early. Building the trie is O(total characters).

    Edge cases

    Duplicate words in the list, a word that is a prefix of another (both are found, because finding one does not stop the walk), words longer than the number of cells.

    Transfer lesson

    An optional optimization removes trie leaves after their word is found, so later searches skip exhausted branches. More generally, when you would run the same search for many keys, ask whether a trie (or a hash of all prefixes) lets one search serve them all.

Go deeper

Binary tries for XOR problems

Numbers are strings of bits. A trie over the 31 bits of each number (most significant first) lets you find, for any x, the stored number that maximizes x ^ y: at each level, prefer the child with the opposite bit. Maximum XOR of Two Numbers (LC 421) is O(31 n).

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on

Any correct brute force counts. Note where you got stuck: the lesson below is about exactly that.

Show a hint
Walk the prefix, then collect up to 3 words
Need Best tool Why
Exact membership only HashSet<String> Simplest; O(L) per lookup to hash
Many prefix queries on a fixed list Trie, or sorted list + binary search for the prefix range Trie is O(L) per query; sorting is O(L log n)
Autocomplete with the top few results Trie with results cached on nodes Answer read directly at the prefix node
Wildcards or grid search with many words Trie Branching and pruning by prefix
Shortest root that prefixes a word Trie Stop at the first end node while walking
Memory is tight HashSet of words (or of all prefixes, if few) Tries cost up to 26 references per node

Common mistakes

  • search returning true for a prefix that is not a word (forgot isEnd).
  • Building a new trie per query instead of once.
  • Assuming lowercase letters when the input can contain other characters.
  • Recursing into all 26 children for every character instead of only for wildcards.

Module 12: Graphs
