12.1Graph fundamentals and representation

Try it first2 minutes, before you read on

Undirected edges [[0,1], [1,2], [2,0], [3,4]] with n = 5. Write the adjacency list. How many connected components are there?

Reveal the answer

0: [1, 2], 1: [0, 2], 2: [1, 0], 3: [4], 4: [3]. Two components: {0, 1, 2} and {3, 4}. Each undirected edge is stored twice, once in each direction.

What it solves

Relationships between items. A tree is a graph with no cycles and one path between any two nodes; general graphs can have cycles, multiple paths, directions, and weights, which is why they need a visited set.

Term Meaning
Vertex (node), edge Items and the connections between them; V and E denote their counts
Directed / undirected One-way (u -> v) or two-way connections
Weighted / unweighted Edges carry a cost, or all count as 1
Degree, in-degree, out-degree Number of edges at a node; in directed graphs, incoming vs outgoing
Path, cycle A sequence of edges; a path that returns to its start
Connected component A maximal set of nodes that can all reach each other (undirected)
DAG Directed acyclic graph: a directed graph with no cycles (it has a topological order)
Dense / sparse E close to V^2, or E close to V
Go deeper

Representations

Representation Space Check edge (u, v) List neighbors of u Use when
Adjacency list O(V + E) O(degree) O(degree) Default for interviews; sparse graphs
Adjacency matrix O(V^2) O(1) O(V) Dense graphs, small V (<= ~1000), Floyd-Warshall
Edge list O(E) O(E) O(E) Kruskal, Bellman-Ford
Implicit (grid, state space) O(1) to describe computed computed (4 or 8 neighbors) Grids, puzzles, word ladders
Java
// Adjacency list from an edge list. Undirected -> add both directions.
static List<List<Integer>> buildGraph(int n, int[][] edges, boolean directed) {
    List<List<Integer>> adj = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) adj.add(new ArrayList<>());
    for (int[] e : edges) {
        adj.get(e[0]).add(e[1]);
        if (!directed) adj.get(e[1]).add(e[0]);
    }
    return adj;
}

For weighted graphs, store pairs: List<List<int[]>> where each entry is {neighbor, weight}. For grids, do not build a graph at all; compute neighbors with a direction array.

12.2BFS, DFS, and connected components

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
200Number of IslandsMedium

Stuck after 15 minutes? The guided solve in this lesson walks through this exact problem, one question at a time.

Show a hint
Count DFS launches over unvisited land
What it solves

Visiting everything reachable from a start: reachability, counting components (islands, provinces), flood fill, cloning, marking regions.

Pattern cardGraph traversal (BFS / DFS)
Signal
Connections, reachability, islands, regions, 'can you get from A to B', components. Grids are graphs.
Required condition
You can list each node's neighbors. Mark visited to avoid infinite loops.
Mental model, core operation, limits, and what to use instead
Mental model
Spreading a rumor: everyone who hears it tells their friends, and nobody is told twice.
Core operation
Start from a source, push it, mark visited, expand neighbors until the frontier is empty.
Complexity benefit
O(V + E) to explore everything reachable.
Limitations
DFS recursion depth on large grids (10^5 to 10^6 cells) can overflow the stack.
Alternative
Union-Find for connectivity with incremental edges; iterative DFS with an explicit stack.
Go deeper

The visited rule

In a graph, unlike a tree, a node can be reached along several paths. Without a visited mark, traversal loops forever on a cycle or does exponential work. Two rules:

  • Mark when you add to the queue or stack, not when you remove. Otherwise the same node is queued many times (correct for reachability, but wasteful, and wrong for BFS distances in some implementations).
  • The visited structure can be the input (overwrite grid cells), a boolean array, a Set, or a map you are already building (Clone Graph's original -> clone map).
Go deeper

BFS vs DFS for traversal

Both visit every reachable node in O(V + E). Use BFS when distances or levels matter; use DFS when you need to follow a path to its end (cycle detection, topological order, backtracking) or when recursion is simply shorter. On large grids (10^6 cells), recursive DFS can overflow the stack; switch to BFS or an explicit stack.

Java
// BFS from a source: dist[v] = fewest edges from source (-1 = unreachable).
// Mark visited when ENQUEUING, so a node is never added twice.
static int[] bfsDistances(List<List<Integer>> adj, int source) {
    int[] dist = new int[adj.size()];
    Arrays.fill(dist, -1);
    Deque<Integer> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
    dist[source] = 0;
    queue.offer(source);
    while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
        int u = queue.poll();
        for (int v : adj.get(u)) {
            if (dist[v] == -1) {
                dist[v] = dist[u] + 1;
                queue.offer(v);
            }
        }
    }
    return dist;
}
Guided solveLC 200. Number of IslandsFive questions, each with a reveal

Problem: 200Number of IslandsMedium. Answer each question on paper first, then reveal.

  1. 1
    Understand the problem

    Say in one sentence what is asked. Which constraint sets the time budget?

    Reveal step 1
    Problem decoding

    In a grid of '1' (land) and '0' (water), count groups of land connected horizontally or vertically.

    Input analysis

    Up to 300 x 300 = 9 * 10^4 cells. The grid is an implicit graph: each cell connects to its four neighbors.

  2. 2
    Brute force, then a pattern

    What is the simplest correct approach and what does it cost? Which pattern could beat it, and why does it apply?

    Reveal step 2
    Pattern discovery

    "Groups of connected things" is connected components. Each traversal from an unvisited land cell discovers one entire island.

    Brute force

    There is nothing simpler that is also correct: any solution must look at each cell. The question is only how to avoid double counting.

  3. 3
    The key observation

    What single fact removes the repeated work? Trace a tiny input on paper until you see it.

    Reveal step 3

    Key idea. count how many times a DFS has to be started

    Key observation

    After a traversal "sinks" an island (marks all its cells), the outer scan can never start a second traversal inside it. So the number of traversals started equals the number of islands.

    Visualization
    1 1 0 0 0        scan finds (0,0): DFS sinks the 2x2 block        count 1
1 1 0 0 0        scan finds (2,2): DFS sinks one cell              count 2
0 0 1 0 0        scan finds (3,3): DFS sinks (3,3), (3,4)          count 3
0 0 0 1 1
  4. 4
    Build it

    Write the algorithm in three or four lines, then code it. Reveal after you have run one small input by hand.

    Reveal step 4
    Algorithm

    Scan every cell. On '1', increment the count and DFS from it, setting each visited land cell to '0'.

    Java implementation
    Java
    // LC 200. Each DFS launch from unvisited land discovers one whole island.
static int numIslands(char[][] grid) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < grid.length; r++)
        for (int c = 0; c < grid[0].length; c++)
            if (grid[r][c] == '1') {
                count++;
                sink(grid, r, c);
            }
    return count;
}

private static void sink(char[][] grid, int r, int c) {
    if (r < 0 || c < 0 || r >= grid.length || c >= grid[0].length || grid[r][c] != '1') return;
    grid[r][c] = '0';                    // mark visited by modifying the input
    sink(grid, r + 1, c); sink(grid, r - 1, c);
    sink(grid, r, c + 1); sink(grid, r, c - 1);
}
    Dry run

    The trace above gives 3.

  5. 5
    Check it

    State time and space with a reason, name three inputs that could break the code, and say what this problem teaches beyond itself.

    Reveal step 5
    Complexity

    O(R * C) time: each cell is sunk at most once, and each sink checks 4 neighbors. Space O(R * C) recursion depth in the worst case (a grid that is all land in a snake shape).

    Edge cases

    All water (0), all land (1), a single row or column. If modifying the input is not allowed, use a boolean[][] visited array.

    Transfer lesson

    Count components (LC 547), measure them (Max Area of Island, LC 695: DFS returns the size), or classify them (Surrounded Regions, LC 130, and Number of Enclaves, LC 1020: start from the border first and mark what escapes). Union-Find solves the same problem when cells or edges arrive over time.

Reverse thinking for regions. "Which cells can reach the border?" is expensive per cell but cheap in reverse: start a traversal from every border cell and mark what it reaches (LC 130, 417, 1020). When a question asks "can X reach Y" for many X, search backward from Y.

12.3Shortest paths in unweighted graphs and multi-source BFS

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
994Rotting OrangesMedium

Stuck after 15 minutes? The guided solve in this lesson walks through this exact problem, one question at a time.

Show a hint
Multi-source BFS; levels are minutes
What it solves

Fewest moves, fewest edges, minimum minutes, nearest X: whenever every move costs the same.

Pattern cardBFS shortest path (unweighted, multi-source)
Signal
Fewest steps, minimum moves, nearest X from every cell, spreading per minute. All moves cost the same.
Required condition
Every edge has equal weight. (0/1 weights: 0-1 BFS with a deque.)
Mental model, core operation, limits, and what to use instead
Mental model
Ripples: a node's first visit happens at its shortest distance.
Core operation
Queue all sources at distance 0, expand level by level, mark visited when enqueuing.
Complexity benefit
Shortest paths in O(V + E) instead of Dijkstra's O(E log V).
Limitations
Weighted edges break it: the first visit is no longer the cheapest.
Alternative
Dijkstra for non-negative weights; Bellman-Ford rounds for edge-count limits or negative weights.

Why the first visit is the shortest. The queue always holds nodes of distance d followed by nodes of distance d + 1 (never more than two consecutive distances, in that order). So nodes are discovered in non-decreasing order of distance, and a node discovered later could only have a larger or equal distance.

Go deeper

Multi-source BFS

When the question is "distance to the nearest source" from every cell, put all sources into the queue at distance 0 before starting. The BFS then behaves as if a single super-source were connected to all of them.

Guided solveLC 994. Rotting OrangesFive questions, each with a reveal

Problem: 994Rotting OrangesMedium. Answer each question on paper first, then reveal.

  1. 1
    Understand the problem

    Say in one sentence what is asked. Which constraint sets the time budget?

    Reveal step 1
    Problem decoding

    Every minute, fresh oranges adjacent to a rotten one become rotten. Return the minutes until none are fresh, or -1 if some never rot.

    Input analysis

    Grid up to 10 x 10. Values 0 (empty), 1 (fresh), 2 (rotten). Several rotten oranges at the start.

  2. 2
    Brute force, then a pattern

    What is the simplest correct approach and what does it cost? Which pattern could beat it, and why does it apply?

    Reveal step 2
    Pattern discovery

    Spreading one step per minute in all directions is BFS levels. Several starting points mean multi-source.

    Brute force

    Simulate minute by minute, scanning the whole grid each minute: O((R * C)^2).

  3. 3
    The key observation

    What single fact removes the repeated work? Trace a tiny input on paper until you see it.

    Reveal step 3

    Key idea. all rotten oranges start the BFS together; levels are minutes

    Key observation

    An orange rots at minute = its BFS distance to the nearest initially rotten orange. A multi-source BFS computes exactly that in one pass.

    Visualization
  4. 4
    Build it

    Write the algorithm in three or four lines, then code it. Reveal after you have run one small input by hand.

    Reveal step 4
    Algorithm

    Queue all rotten cells and count fresh ones. Process level by level; each fresh neighbor becomes rotten (mark on enqueue), decrementing the fresh count. Count levels until no fresh remain. If fresh oranges are left when the queue empties, return -1.

    Java implementation
    Java
    // LC 994. Multi-source BFS: every rotten orange starts in the queue at minute 0.
static int orangesRotting(int[][] grid) {
    int rows = grid.length, cols = grid[0].length, fresh = 0;
    Deque<int[]> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
    for (int r = 0; r < rows; r++)
        for (int c = 0; c < cols; c++) {
            if (grid[r][c] == 2) queue.offer(new int[]{r, c});
            else if (grid[r][c] == 1) fresh++;
        }
    int[][] dirs = {{1, 0}, {-1, 0}, {0, 1}, {0, -1}};
    int minutes = 0;
    while (!queue.isEmpty() && fresh > 0) {
        int size = queue.size();                  // one level = one minute
        for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
            int[] cell = queue.poll();
            for (int[] d : dirs) {
                int nr = cell[0] + d[0], nc = cell[1] + d[1];
                if (nr < 0 || nc < 0 || nr >= rows || nc >= cols || grid[nr][nc] != 1) continue;
                grid[nr][nc] = 2;                 // rot when enqueued
                fresh--;
                queue.offer(new int[]{nr, nc});
            }
        }
        minutes++;
    }
    return fresh == 0 ? minutes : -1;
}
    Dry run

    Example above: levels 1 to 4, fresh count reaches 0, return 4. The loop condition fresh > 0 avoids counting an extra minute after the last orange rots.

  5. 5
    Check it

    State time and space with a reason, name three inputs that could break the code, and say what this problem teaches beyond itself.

    Reveal step 5
    Complexity

    O(R * C) time and space.

    Edge cases

    No fresh oranges at all (0, even with no rotten ones), a fresh orange walled off by empty cells (-1), no rotten oranges but some fresh (-1).

    Transfer lesson

    01 Matrix (LC 542), As Far from Land as Possible (LC 1162), and "walls and gates" style problems are the same multi-source BFS. Shortest Bridge (LC 934) combines a DFS to collect one island as the source set with a BFS outward.

Go deeper

BFS over states

The nodes do not have to be cells. In Open the Lock (LC 752) a node is a 4-digit combination; in Word Ladder (LC 127) a node is a word; in Shortest Path with Obstacles Elimination (LC 1293) a node is (row, col, removals left). The state must contain everything that affects future moves. If two arrivals at the same cell can behave differently later, they are different states.

Java
// LC 127. BFS over words; neighbors differ by one letter. Generating neighbors by
// changing each position to a..z costs O(L * 26) per word instead of O(N * L) per word.
static int ladderLength(String begin, String end, List<String> wordList) {
    Set<String> words = new HashSet<>(wordList);
    if (!words.contains(end)) return 0;
    Deque<String> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
    queue.offer(begin);
    words.remove(begin);
    for (int steps = 1; !queue.isEmpty(); steps++) {
        for (int size = queue.size(); size > 0; size--) {
            char[] w = queue.poll().toCharArray();
            for (int i = 0; i < w.length; i++) {
                char original = w[i];
                for (char c = 'a'; c <= 'z'; c++) {
                    if (c == original) continue;
                    w[i] = c;
                    String next = new String(w);
                    if (!words.contains(next)) continue;
                    if (next.equals(end)) return steps + 1;
                    words.remove(next);          // removing = marking visited
                    queue.offer(next);
                }
                w[i] = original;
            }
        }
    }
    return 0;
}

12.4Cycles, bipartite graphs, and topological sort

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
207Course ScheduleMedium

Stuck after 15 minutes? The guided solve in this lesson walks through this exact problem, one question at a time.

Show a hint
Kahn's algorithm: processed count < n means a cycle
Go deeper

Cycle detection

Graph Method A cycle exists when
Undirected DFS/BFS with parent tracking A visited neighbor is not the node you came from
Undirected Union-Find An edge joins two nodes already in the same set
Directed DFS with three colors An edge reaches a GRAY node (one on the current DFS path)
Directed Kahn's algorithm Fewer than V nodes get processed
Java
// Directed cycle detection with three colors.
// WHITE = unvisited, GRAY = on the current DFS path, BLACK = fully explored.
// An edge to a GRAY node closes a cycle.
static boolean hasDirectedCycle(List<List<Integer>> adj) {
    int[] color = new int[adj.size()];             // 0 white, 1 gray, 2 black
    for (int u = 0; u < adj.size(); u++)
        if (color[u] == 0 && dfsCycle(adj, u, color)) return true;
    return false;
}

private static boolean dfsCycle(List<List<Integer>> adj, int u, int[] color) {
    color[u] = 1;
    for (int v : adj.get(u)) {
        if (color[v] == 1) return true;                       // back edge
        if (color[v] == 0 && dfsCycle(adj, v, color)) return true;
    }
    color[u] = 2;
    return false;
}

// Undirected cycle detection: a visited neighbor that is not the parent closes a cycle.
static boolean hasUndirectedCycle(List<List<Integer>> adj) {
    boolean[] seen = new boolean[adj.size()];
    for (int s = 0; s < adj.size(); s++) {
        if (seen[s]) continue;
        Deque<int[]> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();        // {node, parent}
        stack.push(new int[]{s, -1});
        seen[s] = true;
        while (!stack.isEmpty()) {
            int[] top = stack.pop();
            for (int v : adj.get(top[0])) {
                if (v == top[1]) continue;              // the edge we came in on
                if (seen[v]) return true;
                seen[v] = true;
                stack.push(new int[]{v, top[0]});
            }
        }
    }
    return false;
}

Why three colors in directed graphs? A visited node that is fully explored (BLACK) is not necessarily on the current path: in 0 -> 1, 0 -> 2, 1 -> 2, node 2 is reached twice without any cycle. Only an edge back to a node still on the current path (GRAY) closes a cycle.

Go deeper

Bipartite graphs

A graph is bipartite if its nodes split into two groups with every edge going across. Equivalently, it has no odd-length cycle. Test it by two-coloring with BFS or DFS: neighbors get opposite colors, and a conflict means not bipartite. Start from every uncolored node, because the graph may be disconnected.

Java
// LC 785. Two-color with BFS. Graph may be disconnected: start from every uncolored node.
static boolean isBipartite(int[][] graph) {
    int[] color = new int[graph.length];            // 0 = uncolored, 1 / -1 = the two sides
    for (int s = 0; s < graph.length; s++) {
        if (color[s] != 0) continue;
        Deque<Integer> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
        queue.offer(s);
        color[s] = 1;
        while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
            int u = queue.poll();
            for (int v : graph[u]) {
                if (color[v] == color[u]) return false;   // edge inside one side
                if (color[v] == 0) {
                    color[v] = -color[u];
                    queue.offer(v);
                }
            }
        }
    }
    return true;
}

Possible Bipartition (LC 886) is the same test after building a graph from "dislikes" pairs: recognizing that "split into two groups so that no pair is in the same group" means bipartite is the modeling step.

Go deeper

Topological sort

What it solves

Ordering tasks so every task comes after its prerequisites, deciding whether such an order exists, and dynamic programming over a DAG.

Pattern cardTopological sort and cycle detection
Signal
Prerequisites, dependencies, build order, 'is it possible to finish', ordering with constraints.
Required condition
Directed graph. A valid order exists if and only if there is no directed cycle.
Mental model, core operation, limits, and what to use instead
Mental model
Getting dressed: socks before shoes. Always do something whose prerequisites are all done.
Core operation
Kahn: queue in-degree-0 nodes, remove them, decrement neighbors. DFS: postorder reversed, three colors for cycles.
Complexity benefit
O(V + E) to order or detect a cycle.
Limitations
Undirected graphs need a different cycle test (parent check or DSU).
Alternative
DFS three-color for cycle detection; DP over the topological order for longest paths in a DAG.
Guided solveLC 207 and 210. Course Schedule I and IIFive questions, each with a reveal

Problem: 207Course ScheduleMedium. Answer each question on paper first, then reveal.

  1. 1
    Understand the problem

    Say in one sentence what is asked. Which constraint sets the time budget?

    Reveal step 1
    Problem decoding

    numCourses courses and pairs [a, b] meaning "b before a". Can all courses be finished (207)? If so, return an order (210).

    Input analysis

    Up to 2000 courses and 5000 pairs. Dependencies between items: a directed graph with edges b -> a.

  2. 2
    Brute force, then a pattern

    What is the simplest correct approach and what does it cost? Which pattern could beat it, and why does it apply?

    Reveal step 2
    Pattern discovery

    "Prerequisites" and "order" are the signals for topological sort. "Possible to finish" is "the graph has no directed cycle".

    Brute force

    Repeatedly scan all courses for one whose prerequisites are done: O(V * (V + E)).

  3. 3
    The key observation

    What single fact removes the repeated work? Trace a tiny input on paper until you see it.

    Reveal step 3

    Key idea. repeatedly take a course whose prerequisites are all done

    Key observation

    Track how many unmet prerequisites each course has (in-degree). Finishing a course decrements its dependents' counts, and any course that reaches zero becomes available. A queue of available courses makes each step O(1) amortized.

    Visualization

    The figure above: order 0, 1, 2, 3 (or 0, 2, 1, 3; both are valid).

  4. 4
    Build it

    Write the algorithm in three or four lines, then code it. Reveal after you have run one small input by hand.

    Reveal step 4
    Algorithm

    Build adjacency lists and in-degrees. Queue all in-degree-0 nodes. Pop a node, append it to the order, decrement its neighbors, and queue any that reach 0. If the order has all nodes, return it; otherwise a cycle blocked the rest.

    Java implementation
    Java
    // LC 210. Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly take a node with no remaining prerequisites.
// Edge [course, pre] means pre -> course.
static int[] findOrder(int numCourses, int[][] prerequisites) {
    List<List<Integer>> adj = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < numCourses; i++) adj.add(new ArrayList<>());
    int[] indegree = new int[numCourses];
    for (int[] p : prerequisites) {
        adj.get(p[1]).add(p[0]);
        indegree[p[0]]++;
    }
    Deque<Integer> ready = new ArrayDeque<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < numCourses; i++) if (indegree[i] == 0) ready.offer(i);
    int[] order = new int[numCourses];
    int done = 0;
    while (!ready.isEmpty()) {
        int u = ready.poll();
        order[done++] = u;
        for (int v : adj.get(u))
            if (--indegree[v] == 0) ready.offer(v);   // last prerequisite just finished
    }
    return done == numCourses ? order : new int[0];  // fewer than n -> a cycle blocked some nodes
}
    Dry run

    [[1,0],[0,1]]: both nodes have in-degree 1, the queue starts empty, 0 nodes are processed: cycle, return empty.

  5. 5
    Check it

    State time and space with a reason, name three inputs that could break the code, and say what this problem teaches beyond itself.

    Reveal step 5
    Complexity

    O(V + E) time and space.

    Edge cases

    No prerequisites (any order), self-dependency [a, a] (a cycle), duplicate pairs (in-degree counted twice and decremented twice; consistent), disconnected components (all start in the queue).

    Transfer lesson

    Kahn's order lets you do DP in dependency order: longest path in a DAG, propagate reachability (Course Schedule IV, LC 1462), resolve recipes from supplies (LC 2115). Peeling leaves layer by layer (Minimum Height Trees, LC 310) is the same idea on an undirected tree with degree 1 instead of in-degree 0.

DFS-based topological order. Reverse postorder: a node is finished only after everything it points to, so listing nodes in reverse finish order puts each before its dependents. Combine with three colors to detect cycles in the same pass.

Java
// Topological order by DFS: a node is added AFTER all its descendants (postorder);
// reversing the postorder puts every node before the nodes it points to.
static List<Integer> topoOrderDfs(List<List<Integer>> adj) {
    int n = adj.size();
    boolean[] seen = new boolean[n];
    Deque<Integer> order = new ArrayDeque<>();
    for (int u = 0; u < n; u++) if (!seen[u]) post(adj, u, seen, order);
    return new ArrayList<>(order);
}

private static void post(List<List<Integer>> adj, int u, boolean[] seen, Deque<Integer> order) {
    seen[u] = true;
    for (int v : adj.get(u)) if (!seen[v]) post(adj, v, seen, order);
    order.push(u);            // push to the front = reversed postorder
}

12.5Weighted shortest paths

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
743Network Delay TimeMedium

Stuck after 15 minutes? The guided solve in this lesson walks through this exact problem, one question at a time.

Show a hint
Plain Dijkstra; answer is the max distance
What it solves

Minimum total cost when edges have different non-negative weights: network delay, cheapest route, least effort.

Pattern cardDijkstra (weighted shortest path)
Signal
Minimum total cost, time, or effort over weighted edges; 'cheapest', 'fastest', 'least effort path'.
Required condition
All edge weights are non-negative, and the path cost never decreases as you extend a path.
Mental model, core operation, limits, and what to use instead
Mental model
Water flooding a pipe network: the closest junction fills first.
Core operation
Min-heap of (dist, node); pop the closest, skip if stale, relax its edges.
Complexity benefit
O((V + E) log V) single-source shortest paths.
Limitations
Negative edges break the 'finalized when popped' guarantee. Extra constraints (stop limits) need state expansion or Bellman-Ford.
Alternative
BFS when weights are equal; 0-1 BFS for weights 0/1; Bellman-Ford for negatives or k-edge limits; Floyd-Warshall for all pairs with small V.
Go deeper

Why Dijkstra works, and why it needs non-negative weights

The heap always pops the unfinalized node with the smallest tentative distance d. Any other path to that node would have to leave the finalized region through some node with tentative distance >= d, and with non-negative edges it can only get longer from there. So d is final. A negative edge breaks this: a longer-looking path could later become shorter.

Guided solveLC 743. Network Delay TimeFive questions, each with a reveal

Problem: 743Network Delay TimeMedium. Answer each question on paper first, then reveal.

  1. 1
    Understand the problem

    Say in one sentence what is asked. Which constraint sets the time budget?

    Reveal step 1
    Problem decoding

    A signal starts at node k and travels along directed weighted edges. How long until all nodes receive it? -1 if some never do.

    Input analysis

    Up to 100 nodes and 6000 edges, weights 0 to 100 (non-negative).

  2. 2
    Brute force, then a pattern

    What is the simplest correct approach and what does it cost? Which pattern could beat it, and why does it apply?

    Reveal step 2
    Pattern discovery

    "Time for a signal to reach each node" is the shortest path from k to each node, with weights: Dijkstra. All nodes receive it when the farthest one does: take the max.

    Brute force

    Bellman-Ford: relax all edges V - 1 times, O(V * E). Fine here, but Dijkstra is the expected answer.

  3. 3
    The key observation

    What single fact removes the repeated work? Trace a tiny input on paper until you see it.

    Reveal step 3

    Key idea. single-source shortest paths, answer is the largest distance

    Key observation

    Non-negative weights mean the closest unfinalized node can be finalized, so a min-heap processes nodes in order of distance.

    Visualization
    Pop Distance Relaxations Heap after
    A 0 B = 4, C = 1 (1, C), (4, B)
    C 1 B = min(4, 3) = 3, D = 6 (3, B), (4, B), (6, D)
    B 3 D = min(6, 4) = 4 (4, B), (4, D), (6, D)
    B 4 stale (4 > 3), skip (4, D), (6, D)
    D 4 none (6, D)
    D 6 stale, skip empty
  4. 4
    Build it

    Write the algorithm in three or four lines, then code it. Reveal after you have run one small input by hand.

    Reveal step 4
    Algorithm

    dist[k] = 0, heap of (dist, node). Pop; skip if stale; relax each outgoing edge, pushing improved distances. Answer: max over dist, or -1 if any is infinite.

    Java implementation
    Java
    // LC 743. Dijkstra with a min-heap of (distance, node) and lazy deletion.
// Requires non-negative weights.
static int networkDelayTime(int[][] times, int n, int k) {
    List<List<int[]>> adj = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) adj.add(new ArrayList<>());
    for (int[] t : times) adj.get(t[0]).add(new int[]{t[1], t[2]});   // u -> (v, w)

    int[] dist = new int[n + 1];
    Arrays.fill(dist, Integer.MAX_VALUE);
    dist[k] = 0;
    PriorityQueue<int[]> heap = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]));
    heap.offer(new int[]{0, k});
    while (!heap.isEmpty()) {
        int[] top = heap.poll();
        int d = top[0], u = top[1];
        if (d > dist[u]) continue;            // stale entry: a shorter path was already found
        for (int[] edge : adj.get(u)) {
            int v = edge[0], nd = d + edge[1];
            if (nd < dist[v]) {               // relax
                dist[v] = nd;
                heap.offer(new int[]{nd, v});
            }
        }
    }
    int answer = 0;
    for (int v = 1; v <= n; v++) {
        if (dist[v] == Integer.MAX_VALUE) return -1;
        answer = Math.max(answer, dist[v]);
    }
    return answer;
}
    Dry run

    The table above, using the figure's graph.

  5. 5
    Check it

    State time and space with a reason, name three inputs that could break the code, and say what this problem teaches beyond itself.

    Reveal step 5
    Complexity

    O((V + E) log V) with lazy deletion (the heap can hold up to E entries, and log E = O(log V)). Space O(V + E).

    Edge cases

    Unreachable nodes (-1), zero-weight edges (still fine), self-loops and parallel edges (relaxation handles them).

    Transfer lesson

    Change what "distance" means and keep the algorithm: max of edge weights on the path (Path With Minimum Effort, LC 1631; Swim in Rising Water, LC 778), product of probabilities with a max-heap (LC 1514), number of shortest paths (LC 1976, count ways when nd == dist[v]). This works whenever extending a path never makes its cost better.

Go deeper

Variants and the other shortest-path tools

0-1 BFS. When weights are only 0 or 1, a deque replaces the heap: 0-cost moves go to the front, 1-cost moves to the back. O(V + E).

Java
// LC 2290. Edge cost 0 (empty cell) or 1 (obstacle). Deque: cost-0 moves go to the front,
// cost-1 moves to the back, so the deque stays sorted by distance like Dijkstra's heap.
static int minimumObstacles(int[][] grid) {
    int rows = grid.length, cols = grid[0].length;
    int[][] dist = new int[rows][cols];
    for (int[] row : dist) Arrays.fill(row, Integer.MAX_VALUE);
    Deque<int[]> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();
    dist[0][0] = 0;
    dq.offerFirst(new int[]{0, 0});
    int[][] dirs = {{1, 0}, {-1, 0}, {0, 1}, {0, -1}};
    while (!dq.isEmpty()) {
        int[] cell = dq.pollFirst();
        int r = cell[0], c = cell[1];
        for (int[] d : dirs) {
            int nr = r + d[0], nc = c + d[1];
            if (nr < 0 || nc < 0 || nr >= rows || nc >= cols) continue;
            int nd = dist[r][c] + grid[nr][nc];
            if (nd < dist[nr][nc]) {
                dist[nr][nc] = nd;
                if (grid[nr][nc] == 0) dq.offerFirst(new int[]{nr, nc});
                else dq.offerLast(new int[]{nr, nc});
            }
        }
    }
    return dist[rows - 1][cols - 1];
}

Bellman-Ford with an edge limit. "At most k stops" (LC 787) breaks Dijkstra, because the cheapest path to a node may use too many edges, and a pricier path with fewer edges might be the one that reaches the destination in time. Run k + 1 rounds of relaxing all edges, each round reading only the previous round's distances, so a round can extend any path by at most one edge.

Java
// LC 787. At most k stops = at most k + 1 edges. Run k + 1 relaxation rounds,
// each reading only the PREVIOUS round's distances.
static int findCheapestPrice(int n, int[][] flights, int src, int dst, int k) {
    int[] dist = new int[n];
    Arrays.fill(dist, Integer.MAX_VALUE);
    dist[src] = 0;
    for (int round = 0; round <= k; round++) {
        int[] next = dist.clone();                     // snapshot prevents chaining edges in one round
        for (int[] f : flights) {
            int u = f[0], v = f[1], price = f[2];
            if (dist[u] != Integer.MAX_VALUE && dist[u] + price < next[v]) next[v] = dist[u] + price;
        }
        dist = next;
    }
    return dist[dst] == Integer.MAX_VALUE ? -1 : dist[dst];
}

Floyd-Warshall gives all-pairs shortest paths in O(V^3) with three nested loops. Use it when V is at most a few hundred and you need distances between many pairs.

Java
// LC 1334. All-pairs shortest paths for small n (here n <= 100): O(n^3).
// After processing k, dist[i][j] is the shortest path using only intermediates 0..k.
static int findTheCity(int n, int[][] edges, int threshold) {
    int INF = 1_000_000_000;
    int[][] dist = new int[n][n];
    for (int[] row : dist) Arrays.fill(row, INF);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) dist[i][i] = 0;
    for (int[] e : edges) { dist[e[0]][e[1]] = e[2]; dist[e[1]][e[0]] = e[2]; }
    for (int k = 0; k < n; k++)                    // k must be the OUTER loop
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
            for (int j = 0; j < n; j++)
                if (dist[i][k] + dist[k][j] < dist[i][j]) dist[i][j] = dist[i][k] + dist[k][j];
    int best = -1, fewest = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        int reach = 0;
        for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) if (i != j && dist[i][j] <= threshold) reach++;
        if (reach <= fewest) { fewest = reach; best = i; }   // ties go to the larger index
    }
    return best;
}
Situation Tool Cost
Unweighted BFS O(V + E)
Weights 0 or 1 0-1 BFS O(V + E)
Non-negative weights, one source Dijkstra O((V + E) log V)
Edge-count limit, or negative weights (no negative cycles) Bellman-Ford O(V * E) or O(k * E)
All pairs, small V Floyd-Warshall O(V^3)
DAG, any weights DP in topological order O(V + E)

12.6Union-Find and minimum spanning trees

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
684Redundant ConnectionMedium

Any correct brute force counts. Note where you got stuck: the lesson below is about exactly that.

Show a hint
The first edge joining an already-connected pair
What it solves

Grouping items as connections arrive, answering "are these two in the same group?", counting groups, detecting the edge that creates a cycle, and building minimum spanning trees.

Pattern cardUnion-Find (disjoint set union)
Signal
Grouping by connections that arrive over time, 'are A and B connected', counting components, redundant edge, Kruskal.
Required condition
Only unions happen (no edge deletions). Undirected relationships.
Mental model, core operation, limits, and what to use instead
Mental model
Clubs merging: each club has a president; to compare two people, compare their presidents.
Core operation
find with path compression, union by size; union returns false if already connected.
Complexity benefit
Near O(1) amortized per operation versus re-running BFS after each edge.
Limitations
No deletions; no paths; directed reachability is not supported.
Alternative
BFS/DFS when the graph is static and queried once.
Java
// Disjoint Set Union with path compression and union by size.
// Both together make find/union effectively O(1) amortized (inverse Ackermann).
static class UnionFind {
    private final int[] parent, size;
    private int components;

    UnionFind(int n) {
        parent = new int[n];
        size = new int[n];
        components = n;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { parent[i] = i; size[i] = 1; }
    }

    int find(int x) {
        while (parent[x] != x) {
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];   // path halving: point to grandparent
            x = parent[x];
        }
        return x;
    }

    boolean union(int a, int b) {            // false if already connected
        int ra = find(a), rb = find(b);
        if (ra == rb) return false;
        if (size[ra] < size[rb]) { int t = ra; ra = rb; rb = t; }
        parent[rb] = ra;                     // attach the smaller tree under the larger
        size[ra] += size[rb];
        components--;
        return true;
    }

    int components() { return components; }
}

// LC 684. The first edge whose endpoints are already connected creates the cycle.
static int[] findRedundantConnection(int[][] edges) {
    UnionFind uf = new UnionFind(edges.length + 1);   // nodes are 1..n
    for (int[] e : edges)
        if (!uf.union(e[0], e[1])) return e;
    return new int[0];
}

Why both optimizations. Union by size keeps trees shallow (height O(log n) on its own); path compression flattens them further as they are used. Together, any sequence of m operations takes O(m * alpha(n)), where alpha is the inverse Ackermann function, at most 4 for any realistic n. Say "effectively constant amortized time".

Union-Find vs BFS/DFS. For a fixed graph queried once, BFS/DFS is just as good. Union-Find wins when edges arrive over time with connectivity questions in between, when you need to merge groups by a shared key (Accounts Merge, LC 721), or inside Kruskal.

Go deeper

Minimum spanning tree

A spanning tree connects all V nodes with V - 1 edges; the minimum one has the smallest total weight. The cut property makes greedy correct: for any split of the nodes into two sides, the cheapest edge crossing the split belongs to some MST.

Kruskal Prim
Idea Sort edges; add the cheapest that joins two components (Union-Find) Grow one tree; repeatedly add the cheapest edge leaving it
Cost O(E log E) O(E log V) with a heap; O(V^2) with arrays (best for dense graphs)
Best for Sparse graphs, edges given as a list Dense or complete graphs (all pairs of points)
Java
// LC 1584 with Kruskal: sort all edges, add the cheapest that joins two components.
static int minCostConnectPointsKruskal(int[][] points) {
    int n = points.length;
    List<int[]> edges = new ArrayList<>();                 // {cost, i, j}
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++)
            edges.add(new int[]{manhattan(points, i, j), i, j});
    edges.sort((a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]));
    UnionFind uf = new UnionFind(n);
    int total = 0, used = 0;
    for (int[] e : edges) {
        if (uf.union(e[1], e[2])) {
            total += e[0];
            if (++used == n - 1) break;                    // a tree has n - 1 edges
        }
    }
    return total;
}

// LC 1584 with Prim (O(n^2), best for dense graphs): grow one tree,
// always attaching the closest outside point.
static int minCostConnectPointsPrim(int[][] points) {
    int n = points.length, total = 0;
    int[] best = new int[n];                    // cheapest edge from the tree to each point
    Arrays.fill(best, Integer.MAX_VALUE);
    boolean[] inTree = new boolean[n];
    best[0] = 0;
    for (int added = 0; added < n; added++) {
        int u = -1;
        for (int v = 0; v < n; v++)
            if (!inTree[v] && (u == -1 || best[v] < best[u])) u = v;
        inTree[u] = true;
        total += best[u];
        for (int v = 0; v < n; v++)
            if (!inTree[v]) best[v] = Math.min(best[v], manhattan(points, u, v));
    }
    return total;
}

private static int manhattan(int[][] p, int i, int j) {
    return Math.abs(p[i][0] - p[j][0]) + Math.abs(p[i][1] - p[j][1]);
}

For Min Cost to Connect All Points (LC 1584) the graph is complete (about n^2 / 2 edges), so the O(V^2) Prim avoids building and sorting all edges.

12.8Choosing the algorithm

Try it first3 minutes, before you read on

Module 14: Dynamic programming

Dynamic programming is recursion that remembers. If a brute-force recursion solves the same subproblem many times, store each answer once and reuse it. Every DP in this module is derived with the same six steps; no transition is memorized.

14.1What DP is and when it applies

Try it first2 minutes, before you read on

Plain recursive fib(40) (two calls per call) makes about how many calls? How many distinct values does it actually compute?

Reveal the answer

About 3.3 * 10^8 calls (331,160,281). There are only 41 distinct values, fib(0) to fib(40). Caching each one the first time turns exponential work into O(n): that gap is what dynamic programming removes.

What it solves

Counting ways, minimizing or maximizing cost, and yes/no feasibility, where the answer is built from a sequence of decisions and later decisions depend on earlier ones.

Intuition

Climbing a staircase where you can take 1 or 2 steps. The number of ways to reach step 10 is (ways to reach step 9) + (ways to reach step 8), because your last move came from one of them. You do not need to know how anyone got to step 9; you only need how many ways there are. Compute each step's count once, from the bottom up.

Pattern cardDynamic programming
Signal
Count the ways, min/max cost, 'is it possible', with choices at each step where later choices depend on earlier ones. A brute-force recursion re-solves the same subproblems.
Required condition
Optimal substructure (the best answer is built from best sub-answers) and overlapping subproblems.
Mental model, core operation, limits, and what to use instead
Mental model
Filling a table where every cell is a smaller version of the question, answered once and reused.
Core operation
Define state, write the transition from the last decision, set base cases, fill in dependency order.
Complexity benefit
Exponential recursion becomes polynomial: number of states times work per state.
Limitations
Needs a small state; if you must list every answer, output size dominates (backtracking).
Alternative
Greedy when a choice is provably safe; backtracking when you need all solutions; graph shortest path when states form a weighted graph.
Go deeper

The two properties

  • Optimal substructure: the best answer for a problem can be built from the best answers of smaller subproblems. (Shortest path: the best route to B through A uses the best route to A.)
  • Overlapping subproblems: the recursion reaches the same subproblem along many different paths. Without overlap, plain recursion or divide and conquer is enough.

How to detect overlap quickly: write the brute-force recursion's signature, e.g. best(i) or ways(i, j). If the result depends only on those arguments, and the number of distinct argument values is small (n, n^2, n * W) while the number of calls is exponential, it is DP.

Go deeper

Recognizing a DP problem

Signal Example
"Number of ways", often "modulo 10^9 + 7" Climbing Stairs, Decode Ways, Unique Paths
"Minimum / maximum cost, length, profit" with choices at each step House Robber, Coin Change, Edit Distance
"Is it possible" where choices interact Word Break, Partition Equal Subset Sum
Two strings or sequences compared position by position LCS, Edit Distance, Interleaving String
Greedy has a counterexample Coin change with
Backtracking would explore many paths that end in the same state Word Break, Target Sum

14.2The six-step derivation process

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
198House RobberMedium

Stuck after 15 minutes? The guided solve in this lesson walks through this exact problem, one question at a time.

Show a hint
Take or skip at each house

Use these steps for every DP problem in this module. Write the answers down before coding.

Step Question House Robber (LC 198)
1. State What subproblem does one value answer? Say it in words. best(i) = most money from houses i..n-1
2. Transition What is the last (or first) decision, and what is left after it? Rob house i (then skip i + 1) or skip it: best(i) = max(best(i+1), nums[i] + best(i+2))
3. Base cases Where does the recursion stop? No houses left: best(n) = best(n+1) = 0
4. Answer Which state is the original question? best(0)
5. Order Which states must be computed before which? best(i) needs i+1 and i+2: fill from n-1 down to 0
6. Space Which previous values are still needed? Only the next two: two variables

Finding the transition is the step that feels like magic, and it is not. Ask: "Consider an optimal solution. What happened at the last (or first) position? What are all the possibilities, and what subproblem remains in each case?" Each possibility becomes one term in the max, min, sum, or OR.

Choosing the state. The state must contain everything the future depends on. If two partial solutions with the same state could have different best futures, the state is missing a variable (see the multi-state section below).

Go deeper

Memoization vs tabulation

Memoization (top-down) Tabulation (bottom-up)
How Recursive function + cache Loops filling a table in dependency order
Computes Only the states actually reached Every state
Order Automatic (recursion handles it) You must choose it (step 5)
Risk Stack depth for large n Getting the loop order wrong
Space optimization Hard Natural: keep only the rows or cells still read
Best for Deriving and explaining; sparse state spaces Final versions; tight memory

In an interview, deriving with memoization and then converting is a strong, communicative path. Either form is a complete answer.

Guided solveLC 198. House Robber, all four formsFive questions, each with a reveal

Problem: 198House RobberMedium. Answer each question on paper first, then reveal.

  1. 1
    Understand the problem

    Say in one sentence what is asked. Which constraint sets the time budget?

    Reveal step 1
    Problem decoding

    Houses in a row with money; you cannot rob two adjacent houses. Maximize the total.

    Input analysis

    Up to 100 houses, values up to 400. Even O(n^2) would pass, but the natural DP is O(n).

  2. 2
    Brute force, then a pattern

    What is the simplest correct approach and what does it cost? Which pattern could beat it, and why does it apply?

    Reveal step 2
    Pattern discovery

    A sequence of take/skip decisions where taking constrains the next decision. Greedy fails: on [2, 1, 1, 2], taking every other house gives 3 either way, but houses 0 and 3 give 4. The subproblem "best from house i onward" repeats along many decision paths.

    Brute force

    Recursion over take/skip: O(2^n), because best(i + 2) is reached both by "take i" and by "skip i, skip i + 1".

  3. 3
    The key observation

    What single fact removes the repeated work? Trace a tiny input on paper until you see it.

    Reveal step 3

    Key idea. rob this house and skip the next, or skip this house

    Key observation

    best(i) depends only on i. There are n distinct states and two choices per state: O(n).

    Visualization
  4. 4
    Build it

    Write the algorithm in three or four lines, then code it. Reveal after you have run one small input by hand.

    Reveal step 4
    Algorithm

    State, transition, base cases, and order from the table above.

    Java implementation

    Memoized recursion, then the table, then two variables:

    Java
    // LC 198, step 1: recursion that follows the decision directly.
// best(i) = max money from houses i..n-1
//         = max(skip i -> best(i + 1), rob i -> nums[i] + best(i + 2))
static int robMemo(int[] nums) {
    int[] memo = new int[nums.length];
    Arrays.fill(memo, -1);                       // -1 = not computed (answers are >= 0)
    return best(nums, 0, memo);
}

private static int best(int[] nums, int i, int[] memo) {
    if (i >= nums.length) return 0;              // base case: no houses left
    if (memo[i] != -1) return memo[i];
    int skip = best(nums, i + 1, memo);
    int rob = nums[i] + best(nums, i + 2, memo);
    return memo[i] = Math.max(skip, rob);
}
    Java
    // Step 2: the same recurrence as a table. dp[i] depends on dp[i+1] and dp[i+2],
// so fill i from right to left. dp has 2 extra slots for the base cases.
static int robTab(int[] nums) {
    int n = nums.length;
    int[] dp = new int[n + 2];                   // dp[n] = dp[n+1] = 0
    for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--)
        dp[i] = Math.max(dp[i + 1], nums[i] + dp[i + 2]);
    return dp[0];
}

// Step 3: only two later values are ever read, so keep two variables.
static int robO1(int[] nums) {
    int next1 = 0, next2 = 0;                    // dp[i+1], dp[i+2]
    for (int i = nums.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        int cur = Math.max(next1, nums[i] + next2);
        next2 = next1;
        next1 = cur;
    }
    return next1;
}
    Dry run

    The figure: dp[4] = 1, dp[3] = max(1, 3) = 3, dp[2] = max(3, 9 + 1) = 10, dp[1] = max(10, 7 + 3) = 10, dp[0] = max(10, 2 + 10) = 12.

  5. 5
    Check it

    State time and space with a reason, name three inputs that could break the code, and say what this problem teaches beyond itself.

    Reveal step 5
    Complexity

    O(n) time. Memo and table: O(n) space; the final version O(1).

    Edge cases

    Empty array (0), one house, two houses, all zeros.

    Transfer lesson

    "Take this and jump, or skip this" is the shape of Delete and Earn (LC 740, after bucketing values), House Robber II (LC 213, run twice excluding the first or the last house), and Solving Questions With Brainpower (LC 2140, the jump length varies). The circular variant shows a general trick: break a cycle by fixing one decision and solving the linear problem for each case.

14.3One-dimensional and linear DP

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
91Decode WaysMedium

Any correct brute force counts. Note where you got stuck: the lesson below is about exactly that.

Show a hint
One-digit and two-digit transitions with zero rules
State shape

dp[i] = the answer for a prefix (or suffix) of length i, or "ending exactly at i". The transition looks back a fixed number of steps or over all earlier positions.

Problem State Transition
Climbing Stairs (LC 70) ways to reach step i dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]
Min Cost Climbing Stairs (LC 746) cheapest cost to stand on step i min(dp[i-1] + cost[i-1], dp[i-2] + cost[i-2])
Decode Ways (LC 91) ways to decode s[0..i) dp[i-1] if the last digit is valid, plus dp[i-2] if the last two are 10..26
Word Break (LC 139) can s[0..i) be segmented OR over j of dp[j] && word(s[j..i))
Minimum Cost For Tickets (LC 983) cheapest cover of days up to i min over 1-, 7-, 30-day passes ending today
Java
// LC 91. dp[i] = ways to decode s[0..i). Last step used one digit or two digits.
static int numDecodings(String s) {
    int n = s.length();
    int[] dp = new int[n + 1];
    dp[0] = 1;                                           // empty prefix: one way (decode nothing)
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        char one = s.charAt(i - 1);
        if (one != '0') dp[i] += dp[i - 1];              // s[i-1] alone is 1..9
        if (i >= 2) {
            int two = (s.charAt(i - 2) - '0') * 10 + (one - '0');
            if (two >= 10 && two <= 26) dp[i] += dp[i - 2];   // "10".."26"; "05" is not valid
        }
    }
    return dp[n];
}

Decode Ways shows how base cases encode meaning: dp[0] = 1 says "there is one way to decode an empty prefix", which makes the first real step add correctly. Zeros are the trap: "06" has no decodings, and "10" only one.

Java
// LC 139. dp[i] = s[0..i) can be segmented. Check every word that could end at i.
static boolean wordBreak(String s, List<String> wordDict) {
    Set<String> words = new HashSet<>(wordDict);
    boolean[] dp = new boolean[s.length() + 1];
    dp[0] = true;                                    // empty prefix
    for (int i = 1; i <= s.length(); i++)
        for (int j = 0; j < i && !dp[i]; j++)
            if (dp[j] && words.contains(s.substring(j, i))) dp[i] = true;
    return dp[s.length()];
}

Common mistakes

  • Base case off by one (dp[0] meaning "empty prefix" vs "first element").
  • Forgetting a case in the transition (Decode Ways: a zero can only be the second digit of 10 or 20).
  • Using greedy reasoning in a DP problem ("just pick the bigger neighbor").

14.4Grid and path DP

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
62Unique PathsMedium

Any correct brute force counts. Note where you got stuck: the lesson below is about exactly that.

Show a hint
Paths into a cell = from top + from left
State shape

dp[r][c] = the answer for reaching (or leaving) cell (r, c). Moves are usually right/down, so each cell depends on its top and left neighbors.

Java
// LC 62. dp[c] in the current row = paths from top (old dp[c]) + from left (dp[c - 1]).
static int uniquePaths(int m, int n) {
    int[] dp = new int[n];
    Arrays.fill(dp, 1);                          // first row: one way to each cell
    for (int r = 1; r < m; r++)
        for (int c = 1; c < n; c++)
            dp[c] += dp[c - 1];                  // dp[c] (top) + dp[c - 1] (left)
    return dp[n - 1];
}

Rolling one row. Because row r only reads row r - 1 and the current row, a single 1D array works: before updating, dp[c] still holds the value from the row above, and dp[c - 1] already holds the current row's value to the left.

Problem Twist
Unique Paths II (LC 63) Obstacle cells are 0; the first row and column stop at the first obstacle
Minimum Path Sum (LC 64) grid[r][c] + min(top, left)
Triangle (LC 120) Bottom-up removes boundary checks: dp[c] = tri[r][c] + min(dp[c], dp[c+1])
Maximal Square (LC 221) 1 + min(top, left, diagonal) = side of the largest square ending here
Dungeon Game (LC 174) Fill from the destination backward: the needed health depends on the future, not the past
Cherry Pickup II (LC 1463) Two robots moving down together: state (row, col1, col2)

Direction matters. Dungeon Game cannot be solved forward because the minimum health needed at a cell depends on what comes after it. When the constraint is about the future, define the state as "from here to the end" and fill backward.

14.5The knapsack family: subset sum, partition, coin change

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
322Coin ChangeMedium

Stuck after 15 minutes? The guided solve in this lesson walks through this exact problem, one question at a time.

Show a hint
Unbounded knapsack for a minimum count
State shape

dp[c] = the best value (or feasibility, or count) using capacity c, after considering some prefix of the items. Each item is a decision: take it or not.

Go deeper

0/1 vs unbounded

0/1 knapsack (each item once) Unbounded (items reusable)
Transition dp[c] = best(dp[c], dp[c - w] + v) using the dp from before this item same, using the dp including this item
1D loop over capacity Downward, so dp[c - w] is still the old value Upward, so dp[c - w] may already include this item
Problems Partition Equal Subset Sum, Target Sum, Ones and Zeroes, Last Stone Weight II Coin Change, Coin Change II, Perfect Squares, Combination Sum IV
Guided solveLC 416. Partition Equal Subset SumFive questions, each with a reveal

Problem: 416Partition Equal Subset SumMedium. Answer each question on paper first, then reveal.

  1. 1
    Understand the problem

    Say in one sentence what is asked. Which constraint sets the time budget?

    Reveal step 1
    Problem decoding

    Can the array be split into two subsets with equal sums?

    Input analysis

    Up to 200 numbers, each up to 100: the total is at most 20,000, so a table indexed by sums is small.

  2. 2
    Brute force, then a pattern

    What is the simplest correct approach and what does it cost? Which pattern could beat it, and why does it apply?

    Reveal step 2
    Pattern discovery

    Two equal halves means one subset sums to total / 2. "Choose a subset hitting an exact sum" is 0/1 knapsack feasibility.

    Brute force

    All 2^n subsets: hopeless for n = 200.

  3. 3
    The key observation

    What single fact removes the repeated work? Trace a tiny input on paper until you see it.

    Reveal step 3

    Key idea. find a subset that sums to half the total

    Key observation

    Whether sum s is reachable using the first i numbers depends only on (i, s). Sums are bounded by 10,000, so the state space is 200 x 10,000.

    Visualization

    See the downward-iteration figure above.

  4. 4
    Build it

    Write the algorithm in three or four lines, then code it. Reveal after you have run one small input by hand.

    Reveal step 4
    Algorithm

    If the total is odd, return false. reachable[0] = true. For each number x, for s from target down to x: reachable[s] |= reachable[s - x]. Answer reachable[target].

    Java implementation
    Java
    // LC 416. 0/1 knapsack: can a subset reach total / 2?
// Iterate capacity DOWNWARD so each number is used at most once.
static boolean canPartition(int[] nums) {
    int total = 0;
    for (int x : nums) total += x;
    if (total % 2 != 0) return false;
    int target = total / 2;
    boolean[] reachable = new boolean[target + 1];
    reachable[0] = true;
    for (int x : nums)
        for (int s = target; s >= x; s--)        // downward: reachable[s - x] is from before x
            reachable[s] = reachable[s] || reachable[s - x];
    return reachable[target];
}
    Dry run

    [1, 5, 11, 5], target 11: after 1: {0, 1}; after 5: {0, 1, 5, 6}; after 11: {0, 1, 5, 6, 11}: done (true). For [1, 2, 5] (target 4), an upward loop would reuse the 2 and wrongly mark 4 as reachable; the correct answer is false, and the test harness checks exactly this case.

  5. 5
    Check it

    State time and space with a reason, name three inputs that could break the code, and say what this problem teaches beyond itself.

    Reveal step 5
    Complexity

    O(n * target) time, O(target) space.

    Edge cases

    Odd total, a single element larger than the target, all equal elements.

    Transfer lesson

    Target Sum (LC 494) becomes "count subsets with sum (total + target) / 2" after algebra on the signs. Last Stone Weight II (LC 1049) becomes "the reachable sum closest to total / 2". Recognizing a disguised subset sum is the main skill in this family.

Guided solveLC 322. Coin ChangeFive questions, each with a reveal

Problem: 322Coin ChangeMedium. Answer each question on paper first, then reveal.

  1. 1
    Understand the problem

    Say in one sentence what is asked. Which constraint sets the time budget?

    Reveal step 1
    Problem decoding

    Fewest coins (unlimited supply of each denomination) that sum to amount, or -1.

    Input analysis

    Up to 12 coin types, amount up to 10^4.

  2. 2
    Brute force, then a pattern

    What is the simplest correct approach and what does it cost? Which pattern could beat it, and why does it apply?

    Reveal step 2
    Pattern discovery

    Minimize a count over choices that repeat: greedy fails for {1, 3, 4}, so DP over amounts.

    Brute force

    Try every coin as the first choice, recurse on the remainder: exponential, with the same remainders reached many times.

  3. 3
    The key observation

    What single fact removes the repeated work? Trace a tiny input on paper until you see it.

    Reveal step 3

    Key idea. the last coin used leaves a smaller amount

    Key observation

    If the last coin in an optimal solution is c, the rest is an optimal solution for amount - c. So dp[a] = 1 + min over coins of dp[a - c].

    Visualization
  4. 4
    Build it

    Write the algorithm in three or four lines, then code it. Reveal after you have run one small input by hand.

    Reveal step 4
    Algorithm

    dp[0] = 0, others "infinity" (amount + 1 is enough). For a from 1 up: try each coin that fits. Answer dp[amount], or -1 if still infinity.

    Java implementation
    Java
    // LC 322. dp[a] = fewest coins to make amount a. Unbounded: each coin reusable.
static int coinChange(int[] coins, int amount) {
    int INF = amount + 1;                        // more coins than could ever be needed
    int[] dp = new int[amount + 1];
    Arrays.fill(dp, INF);
    dp[0] = 0;
    for (int a = 1; a <= amount; a++)
        for (int coin : coins)
            if (coin <= a) dp[a] = Math.min(dp[a], dp[a - coin] + 1);   // last coin used = coin
    return dp[amount] >= INF ? -1 : dp[amount];
}

// LC 518. Number of COMBINATIONS: coins outer loop, so each combination is built
// in one canonical coin order and counted once.
static int change(int amount, int[] coins) {
    int[] ways = new int[amount + 1];
    ways[0] = 1;
    for (int coin : coins)
        for (int a = coin; a <= amount; a++)     // ascending: the same coin may be reused
            ways[a] += ways[a - coin];
    return ways[amount];
}
    Dry run

    The figure. Note how dp[3] = 2 (2 + 1) and dp[6] = 2 (5 + 1) feed later amounts.

  5. 5
    Check it

    State time and space with a reason, name three inputs that could break the code, and say what this problem teaches beyond itself.

    Reveal step 5
    Complexity

    O(amount * coins) time, O(amount) space.

    Edge cases

    Amount 0 (0 coins), unreachable amounts (stay at infinity), using Integer.MAX_VALUE as infinity and then adding 1 (overflow: hence amount + 1).

    Transfer lesson

    Loop order decides what is counted. For the number of combinations (LC 518), put coins in the outer loop: each combination is built in one fixed coin order and counted once. For the number of ordered sequences (LC 377), put the amount in the outer loop: every order is counted. This is the most common silent bug in counting DPs.

14.6Longest increasing subsequence family

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
300Longest Increasing SubsequenceMedium

Any correct brute force counts. Note where you got stuck: the lesson below is about exactly that.

Show a hint
O(n^2) dp, then patience sorting O(n log n)
State shape

dp[i] = the best answer for a subsequence ending at index i. The transition looks at every earlier j that can precede i.

Java
// LC 300, O(n^2): dp[i] = length of the longest increasing subsequence ENDING at i.
static int lengthOfLISQuadratic(int[] nums) {
    int[] dp = new int[nums.length];
    int best = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        dp[i] = 1;
        for (int j = 0; j < i; j++)
            if (nums[j] < nums[i]) dp[i] = Math.max(dp[i], dp[j] + 1);
        best = Math.max(best, dp[i]);
    }
    return best;
}

// O(n log n): tails[len] = smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length len + 1.
// tails is sorted, so each number finds its slot by binary search.
static int lengthOfLIS(int[] nums) {
    int[] tails = new int[nums.length];
    int size = 0;
    for (int x : nums) {
        int lo = 0, hi = size;                   // lower bound of x in tails[0..size)
        while (lo < hi) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
            if (tails[mid] >= x) hi = mid;
            else lo = mid + 1;
        }
        tails[lo] = x;                           // replace, or extend when lo == size
        if (lo == size) size++;
    }
    return size;                                 // tails itself is NOT a valid subsequence
}
Go deeper

From O(n^2) to O(n log n)

Keep tails[k] = the smallest possible last value of an increasing subsequence of length k + 1. tails is always sorted, so each new number finds its position by binary search: it either extends the longest run or lowers some tail, which can only help future extensions.

Go deeper

Reconstructing the sequence

To return the subsequence itself, record parent[i] = the j that gave dp[i] its value, then walk back from the best ending index. The same idea reconstructs any DP: store the choice that produced each state, or recompute it by comparing neighbors.

Java
// Reconstruct one LIS: remember, for each i, which j it extended (parent[i]).
static List<Integer> lisSequence(int[] nums) {
    int n = nums.length;
    int[] len = new int[n], parent = new int[n];
    int bestEnd = -1;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        len[i] = 1;
        parent[i] = -1;
        for (int j = 0; j < i; j++)
            if (nums[j] < nums[i] && len[j] + 1 > len[i]) { len[i] = len[j] + 1; parent[i] = j; }
        if (bestEnd == -1 || len[i] > len[bestEnd]) bestEnd = i;
    }
    LinkedList<Integer> seq = new LinkedList<>();
    for (int i = bestEnd; i != -1; i = parent[i]) seq.addFirst(nums[i]);   // walk back
    return seq;
}
Problem Twist
Number of LIS (LC 673) Track a count per index alongside the length
Largest Divisible Subset (LC 368) Sort, then "divides" replaces "less than"; reconstruct with parents
Longest String Chain (LC 1048) Sort by length; predecessors found by deleting one character, looked up in a map
Russian Doll Envelopes (LC 354) Sort width ascending and height descending, then LIS on heights in O(n log n)
Longest Arithmetic Subsequence (LC 1027) State (i, difference): one map per index

14.7Two-sequence and string DP

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
1143Longest Common SubsequenceMedium

Stuck after 15 minutes? The guided solve in this lesson walks through this exact problem, one question at a time.

Show a hint
dp[i][j] over prefixes; match vs skip one side
State shape

dp[i][j] = the answer for the prefixes a[0..i) and b[0..j). Row 0 and column 0 are the empty prefixes. The transition considers the last characters a[i-1] and b[j-1]: match them, or drop one of them.

Guided solveLC 1143. Longest Common SubsequenceFive questions, each with a reveal

Problem: 1143Longest Common SubsequenceMedium. Answer each question on paper first, then reveal.

  1. 1
    Understand the problem

    Say in one sentence what is asked. Which constraint sets the time budget?

    Reveal step 1
    Problem decoding

    Length of the longest sequence that appears (not necessarily contiguously) in both strings.

    Input analysis

    Lengths up to 1000 each: a 1001 x 1001 table (10^6 cells) is fine.

  2. 2
    Brute force, then a pattern

    What is the simplest correct approach and what does it cost? Which pattern could beat it, and why does it apply?

    Reveal step 2
    Pattern discovery

    Two sequences compared position by position, with "skip a character" choices: two-sequence DP.

    Brute force

    All subsequences of one string checked against the other: O(2^m * n).

  3. 3
    The key observation

    What single fact removes the repeated work? Trace a tiny input on paper until you see it.

    Reveal step 3

    Key idea. compare the last characters of the two prefixes

    Key observation

    Look at the last characters of the prefixes. If they match, some LCS uses them both, leaving dp[i-1][j-1]. If not, at least one of them is unused: the answer is the better of dropping a[i-1] or dropping b[j-1].

    Visualization
  4. 4
    Build it

    Write the algorithm in three or four lines, then code it. Reveal after you have run one small input by hand.

    Reveal step 4
    Algorithm

    Table of size (m + 1) x (n + 1), zeros on the borders. Fill row by row with the transition above. Answer dp[m][n].

    Java implementation
    Java
    // LC 1143. dp[i][j] = LCS of text1[0..i) and text2[0..j).
static int longestCommonSubsequence(String a, String b) {
    int m = a.length(), n = b.length();
    int[][] dp = new int[m + 1][n + 1];          // row 0 and col 0 = empty prefix = 0
    for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++)
        for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++)
            dp[i][j] = (a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1))
                     ? dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1                      // use the matching pair
                     : Math.max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1]);     // drop one character
    return dp[m][n];
}

// Reconstruction: walk back from dp[m][n] following the choice that produced each cell.
static String lcsString(String a, String b) {
    int m = a.length(), n = b.length();
    int[][] dp = new int[m + 1][n + 1];
    for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++)
        for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++)
            dp[i][j] = (a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1)) ? dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1
                                                            : Math.max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1]);
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
    int i = m, j = n;
    while (i > 0 && j > 0) {
        if (a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1)) { sb.append(a.charAt(i - 1)); i--; j--; }
        else if (dp[i - 1][j] >= dp[i][j - 1]) i--;
        else j--;
    }
    return sb.reverse().toString();
}
    Dry run

    In the figure, row c and column c meet with a match: dp = dp[upper-left] + 1 = 2. The walk back moves diagonally on matches (green) and toward the larger neighbor otherwise.

  5. 5
    Check it

    State time and space with a reason, name three inputs that could break the code, and say what this problem teaches beyond itself.

    Reveal step 5
    Complexity

    O(m * n) time and space. Space can drop to O(min(m, n)) with two rows (or one row plus a saved diagonal), but then reconstruction needs the full table.

    Edge cases

    An empty string (0), identical strings (their length), no common characters (0).

    Transfer lesson

    Delete Operation for Two Strings (LC 583) is m + n - 2 * LCS. Shortest Common Supersequence (LC 1092) is the LCS walk-back that also emits the unmatched characters. Longest Palindromic Subsequence (LC 516) is LCS of a string with its reverse, or an interval DP on (i, j).

Go deeper

Edit distance: three moves, three neighbors

Java
// LC 72. dp[i][j] = edits to turn word1[0..i) into word2[0..j).
static int minDistance(String w1, String w2) {
    int m = w1.length(), n = w2.length();
    int[][] dp = new int[m + 1][n + 1];
    for (int i = 0; i <= m; i++) dp[i][0] = i;    // delete all i characters
    for (int j = 0; j <= n; j++) dp[0][j] = j;    // insert all j characters
    for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++)
        for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) {
            if (w1.charAt(i - 1) == w2.charAt(j - 1)) dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1];
            else dp[i][j] = 1 + Math.min(dp[i - 1][j - 1],             // replace
                                Math.min(dp[i - 1][j],                  // delete from w1
                                         dp[i][j - 1]));                // insert into w1
        }
    return dp[m][n];
}

With dp[i][j] = edits to turn w1[0..i) into w2[0..j): if the last characters match, no edit is needed (dp[i-1][j-1]). Otherwise the last operation was a replace (dp[i-1][j-1] + 1), a delete from w1 (dp[i-1][j] + 1), or an insert into w1 (dp[i][j-1] + 1). The base cases are the cost of deleting or inserting everything.

14.8Multiple state variables: state machines and intervals

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
309Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with CooldownMedium

Any correct brute force counts. Note where you got stuck: the lesson below is about exactly that.

Show a hint
Add a cooldown state and draw the state machine

When one index is not enough. If two partial solutions with the same index can have different best futures, the state is missing information. Add the missing fact as another dimension:

Missing fact Extra state Example
Am I holding a stock? In cooldown? a small enum of modes Stock problems (LC 122, 309, 714, 123)
How many transactions or operations are left? a count k Stock III and IV, Ones and Zeroes
Where are both walkers? a second position Cherry Pickup II
Which items are used (small n) a bitmask Assignment problems with n <= 15
Whose turn is it, or what is the current limit? turn or parameter Stone Game II (index, M)
Go deeper

State machine DP

Draw the states as nodes and the allowed daily actions as arrows. Each arrow becomes one term in the transition.

Java
// LC 309. Three states at the end of each day:
//   hold = own a share, sold = sold today (cooldown tomorrow), rest = free to buy.
static int maxProfitCooldown(int[] prices) {
    int hold = Integer.MIN_VALUE / 2, sold = 0, rest = 0;   // MIN/2: safe to add to
    for (int p : prices) {
        int prevHold = hold, prevSold = sold, prevRest = rest;
        hold = Math.max(prevHold, prevRest - p);    // keep holding, or buy (only from rest)
        sold = prevHold + p;                        // sell what we held
        rest = Math.max(prevRest, prevSold);        // stay free, or finish the cooldown
    }
    return Math.max(sold, rest);
}

Each day reads the previous day's three values (saved in prev* variables first, because all three updates must use yesterday's values). With a transaction fee (LC 714), subtract it on one transition; with at most k transactions, index the states by transactions used.

Go deeper

Interval DP

State shape

dp[l][r] = the answer for the subarray or substring between l and r. Fill by increasing interval length, and choose a split point k inside the interval.

Java
// LC 312. Interval DP. dp[l][r] = best coins from bursting every balloon strictly between l and r.
// Choose k = the LAST balloon burst in (l, r): its neighbors at that moment are l and r.
static int maxCoins(int[] nums) {
    int n = nums.length;
    int[] a = new int[n + 2];
    a[0] = a[n + 1] = 1;                                 // virtual balloons with value 1
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) a[i + 1] = nums[i];
    int[][] dp = new int[n + 2][n + 2];
    for (int len = 2; len <= n + 1; len++)               // shorter intervals first
        for (int l = 0; l + len <= n + 1; l++) {
            int r = l + len;
            for (int k = l + 1; k < r; k++)
                dp[l][r] = Math.max(dp[l][r], dp[l][k] + a[l] * a[k] * a[r] + dp[k][r]);
        }
    return dp[0][n + 1];
}

The key decision in Burst Balloons (LC 312) is choosing k as the last balloon burst in (l, r), not the first. If k is last, its neighbors at that moment are exactly l and r, and the two sides are independent subproblems. Choosing the first balloon would leave sides whose neighbors keep changing. When an interval problem seems to have dependent sides, try "last action" instead of "first action".

14.9DP vs greedy vs backtracking vs plain recursion

Try it first3 minutes, before you read on

Pick DP, greedy, or backtracking: (a) list every subset that sums to 10; (b) count the subsets that sum to 10; (c) the largest number of non-overlapping meetings.

Reveal the answer

(a) Backtracking: you must output each subset, so the cost is at least the size of the output. (b) DP: the count for (items used, remaining sum) repeats across paths. (c) Greedy: sort by end time and take each meeting that fits.

Situation Use Why
Subproblems repeat, and you need a count, best value, or yes/no DP Each state is solved once
Subproblems do not repeat (tree traversal, divide and conquer on disjoint parts) Plain recursion Nothing to cache
You must list every solution Backtracking Output size is exponential anyway
A local choice is provably safe Greedy No need to compare alternatives
States form a graph with costs, and transitions can go in cycles Shortest path (BFS / Dijkstra) DP needs an order without cycles

Common mistakes across all DP

  • A state that does not capture everything the future depends on.
  • Wrong loop order: reading a cell before it is computed, or reading an updated cell that should still be old (0/1 knapsack).
  • Initializing minimization tables with 0 instead of "infinity", or using Integer.MAX_VALUE and then adding to it.
  • Forgetting the modulo on every addition in counting problems (and using long for intermediate products).
  • Optimizing space too early, which makes reconstruction impossible and bugs harder to see.
