Module 15: Bit manipulation

A handful of bit operations, used precisely, replace extra memory or loops: canceling pairs with XOR, counting set bits, testing powers of two, and representing small sets as integers.

5 lessons0 guided solves10 practice problems

On this page

  1. 15.1Binary representation and the operators
  2. 15.2Checking, setting, clearing, toggling
  3. 15.3XOR patterns
  4. 15.4Bitmasks as small sets
  5. 15.5Java-specific pitfalls

15.1Binary representation and the operators

Try it first2 minutes, before you read on

Without running it: what are 6 & 3, 6 | 3, 6 ^ 3, and 6 << 2?

Reveal the answer

6 is 110 and 3 is 011. AND = 010 = 2, OR = 111 = 7, XOR = 101 = 5, and 6 << 2 = 24 (multiply by 2^2).

What it solves

Problems about parity, pairs that cancel, subsets of a small set, flags, and arithmetic without extra space.

Intuition

An integer is a row of 32 light switches. AND keeps a switch on only if both rows have it on, OR turns it on if either does, XOR turns it on if exactly one does, NOT flips every switch, and shifts slide the whole row.

Pattern cardBit manipulation
Signal
'Without extra space', pairs canceling out, powers of two, subsets of a small set, flags, XOR in the statement.
Required condition
Values fit in a fixed width (32 or 64 bits); operations act on each bit independently.
Mental model, core operation, limits, and what to use instead
Mental model
A row of light switches: AND keeps, OR sets, XOR flips.
Core operation
Masks with 1 << i; x & (x - 1) clears the lowest set bit; XOR cancels pairs.
Complexity benefit
O(1) extra space and constant-time set operations on up to 64 items.
Limitations
Readability; Java's signed ints and shift rules (>> vs >>>, shift mod 32).
Alternative
HashSet or boolean arrays when clarity matters more than space.
Operator Java Bit rule Typical use
AND a & b 1 if both are 1 Test or clear bits (masking)
OR a | b 1 if either is 1 Set bits
XOR a ^ b 1 if they differ Toggle bits, cancel pairs
NOT ~a Flip every bit ~a == -a - 1 in two's complement
Left shift a << k Multiply by 2^k (until overflow) Build masks 1 << i
Signed right shift a >> k Divide by 2^k, rounding toward negative infinity; copies the sign bit Halving signed values
Unsigned right shift a >>> k Shift in zeros Treating int as unsigned; safe midpoints (lo + hi) >>> 1

Two's complement. Java int is 32 bits; negative numbers are stored as ~x + 1. So -1 is all ones, Integer.MIN_VALUE is 1 followed by 31 zeros, and -x equals ~x + 1. This is why x & -x isolates the lowest set bit.

15.2Checking, setting, clearing, toggling

Try it first2 minutes, before you read on

x = 11 (1011 in binary). Write the expression and the result to: check bit 2, set bit 2, clear bit 0, toggle bit 3.

Reveal the answer

Check: (x >> 2) & 1 = 0. Set: x | (1 << 2) = 1111 = 15. Clear: x & ~1 = 1010 = 10. Toggle: x ^ (1 << 3) = 0011 = 3.

Java
static boolean isSet(int x, int i)  { return (x & (1 << i)) != 0; }   // check bit i
static int setBit(int x, int i)     { return x | (1 << i); }          // force bit i to 1
static int clearBit(int x, int i)   { return x & ~(1 << i); }         // force bit i to 0
static int toggleBit(int x, int i)  { return x ^ (1 << i); }          // flip bit i
static int lowestSetBit(int x)      { return x & -x; }                // e.g. 12 (1100) -> 4 (0100)
static int clearLowestSetBit(int x) { return x & (x - 1); }           // 12 (1100) -> 8 (1000)
static boolean isPowerOfTwo(int n)  { return n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) == 0; }

static void javaPitfalls() {
    int neg = -8;                       // 11111111 11111111 11111111 11111000
    int arith = neg >> 1;               // -4: sign bit is copied in
    int logical = neg >>> 1;            // 2147483644: zeros shifted in
    int wrap = 1 << 32;                 // 1, not 0: int shift distance is taken mod 32
    long big = 1L << 40;                // use a long literal for shifts >= 31
    boolean wrong = (5 & 1) == 1;       // parenthesize: == binds tighter than &
    if (arith != -4 || logical != 2147483644 || wrap != 1 || big != 1099511627776L || !wrong)
        throw new AssertionError();
    // Integer.bitCount(x), Integer.toBinaryString(x), Integer.highestOneBit(x),
    // Integer.numberOfTrailingZeros(x) are built in and O(1).
}

Counting set bits. x & (x - 1) removes one set bit per iteration, so the loop runs once per set bit (Brian Kernighan's method). Integer.bitCount(x) does it in O(1). Counting Bits (LC 338) for all numbers up to n uses DP: bits[i] = bits[i >> 1] + (i & 1).

Power of two. A positive power of two has exactly one set bit: n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) == 0. The n > 0 check excludes 0 and Integer.MIN_VALUE.

15.3XOR patterns

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
260Single Number IIIMedium

Any correct brute force counts. Note where you got stuck: the lesson below is about exactly that.

Show a hint
Split the group by any set bit of a ^ b

XOR has three properties that do all the work: x ^ x = 0, x ^ 0 = x, and it is commutative and associative (order does not matter).

Java
// LC 136. Pairs cancel: a ^ a = 0, and XOR is order-independent.
static int singleNumber(int[] nums) {
    int x = 0;
    for (int v : nums) x ^= v;
    return x;
}

// LC 191. Each n & (n - 1) removes one set bit: loop runs popcount times.
static int hammingWeight(int n) {
    int count = 0;
    while (n != 0) {          // != 0, not > 0: works for negative (unsigned) inputs
        n &= n - 1;
        count++;
    }
    return count;
}

// LC 260. a ^ b != 0 has some set bit; that bit splits a and b into different groups.
static int[] singleNumberIII(int[] nums) {
    int xorAll = 0;
    for (int v : nums) xorAll ^= v;
    int diffBit = xorAll & -xorAll;
    int a = 0, b = 0;
    for (int v : nums) {
        if ((v & diffBit) != 0) a ^= v;
        else b ^= v;
    }
    return new int[]{Math.min(a, b), Math.max(a, b)};
}
Problem XOR idea
Single Number (LC 136) XOR everything; pairs cancel
Missing Number (LC 268) XOR all indices 0..n with all values; the missing one remains
Single Number III (LC 260) xorAll = a ^ b has a set bit where a and b differ; split by that bit and XOR each group
Single Number II (LC 137) XOR does not cancel triples; count each bit position modulo 3 instead
Count Triplets with Equal XOR (LC 1442) prefix[i] == prefix[k + 1] means the XOR of i..k is 0: prefix XOR plus counting
Sum of Two Integers (LC 371) a ^ b is the sum without carries; (a & b) << 1 is the carry; repeat until no carry

15.4Bitmasks as small sets

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
1239Maximum Length of a Concatenated String with Unique CharactersMedium

Any correct brute force counts. Note where you got stuck: the lesson below is about exactly that.

Show a hint
Represent each word as a bitmask; skip overlapping masks

An int can represent a subset of up to 31 items (a long, 63): bit i set means item i is in the set. Union is |, intersection &, membership (mask >> i) & 1, and enumerating all subsets is a loop from 0 to (1 << n) - 1.

Java
// Enumerate all subsets of n items: mask bit i = 1 means item i is chosen.
static List<List<Integer>> subsetsByMask(int[] nums) {
    int n = nums.length;
    List<List<Integer>> all = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int mask = 0; mask < (1 << n); mask++) {     // 2^n masks; fine for n <= ~20
        List<Integer> subset = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
            if ((mask & (1 << i)) != 0) subset.add(nums[i]);
        all.add(subset);
    }
    return all;
}

Use bitmasks when n is at most about 20 and you need to store or compare subsets compactly: DP over subsets (assignment problems), or carrying a set of seen characters or parities along a path (Pseudo-Palindromic Paths, LC 1457: toggle bit val at each node, and a path can form a palindrome if at most one bit is set at the leaf).

15.5Java-specific pitfalls

Try it first2 minutes, before you read on

In Java, what are -8 >> 1, -8 >>> 1, and 1 << 32?

Reveal the answer

-8 >> 1 = -4 (the sign bit is copied in). -8 >>> 1 = 2147483644 (a zero is shifted in, so the result is a large positive number). 1 << 32 = 1, because the shift distance of an int is taken modulo 32; use 1L << k for large k.

  • Precedence: == binds tighter than &, |, ^. Write (x & 1) == 1, never x & 1 == 1 (which does not compile for ints, but does odd things with booleans).
  • Shift distance is taken modulo 32 for int (modulo 64 for long): 1 << 32 == 1. Use 1L << k when k can be 31 or more.
  • >> vs >>> on negative numbers: -8 >> 1 == -4, but -8 >>> 1 == 2147483644.
  • Loops on negative inputs: while (n > 0) never runs for a negative n treated as unsigned (LC 191); use while (n != 0).
  • Overflow in shifts: 1 << 31 is Integer.MIN_VALUE, a negative number.
  • Built-ins: Integer.bitCount, Integer.highestOneBit, Integer.numberOfTrailingZeros, Integer.toBinaryString (useful for debugging).

Interview math is a short list: GCD and LCM, primes, modular arithmetic, fast exponentiation, overflow-safe arithmetic, and a little counting. Each one has a standard implementation worth knowing exactly.

Pattern cardNumber theory essentials
Signal
Divisibility, primes, 'answer modulo 10^9 + 7', huge exponents, counting arrangements.
Required condition
Integer arithmetic with known identities (Euclid, Fermat, Pascal).
Mental model, core operation, limits, and what to use instead
Mental model
Clock arithmetic: after 12 comes 1; only the remainder matters.
Core operation
gcd via Euclid, sieve for many primes, fast power by squaring, reduce modulo after each operation.
Complexity benefit
O(log n) gcd and power instead of O(n); sieve gives all primes up to n in O(n log log n).
Limitations
Overflow before the modulo; negative remainders in Java; division under a modulus needs an inverse.
Alternative

16.1GCD and LCM

Try it first2 minutes, before you read on

Compute gcd(84, 36) with the Euclidean algorithm, one step per line. Then compute lcm(84, 36).

Reveal the answer

gcd(84, 36) = gcd(36, 12) = gcd(12, 0) = 12. lcm = 84 / 12 * 36 = 252. Divide before multiplying to keep the intermediate small.

What it solves

Divisibility relationships: simplifying ratios, grouping by common periods, repeating patterns (GCD of Strings, LC 1071), counting multiples (LCM inside inclusion-exclusion).

Euclid's algorithm. gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b), with gcd(a, 0) = a. Every two steps the larger number at least halves, so it runs in O(log min(a, b)).

Java
// Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b). O(log min(a, b)).
static long gcd(long a, long b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        long t = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = t;
    }
    return Math.abs(a);
}

// Divide BEFORE multiplying so the intermediate value stays small.
static long lcm(long a, long b) {
    return a / gcd(a, b) * b;
}

lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) * b: divide first, or a * b can overflow before the division.

16.2Primes and the Sieve of Eratosthenes

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
204Count PrimesMedium

Any correct brute force counts. Note where you got stuck: the lesson below is about exactly that.

Show a hint
Sieve of Eratosthenes starting at i * i

Checking one number. A composite n has a divisor at most sqrt(n), so trial division up to sqrt(n) is O(sqrt n). Loop with d * d <= n in long (or d <= n / d) to avoid overflow.

All primes below n. The sieve crosses out multiples of each prime, starting at p * p (smaller multiples were already crossed out by smaller primes). Total work is O(n log log n), effectively linear.

Java
// Trial division up to sqrt(n): a composite n has a factor <= sqrt(n).
static boolean isPrime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) return false;
    for (long d = 2; d * d <= n; d++)      // long: d * d can overflow int
        if (n % d == 0) return false;
    return true;
}

// LC 204. Sieve of Eratosthenes: O(n log log n). Count primes strictly less than n.
static int countPrimes(int n) {
    if (n < 3) return 0;
    boolean[] composite = new boolean[n];
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = 2; i < n; i++) {
        if (composite[i]) continue;
        count++;
        for (long j = (long) i * i; j < n; j += i)   // smaller multiples were crossed already
            composite[(int) j] = true;
    }
    return count;
}

n = 20
p = 2: cross 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18
p = 3: cross 9, 15  (6, 12, 18 already crossed)
p = 5: 25 > 20, stop crossing
primes: 2 3 5 7 11 13 17 19

16.3Modular arithmetic

Try it first2 minutes, before you read on

In Java, what is -7 % 3? How do you get a remainder in the range 0 to 2 instead?

Reveal the answer

-1: Java's % takes the sign of the left operand. Use ((a % m) + m) % m, which gives 2 here, or Math.floorMod(a, m).

What it solves

Counting problems whose answers are huge ("return the answer modulo 10^9 + 7"). Reduce after every operation so values stay small.

Rules. (a + b) mod m = ((a mod m) + (b mod m)) mod m, and the same for subtraction and multiplication. Division does not work this way; it needs a modular inverse (for a prime m, a^(m - 2) mod m by Fermat's little theorem), which is rarely needed in interviews.

Java
static final int MOD = 1_000_000_007;

static void modularRules() {
    long a = 999_999_999L, b = 888_888_888L;
    long sum = (a + b) % MOD;                      // (a + b) mod m
    long product = (a % MOD) * (b % MOD) % MOD;     // operands < 2^30, product < 2^60: fits in long
    long diff = ((a - b) % MOD + MOD) % MOD;        // Java % can be negative: add MOD back
    int negMod = -7 % 3;                            // -1 in Java, not 2
    int fixed = Math.floorMod(-7, 3);               // 2
    if (sum < 0 || product < 0 || diff < 0 || negMod != -1 || fixed != 2) throw new AssertionError();
}

// LC 7. Check for overflow BEFORE the multiply-and-add.
static int reverse(int x) {
    int result = 0;
    while (x != 0) {
        int digit = x % 10;                         // negative for negative x
        if (result > Integer.MAX_VALUE / 10 || result < Integer.MIN_VALUE / 10) return 0;
        result = result * 10 + digit;
        x /= 10;
    }
    return result;
}

Why 10^9 + 7: it is prime, and any two residues below it multiply to less than about 10^18, which fits in a long (max about 9.2 x 10^18). Two int-sized residues multiplied as int overflow; always multiply in long.

16.4Fast exponentiation

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
50Pow(x, n)Medium

Any correct brute force counts. Note where you got stuck: the lesson below is about exactly that.

Show a hint
Fast exponentiation; n = Integer.MIN_VALUE edge case
What it solves

x^n for huge n (Pow(x, n), LC 50; Count Good Numbers, LC 1922) in O(log n) multiplications instead of n.

Idea. Write n in binary. x^13 = x^8 * x^4 * x^1 because 13 = 1101. Square the base each step; multiply it into the result when the current bit of the exponent is 1.

Java
// Fast exponentiation: square the base, use the bits of the exponent. O(log exp).
static long modPow(long base, long exp, long mod) {
    long result = 1;
    base %= mod;
    while (exp > 0) {
        if ((exp & 1) == 1) result = result * base % mod;   // this bit contributes base^(2^k)
        base = base * base % mod;
        exp >>= 1;
    }
    return result;
}

// LC 50. Handle negative n with a long: -Integer.MIN_VALUE does not fit in an int.
static double myPow(double x, int n) {
    long e = n;
    if (e < 0) { x = 1 / x; e = -e; }
    double result = 1;
    while (e > 0) {
        if ((e & 1) == 1) result *= x;
        x *= x;
        e >>= 1;
    }
    return result;
}

The myPow version shows two classic edge cases: a negative exponent becomes 1 / x with a positive exponent, and -Integer.MIN_VALUE does not fit in an int, so the exponent is widened to long before negating.

16.5Safe arithmetic and integer overflow

Try it first2 minutes, before you read on

int a = 50000, b = 50000; long c = a * b; What is c?

Reveal the answer

-1,794,967,296. a * b is computed in int and overflows before it is widened to long. Write (long) a * b.

Danger Example Fix
Sum of many ints 10^5 values of 10^9 Accumulate in long
Product of two ints a * b with a, b up to 10^5 (long) a * b (cast before multiplying)
Midpoint (lo + hi) / 2 near 2^31 lo + (hi - lo) / 2
Negation -Integer.MIN_VALUE is still negative Widen to long, or handle separately
Comparator subtraction a - b Integer.compare(a, b)
Building a number digit by digit result * 10 + d Check result > (MAX - d) / 10 first
Absolute value Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) is negative Widen first

Math.addExact, Math.multiplyExact, and Math.toIntExact throw on overflow, which is useful while debugging.

16.6Basic combinatorics

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
1641Count Sorted Vowel StringsMedium

Any correct brute force counts. Note where you got stuck: the lesson below is about exactly that.

Show a hint
Stars and bars: C(n + 4, 4)
Question Formula Example
Ordered arrangements of n distinct items n! Permutations
Choose k of n, order irrelevant C(n, k) = n! / (k! (n - k)!) Unique Paths: C(m + n - 2, m - 1)
Distribute n identical items into k groups (stars and bars) C(n + k - 1, k - 1) Count Sorted Vowel Strings (LC 1641): C(n + 4, 4)
Pairs among n items n (n - 1) / 2 Counting unreachable pairs, equal pairs
Count with an exclusion inclusion-exclusion: |A or B| = |A| + |B| - |A and B| Ugly Number III (LC 1201): multiples of a, b, or c up to x
Java
// nCr with Pascal's rule C(n, r) = C(n-1, r-1) + C(n-1, r), modulo MOD.
static long[][] pascal(int n) {
    long[][] c = new long[n + 1][n + 1];
    for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) {
        c[i][0] = 1;
        for (int r = 1; r <= i; r++) c[i][r] = (c[i - 1][r - 1] + c[i - 1][r]) % MOD;
    }
    return c;
}

// Exact small nCr without overflow-prone factorials: multiply and divide alternately.
static long nCr(int n, int r) {
    r = Math.min(r, n - r);
    long result = 1;
    for (int i = 1; i <= r; i++) result = result * (n - r + i) / i;   // always an integer
    return result;
}

Computing C(n, k) by multiplying and dividing alternately keeps every intermediate value an exact integer and avoids computing huge factorials. For many binomials modulo a prime, build Pascal's triangle (O(n^2)) or precompute factorials and inverse factorials.

Factorial trailing zeros (LC 172) is a counting question in disguise: each zero needs a factor 10 = 2 x 5, and 2s are plentiful, so count factors of 5: n/5 + n/25 + n/125 + ....

Module 17: Data structure design

Design questions give you a list of operations and a time limit for each. No single structure meets every limit, so you combine two or three, and keep them consistent on every update. This module does not reteach the structures; it shows how they combine.

17.1How to design from a list of operations

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
1472Design Browser HistoryMedium

Any correct brute force counts. Note where you got stuck: the lesson below is about exactly that.

Show a hint
Array with a cursor and a logical end replaces a stack pair
Pattern cardData structure design
Signal
'Design a class' with required time limits per operation: get/put in O(1), getRandom in O(1), min in O(1).
Required condition
List every operation and its target complexity first; each operation needs some structure that supports it.
Mental model, core operation, limits, and what to use instead
Mental model
A kitchen with a pantry (lookup), a conveyor (order), and a scoreboard (extremes): each station does one job fast.
Core operation
Combine structures so each operation is fast in at least one of them, and keep them consistent on every update.
Complexity benefit
Meets per-operation bounds that no single structure can.
Limitations
Every write must update all structures; inconsistent updates are the main bug.
Alternative
Built-ins: LinkedHashMap (LRU), TreeMap (ordered), PriorityQueue with lazy deletion.

Follow these steps before writing a class:

  1. List every operation and its required complexity. Write them as a table. "get in O(1), put in O(1), evict the least recently used in O(1)."
  2. For each operation, name the structure that makes it fast. Lookup by key: hash map. Order by time: linked list or queue. Current min/max: heap or a stack of running mins. Random element: array. Sorted access: TreeMap.
  3. Decide how the structures point at each other. Usually the map stores a reference or index into the other structure, so finding and then moving or deleting an element are both O(1).
  4. Walk through every operation and list every structure it must update. Inconsistency between structures is the main source of bugs.
  5. Handle the edge cases explicitly: empty structure, capacity 1, updating an existing key, deleting the last element.
Required operation Structure that gives it
Find by key in O(1) HashMap
Remove an element you already hold, in O(1) Doubly linked list node (or swap-with-last in an array)
Maintain insertion or usage order Linked list, deque, LinkedHashMap
Uniform random element in O(1) ArrayList (index access)
Current minimum or maximum Heap (with lazy deletion), or running min stored per stack entry
Smallest key >= x, ordered iteration TreeMap / TreeSet
Value at a past version or time Per-key list of (time, value) + binary search

17.2Min Stack: carry the answer with each element

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
155Min StackMedium

Any correct brute force counts. Note where you got stuck: the lesson below is about exactly that.

Show a hint
Store the running min alongside each value
Operations

push, pop, top, getMin, all O(1). A single "current min" variable fails on pop: after removing the minimum, you cannot recover the previous one. Store the minimum as of each push alongside the value. Popping restores the previous minimum automatically.

Java
// LC 155. Each entry remembers the minimum of everything at or below it.
static class MinStack {
    private final Deque<int[]> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();   // {value, minSoFar}

    void push(int val) {
        int min = stack.isEmpty() ? val : Math.min(val, stack.peek()[1]);
        stack.push(new int[]{val, min});
    }
    void pop()    { stack.pop(); }
    int top()     { return stack.peek()[0]; }
    int getMin()  { return stack.peek()[1]; }
}

The same "store the aggregate with each element" idea gives a max stack, or a stack that answers "sum of everything below".

17.3Queue from stacks, stack from queues

Try it first2 minutes, before you read on

Build a queue from two stacks, in and out. Push goes to in. How does pop work, and what does it cost on average over many operations?

Reveal the answer

Pop from out; when out is empty, move everything from in to out first, which reverses the order. Each element is moved at most once in its lifetime, so pop is O(1) amortized even though a single pop can cost O(n).

Queue from two stacks. Push into in. To pop, take from out; when out is empty, pour all of in into it, which reverses the order so the oldest element is on top. Each element is moved at most once in its lifetime, so the amortized cost per operation is O(1) even though a single pop can cost O(n).

Stack from one queue. After each push, rotate the older elements behind the new one so it reaches the front: O(n) push, O(1) pop.

Java
// LC 232. Push to 'in'. Pop from 'out'; refill 'out' only when it is empty.
// Each element moves at most once: amortized O(1) per operation.
static class MyQueue {
    private final Deque<Integer> in = new ArrayDeque<>(), out = new ArrayDeque<>();

    void push(int x) { in.push(x); }
    int pop()        { peek(); return out.pop(); }
    int peek() {
        if (out.isEmpty())
            while (!in.isEmpty()) out.push(in.pop());   // reverses order: oldest on top
        return out.peek();
    }
    boolean empty()  { return in.isEmpty() && out.isEmpty(); }
}

// LC 225. After pushing x, rotate the older elements behind it: x is now at the front.
static class MyStack {
    private final Deque<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>();

    void push(int x) {
        q.offer(x);
        for (int i = 0; i < q.size() - 1; i++) q.offer(q.poll());   // O(n) push
    }
    int pop()       { return q.poll(); }
    int top()       { return q.peek(); }
    boolean empty() { return q.isEmpty(); }
}

These two show the trade-off you should state in an interview: amortized O(1) with occasional O(n) spikes, or a consistent O(n) on one operation.

17.4LRU cache: HashMap + doubly linked list

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
146LRU CacheMedium

Stuck after 15 minutes? The guided solve in this lesson walks through this exact problem, one question at a time.

Show a hint
HashMap for lookup + doubly linked list for recency
Operations

get(key) and put(key, value) in O(1); when full, evict the least recently used key.

Need Structure
Find a key's entry in O(1) HashMap<key, Node>
Move an entry to "most recent" in O(1) Doubly linked list (unlink and relink a node)
Find and remove the least recent in O(1) The node at the tail end of the list
Remove that key from the map The node stores its own key
Guided solveLC 146. LRU CacheFive questions, each with a reveal

Problem: 146LRU CacheMedium. Answer each question on paper first, then reveal.

  1. 1
    Understand the problem

    Say in one sentence what is asked. Which constraint sets the time budget?

    Reveal step 1
    Problem decoding

    Fixed-capacity key-value cache. get returns the value or -1 and marks the key as used. put inserts or updates and marks it used; if the cache is over capacity, evict the least recently used key.

    Input analysis

    Up to 2 * 10^5 calls; O(1) per call is required.

  2. 2
    Brute force, then a pattern

    What is the simplest correct approach and what does it cost? Which pattern could beat it, and why does it apply?

    Reveal step 2
    Pattern discovery

    Two requirements pull in different directions: lookup by key (hash map) and order by recency with O(1) moves (linked list). The design is their combination.

    Brute force

    A list ordered by recency: get is O(n) to find. A map with timestamps: eviction is O(n) to find the oldest.

  3. 3
    The key observation

    What single fact removes the repeated work? Trace a tiny input on paper until you see it.

    Reveal step 3

    Key idea. the map finds nodes, the list orders them

    Key observation

    If the map's value is the list node itself, finding a node is O(1) via the map, and moving or deleting it is O(1) via its prev and next links. A singly linked list is not enough, because unlinking needs the predecessor.

    Visualization
    capacity 2
put(1,1)          list: head <-> 1 <-> tail
put(2,2)          list: head <-> 2 <-> 1 <-> tail
get(1) -> 1       list: head <-> 1 <-> 2 <-> tail     (1 moved to the front)
put(3,3)          full: evict tail.prev = 2           list: head <-> 3 <-> 1 <-> tail
get(2) -> -1
  4. 4
    Build it

    Write the algorithm in three or four lines, then code it. Reveal after you have run one small input by hand.

    Reveal step 4
    Algorithm

    get: look up the node; if present, unlink it, add it after head, return its value. put: if the key exists, update the value and move it to the front. Otherwise, if full, unlink tail.prev and remove its key from the map; then create a node, map it, and add it to the front.

    Java implementation
    Java
    // LC 146. get/put in O(1).
// HashMap: key -> node (find in O(1)). Doubly linked list: recency order (move/remove in O(1)).
// Most recent sits right after head; least recent right before tail.
static class LRUCache {
    private static class Node {
        int key, value;
        Node prev, next;
        Node(int key, int value) { this.key = key; this.value = value; }
    }

    private final int capacity;
    private final Map<Integer, Node> map = new HashMap<>();
    private final Node head = new Node(0, 0), tail = new Node(0, 0);   // sentinels

    LRUCache(int capacity) {
        this.capacity = capacity;
        head.next = tail;
        tail.prev = head;
    }

    int get(int key) {
        Node node = map.get(key);
        if (node == null) return -1;
        unlink(node);
        addFront(node);                       // used -> most recent
        return node.value;
    }

    void put(int key, int value) {
        Node node = map.get(key);
        if (node != null) {                   // update existing
            node.value = value;
            unlink(node);
            addFront(node);
            return;
        }
        if (map.size() == capacity) {         // evict least recent
            Node lru = tail.prev;
            unlink(lru);
            map.remove(lru.key);              // the node stores its key for exactly this
        }
        Node fresh = new Node(key, value);
        map.put(key, fresh);
        addFront(fresh);
    }

    private void unlink(Node n) {
        n.prev.next = n.next;
        n.next.prev = n.prev;
    }

    private void addFront(Node n) {
        n.next = head.next;
        n.prev = head;
        head.next.prev = n;
        head.next = n;
    }
}
    Dry run

    The trace above. The test harness also checks capacity 1 with an update to an existing key, which must not evict anything.

  5. 5
    Check it

    State time and space with a reason, name three inputs that could break the code, and say what this problem teaches beyond itself.

    Reveal step 5
    Complexity

    O(1) per operation, O(capacity) space.

    Edge cases

    Updating an existing key (no eviction, but it becomes most recent), capacity 1, get on a missing key (no change to order).

    Transfer lesson

    Java's LinkedHashMap with accessOrder = true and an overridden removeEldestEntry is an LRU cache in a few lines. Mention it, but expect to build the manual version. LFU Cache (LC 460) extends the idea: a map from frequency to an LRU list, plus a minFreq pointer.

17.5Insert, delete, getRandom in O(1)

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
380Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)Medium

Any correct brute force counts. Note where you got stuck: the lesson below is about exactly that.

Show a hint
Array + index map; delete by swapping with the last
Operations

insert, remove, and return a uniformly random element, all O(1). An ArrayList gives random access; a hash map from value to index gives "where is it". To delete from the middle of the array in O(1), move the last element into the hole and fix its index in the map.

Java
// LC 380. ArrayList gives O(1) random access; the map gives O(1) "where is it?".
// Delete in O(1) by moving the last element into the deleted slot.
static class RandomizedSet {
    private final List<Integer> values = new ArrayList<>();
    private final Map<Integer, Integer> indexOf = new HashMap<>();
    private final Random random = new Random();

    boolean insert(int val) {
        if (indexOf.containsKey(val)) return false;
        indexOf.put(val, values.size());
        values.add(val);
        return true;
    }

    boolean remove(int val) {
        Integer idx = indexOf.get(val);
        if (idx == null) return false;
        int last = values.get(values.size() - 1);
        values.set(idx, last);                 // move last into the hole
        indexOf.put(last, idx);
        values.remove(values.size() - 1);      // removing the last index is O(1)
        indexOf.remove(val);
        return true;
    }

    int getRandom() { return values.get(random.nextInt(values.size())); }
}

Order of updates in remove is the bug magnet: write the last element into the hole, update the last element's index, then remove the last slot, then remove the deleted value from the map. This order also works when the removed element is itself the last one.

Try it first15 minutes, before you read on
1396Design Underground SystemMedium

Any correct brute force counts. Note where you got stuck: the lesson below is about exactly that.

Show a hint
Two maps: in-progress trips and aggregated stats
Problem Combination Why
Time Based Key-Value Store (LC 981) Map<key, List<(time, value)>> + binary search Times arrive in increasing order, so each list is sorted
Snapshot Array (LC 1146) Per-index list of (snapId, value) + binary search Store only changes, not full copies per snapshot
Design Underground System (LC 1396) Map of check-ins by id + map of (from, to) totals Separate in-progress state from aggregated state
Food Rating System (LC 2353) Map food -> rating, map cuisine -> TreeSet ordered by (rating desc, name) Update = remove, change, re-insert
Design Twitter (LC 355) Map user -> tweets, map user -> followees, heap to merge feeds K-way merge of the most recent tweets
Stock Price / leaderboards Map + TreeMap<value, count> Ordered values with deletions
LFU Cache (LC 460) Map key -> node, map freq -> LRU list, minFreq Two levels of ordering

Common mistakes

  • Updating one structure and forgetting the other (the map still points at an evicted node).
  • Using a heap where deletions by key are needed without lazy deletion.
  • Storing values in the list but not keys, so eviction cannot clean the map.
  • Not stating amortized vs worst-case bounds when they differ.

Pattern cheat sheets

Quick-reference pages for revision. Use them after you have studied a module, to check recall, not instead of the module. For choosing between two similar techniques, see the decision tables.

On this page

Signal to pattern

Read the problem, find the matching signals, then verify the required condition before committing. A signal is a hypothesis, not a decision.

If the problem has ... First try Verify that ...
Pair or complement lookup in unsorted data Hash map Order does not matter; O(n) memory is acceptable
Groups of equivalent items Hash map with a canonical key You can build a key that is equal exactly for items in the same group
Range sums, many queries, or "subarray sum equals k" Prefix sums (+ hash map) The operation is invertible (sum, count, XOR)
Many range updates, read once Difference array Updates come before reads
Best contiguous sum or product Kadane Contiguity is required
Sorted array, pairs or triplets with a target Two pointers Moving a pointer safely discards candidates
Partition in place (colors, pivot) Read/write or three pointers The relative order requirement (stable or not)
Every window of size k Fixed sliding window State can be updated on add and remove
Longest or shortest contiguous range with a condition Variable sliding window Shrinking a valid window keeps it valid (no negatives in sums)
"Exactly k" in a window atMost(k) - atMost(k - 1) "At most" is monotonic
Sorted or rotated data, find a position Binary search on data A test at mid tells you which half to discard
"Minimum X such that ...", "minimize the maximum" Binary search on the answer Feasibility is monotonic and cheap to check
Overlaps, merges, rooms, schedules Sort intervals; sweep line Endpoint semantics (closed or half-open)
Keep the most non-overlapping intervals Greedy by earliest end Unweighted (weighted needs DP)
Reverse, reorder, or merge a linked list Pointer rewiring with a dummy You save next before overwriting
Cycle, middle, kth from end, repeating sequence Fast and slow pointers There is a single "next" function
Matching brackets, nested encodings, undo Stack The item you need is the most recent unresolved one
Next or previous greater or smaller element, spans Monotonic stack Beaten elements can never be an answer again
Max or min of every window Monotonic deque Elements expire from the front
"Generate all", "list every" Backtracking n is small (about 20 for subsets, 10 for permutations)
Tree height, diameter, balance, LCA, path through a node Bottom-up tree recursion You know what each node returns to its parent
Root-to-node paths, ancestors' values Top-down parameters You undo mutable state on the way back
Level by level, nearest node Tree BFS Snapshot the queue size per level
BST, sorted order, kth smallest Inorder traversal or bounds Strictness of the BST definition
Top k, kth largest, repeatedly take the extreme Heap (size k) Data arrives over time or k is small
Running median Two heaps Sizes stay balanced
Merge k sorted sources Heap of fronts Each source is sorted
Locally obvious best choice Greedy An exchange argument holds; no small counterexample
Grid regions, connectivity, reachability BFS or DFS Visited marking
Fewest steps, equal costs BFS (multi-source if many starts) All moves cost the same
Prerequisites, ordering constraints Topological sort Directed; detect cycles
Two groups with no conflicting pair together Bipartite check Undirected conflict graph
Cheapest path, weighted Dijkstra No negative weights
Path with at most k edges Bellman-Ford rounds Read only the previous round
Merging groups as connections arrive Union-Find No deletions
Connect everything cheaply Kruskal or Prim Undirected, weighted
Many prefix queries, autocomplete, many words in a grid Trie Keys are sequences sharing prefixes
Count ways, min or max cost, feasibility with interacting choices DP Subproblems repeat; the state captures the future
Pairs canceling, single odd element, small subsets Bits (XOR, masks) Fixed width, Java shift rules
GCD, primes, huge powers, answer modulo 10^9 + 7 Number theory Overflow before the modulo
"Design a class" with per-operation limits Combine structures Every update keeps all structures consistent

Pattern summary

Every pattern card from the modules, condensed to the three fields you check first.

PatternSignalMust be trueIf it is not
Hashing (lookup and counting)
Module 2
You keep asking 'have I seen X?', 'how many X?', or 'where is X?' inside a loop. Pairs that must sum or match. Grouping by an equivalence (anagrams, same pattern).A key that identifies what you are looking for. Order of elements does not matter for the lookup itself.Sorting + two pointers (O(1) extra space), TreeMap for ordered or range queries, a counting array for small value ranges.
Prefix sums
Module 2
Sum (or count, XOR) over a contiguous range, asked many times. 'Subarray sum equals / divisible by k'. Negative numbers allowed.An invertible combine operation (sum, XOR, count): range = prefix[r+1] - prefix[l]. Max and min are NOT invertible.Sliding window when all values are non-negative; difference array for many range updates; Fenwick or segment tree when the array changes.
Kadane (best subarray ending here)
Module 2
Maximum (or minimum) sum or product of a contiguous subarray. 'Best time to buy and sell once'.The best answer ending at i can be built from the best answer ending at i - 1 plus nums[i].Prefix sums with a running minimum prefix (same idea), DP with extra states for deletions or circular arrays.
Two pointers
Module 3
Sorted array or string; pairs or triplets meeting a target; palindromes; in-place removal or partitioning.Moving one pointer must safely discard candidates. Usually needs sorted order or a symmetric structure.Hash map for unsorted pair search; sliding window when the pair bounds a contiguous range with a running condition.
Fixed-size sliding window
Module 3
'Every subarray/substring of length k', anagram or permutation of a pattern, averages over k items.Window state can be updated in O(1) when one element enters and one leaves.Monotonic deque for window max/min; prefix sums for window sums with random access.
Variable-size sliding window
Module 3
Longest or shortest contiguous subarray/substring satisfying a condition; 'at most k' distinct, zeros, or replacements.Monotonic validity: shrinking a valid window keeps it valid (or growing an invalid one keeps it invalid). Typically fails with negative numbers in sum conditions.Prefix sums + hash map (exact sums with negatives); monotonic deque over prefix sums (shortest sum >= k with negatives); exactly(k) = atMost(k) - atMost(k-1).
Binary search on data
Module 4
Sorted or rotated-sorted input, 'first/last position', insertion point, peak, or any O(log n) requirement.A predicate over indices that is false...false true...true (monotonic). Sorting gives one for free.Linear scan when unsorted and queried once; hash set for membership only; TreeMap floor/ceiling for dynamic data.
Binary search on the answer
Module 4
'Minimum largest', 'maximum smallest', 'least capacity/speed/time so that...'. You can check a candidate answer easily but cannot compute it directly.feasible(x) is monotonic: if x works, every larger (or smaller) x also works.Direct formula, greedy, or DP when the answer can be constructed; heap-based simulation for some scheduling problems.
Intervals and sweep line
Module 5
Pairs [start, end]: overlaps, merging, free time, rooms needed, max concurrent events.Sort order exposes the structure: by start for merging, by end for selecting, by event time for counting.Min-heap of end times for rooms; difference array when coordinates are small integers; TreeMap for dynamic calendars.
Linked list pointer manipulation
Module 6
Reverse, reorder, merge, delete, or split a linked list in place.You can only move forward (singly linked); O(1) extra space is usually expected.Copy into an ArrayList when space is allowed and the logic gets simpler; recursion for clarity (O(n) stack).
Fast and slow pointers
Module 6
Cycle detection, middle element, kth from end, a sequence that might repeat (happy number), duplicates in [1..n].A function next(x) that defines a path; a cycle exists if the path revisits a state.HashSet of visited states (simpler, O(n) memory).
Stack (most recent unmatched item)
Module 7
Matching pairs (brackets, tags), undo, nested structure (decode string, calculators), collisions that resolve against the latest item.The element you need next is always the most recently added unresolved one (LIFO).Recursion (an implicit stack), a counter when only one bracket type exists.
Monotonic stack
Module 7
Next/previous greater or smaller element, span/width bounded by a taller or shorter element, 'how far until warmer'.Once a bigger (or smaller) element arrives, the elements it beats can never be the answer for anything later.Monotonic deque when the window also expires from the left; sorting + DSU for some offline variants.
Monotonic deque (window max/min)
Module 7
Max or min of every sliding window; DP where dp[i] needs the best of the last k states.Old elements expire from the front; new elements make worse older ones useless from the back.Heap with lazy deletion (O(n log n)); TreeMap of counts for any order statistic.
Recursion and divide and conquer
Module 8
The problem on input n can be stated using the same problem on a smaller input (n - 1, halves, subtrees, splits).A base case that stops the recursion and a smaller subproblem each call.Iteration with an explicit stack for deep inputs; memoization or DP for overlapping subproblems.
Backtracking
Module 8
'All', 'every', 'generate', 'list all valid' combinations, permutations, partitions, placements. Small n (about 10 to 20).The answer is built by a sequence of choices; partial choices can be undone; output size itself may be exponential.DP (count or optimize), bitmask enumeration for n <= 20, greedy when a choice is provably safe.
Tree recursion (bottom-up return values)
Module 9
Height, diameter, balance, path sums through a node, LCA, subtree properties, 'information from children'.A node's answer can be computed from its children's answers plus its own value.Top-down parameters for ancestor information; BFS for level-based questions; parent pointers + BFS for distance-k.
Tree BFS (level order)
Module 9
'Level by level', 'each row', right side view, minimum depth, width, zigzag.The answer depends on depth or on nodes that share a level.DFS with a depth parameter and a list indexed by depth.
Binary search tree
Module 9
'BST' in the statement, sorted order, kth smallest, floor/ceiling, validate, range sum.Every left-subtree value < node < every right-subtree value (strict, unless stated).TreeMap / TreeSet in Java (red-black tree, guaranteed O(log n)); sorted array + binary search for static data.
Heap / priority queue
Module 10
Top k, kth largest/smallest, 'repeatedly take the smallest/largest', merging sorted sources, scheduling by time or priority.You need fast access to the current extreme while elements keep arriving or changing.Sorting when all data is known up front; quickselect for one kth element (O(n) average); TreeMap when you need removal by key.
Two heaps and k-way merge
Module 10
Running median, balancing two halves, merging k sorted lists, smallest pairs from sorted arrays.The answer is defined by a boundary between two halves, or by the next smallest among k sorted frontiers.TreeMap multiset; divide-and-conquer pairwise merging for k-way merge.
Greedy
Module 11
Optimize one quantity with a natural order (earliest end, largest value per unit, furthest reach); local decision seems obviously safe.Greedy-choice property: some optimal solution starts with the greedy choice. Prove it (exchange argument) or find a counterexample.DP when choices interact; heap-based greedy when the best choice changes as you go.
Graph traversal (BFS / DFS)
Module 12
Connections, reachability, islands, regions, 'can you get from A to B', components. Grids are graphs.You can list each node's neighbors. Mark visited to avoid infinite loops.Union-Find for connectivity with incremental edges; iterative DFS with an explicit stack.
BFS shortest path (unweighted, multi-source)
Module 12
Fewest steps, minimum moves, nearest X from every cell, spreading per minute. All moves cost the same.Every edge has equal weight. (0/1 weights: 0-1 BFS with a deque.)Dijkstra for non-negative weights; Bellman-Ford rounds for edge-count limits or negative weights.
Topological sort and cycle detection
Module 12
Prerequisites, dependencies, build order, 'is it possible to finish', ordering with constraints.Directed graph. A valid order exists if and only if there is no directed cycle.DFS three-color for cycle detection; DP over the topological order for longest paths in a DAG.
Dijkstra (weighted shortest path)
Module 12
Minimum total cost, time, or effort over weighted edges; 'cheapest', 'fastest', 'least effort path'.All edge weights are non-negative, and the path cost never decreases as you extend a path.BFS when weights are equal; 0-1 BFS for weights 0/1; Bellman-Ford for negatives or k-edge limits; Floyd-Warshall for all pairs with small V.
Union-Find (disjoint set union)
Module 12
Grouping by connections that arrive over time, 'are A and B connected', counting components, redundant edge, Kruskal.Only unions happen (no edge deletions). Undirected relationships.BFS/DFS when the graph is static and queried once.
Trie (prefix tree)
Module 13
Many prefix queries, autocomplete, 'words starting with', dictionary with wildcards, word search with many words, max XOR.Keys are sequences (strings, bits) and queries share prefixes.HashSet for exact matches; sorted list + binary search for prefix ranges; HashSet of all prefixes for small inputs.
Dynamic programming
Module 14
Count the ways, min/max cost, 'is it possible', with choices at each step where later choices depend on earlier ones. A brute-force recursion re-solves the same subproblems.Optimal substructure (the best answer is built from best sub-answers) and overlapping subproblems.Greedy when a choice is provably safe; backtracking when you need all solutions; graph shortest path when states form a weighted graph.
Bit manipulation
Module 15
'Without extra space', pairs canceling out, powers of two, subsets of a small set, flags, XOR in the statement.Values fit in a fixed width (32 or 64 bits); operations act on each bit independently.HashSet or boolean arrays when clarity matters more than space.
Number theory essentials
Module 16
Divisibility, primes, 'answer modulo 10^9 + 7', huge exponents, counting arrangements.Integer arithmetic with known identities (Euclid, Fermat, Pascal).BigInteger for exact big values (slow); long arithmetic with careful ordering.
Data structure design
Module 17
'Design a class' with required time limits per operation: get/put in O(1), getRandom in O(1), min in O(1).List every operation and its target complexity first; each operation needs some structure that supports it.Built-ins: LinkedHashMap (LRU), TreeMap (ordered), PriorityQueue with lazy deletion.

Complexity reference

Algorithm or operation Time Extra space
Hash map get / put O(1) average O(n) total
Sorting O(n log n) O(log n) to O(n)
Binary search O(log n) O(1)
Two pointers, sliding window O(n) O(1) or O(alphabet)
Prefix sums build / query O(n) / O(1) O(n)
Monotonic stack or deque O(n) O(n)
Heap push / pop, top-k O(log n), O(n log k) O(k)
Tree traversal O(n) O(h)
BST search / insert / delete O(h) O(h) recursive
BFS / DFS on a graph O(V + E) O(V)
Topological sort O(V + E) O(V)
Dijkstra (binary heap) O((V + E) log V) O(V + E)
Bellman-Ford O(V * E) O(V)
Floyd-Warshall O(V^3) O(V^2)
Union-Find (both optimizations) O(alpha(n)) amortized per op O(n)
Kruskal / Prim (heap) O(E log E) / O(E log V) O(V + E)
Trie insert / search O(L) O(total characters x alphabet)
Subsets / permutations O(2^n * n) / O(n! * n) O(n) plus output
DP states x transitions states (often reducible)
Sieve of Eratosthenes O(n log log n) O(n)
GCD, fast power O(log n) O(1)

Binary search: first true

Aspect Detail
Use when Searching a sorted array for a boundary, or searching an answer range with a monotonic feasibility check
Invariant The first true lies in [left, right]; [left, right) is the live search space
Cost O(log range) calls to the predicate
Mistakes Non-monotonic predicate; bounds that exclude the answer; overflow in the predicate
Changes The predicate and the bounds; "last true" = first true of the negation, minus 1
Java
// Find the FIRST x in [lo, hi] where ok(x) is true, given ok is false...false true...true.
// Returns hi + 1 if ok is never true. Works for indices (data) and for answers.
static int firstTrue(int lo, int hi, IntPredicate ok) {
    int left = lo, right = hi + 1;            // search space [left, right)
    while (left < right) {
        int mid = left + (right - left) / 2;
        if (ok.test(mid)) right = mid;        // mid might be the first true
        else left = mid + 1;                  // mid and everything before are false
    }
    return left;
}
// CHANGE: the predicate and the bounds.
//   lower bound of t in a: firstTrue(0, n - 1, i -> a[i] >= t)
//   min feasible answer:   firstTrue(minAns, maxAns, x -> feasible(x))
//   max feasible answer (true...true false...false): firstTrue(lo, hi, x -> !feasible(x)) - 1

Sliding window and two pointers

Aspect Detail
Use when Window: contiguous range with a condition that stays true when a valid window shrinks. Two pointers: pairs in sorted data
Invariant After the inner loop, [left, right] is the longest valid window ending at right
Cost O(n): each index enters and leaves once
Mistakes if instead of while when shrinking; updating the answer in the wrong place for shortest vs longest; negative numbers
Changes The state, the add and remove steps, the invalid condition, where the answer is updated
Java
// Variable window: longest valid window. The window must stay valid after shrinking,
// and adding elements can only make it "less valid" (monotonic).
static int longestValidWindow(int[] nums, int limit) {
    int left = 0, best = 0;
    long state = 0;                                      // CHANGE: sum, counts map, distinct count...
    for (int right = 0; right < nums.length; right++) {
        state += nums[right];                            // CHANGE: add nums[right] to state
        while (state > limit) {                          // CHANGE: "window invalid" condition
            state -= nums[left++];                       // CHANGE: remove nums[left] from state
        }
        best = Math.max(best, right - left + 1);         // longest: update after shrinking
    }
    return best;
}
// Shortest valid window: move the update INSIDE the while loop, before shrinking.
// Counting windows: add (right - left + 1) after shrinking (for "at most" conditions).

// Opposite-direction two pointers on sorted input.
static boolean pairWithSum(int[] sorted, int target) {
    int left = 0, right = sorted.length - 1;
    while (left < right) {
        int sum = sorted[left] + sorted[right];
        if (sum == target) return true;
        if (sum < target) left++; else right--;          // CHANGE: which pointer and why
    }
    return false;
}

Prefix sums with a hash map

Aspect Detail
Use when Counting subarrays with an exact sum, remainder, or balance, including negative values
Invariant Before processing index i, the map counts prefix values for all earlier positions (including the empty prefix)
Cost O(n) time, O(n) space
Mistakes Missing the 0 -> 1 seed; inserting before querying; negative remainders in Java
Changes The transform of each element; count vs first index (longest)
Java
// Count subarrays whose sum satisfies prefix(i) - prefix(j) == k.
static int countSubarrays(int[] nums, int k) {
    Map<Long, Integer> count = new HashMap<>();
    count.put(0L, 1);                                    // empty prefix: subarrays starting at 0
    long prefix = 0;
    int result = 0;
    for (int x : nums) {
        prefix += x;                                     // CHANGE: transform x (0 -> -1, x % k ...)
        result += count.getOrDefault(prefix - k, 0);     // query first
        count.merge(prefix, 1, Integer::sum);            // then record
    }
    return result;
}
// Longest instead of count: store the FIRST index of each prefix, never overwrite.

Linked list reversal and cycle detection

Aspect Detail
Use when Reversing all or part of a list; detecting cycles or finding middles
Invariant prev heads the reversed part, head heads the rest; fast is twice as far as slow
Cost O(n) time, O(1) space
Mistakes Overwriting next before saving it; forgetting the dummy when the head can change
Changes The range to reverse; the stopping condition for the middle
Java
static ListNode reverse(ListNode head) {
    ListNode prev = null;
    while (head != null) {
        ListNode next = head.next;
        head.next = prev;
        prev = head;
        head = next;
    }
    return prev;
}

static boolean hasCycle(ListNode head) {
    ListNode slow = head, fast = head;
    while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
        slow = slow.next;
        fast = fast.next.next;
        if (slow == fast) return true;
    }
    return false;
}
// Always: dummy node when the head can change; save next before rewiring; draw it first.

Monotonic stack

Aspect Detail
Use when Next or previous greater or smaller element; ranges bounded by nearest larger or smaller values
Invariant Values at stack indices are monotonic; every popped index has found its answer
Cost O(n): each index pushed and popped once
Mistakes Storing values instead of indices; strict vs non-strict comparisons with duplicates; forgetting leftovers
Changes The comparison direction; what is recorded on pop; previous (stack top) vs next (current element)
Java
// Next greater element to the right (value), -1 if none.
static int[] nextGreater(int[] nums) {
    int[] result = new int[nums.length];
    Arrays.fill(result, -1);
    Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();           // indices; values decreasing
    for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        while (!stack.isEmpty() && nums[stack.peek()] < nums[i])   // CHANGE: < vs <=, > for smaller
            result[stack.pop()] = nums[i];               // nums[i] resolves the popped index
        stack.push(i);
    }
    return result;
}
// Previous greater: the element left on the stack top after popping is the answer for i.

Tree DFS and BFS

Aspect Detail
Use when DFS: answers built from children (bottom-up) or from ancestors (parameters). BFS: per-level questions
Invariant DFS returns exactly what the parent needs; BFS processes one full level per round
Cost O(n) time; O(h) DFS stack, O(width) BFS queue
Mistakes Returning the final answer instead of the parent's need; reading queue.size() inside the loop
Changes Base value, combine step, global update, return value
Java
// DFS with a return value: combine children's answers (bottom-up).
static int dfs(TreeNode node) {
    if (node == null) return 0;                          // CHANGE: base value
    int left = dfs(node.left), right = dfs(node.right);
    // CHANGE: update a global answer using left, right, node.val if needed
    return 1 + Math.max(left, right);                    // CHANGE: what the parent needs
}

// BFS by levels.
static List<List<Integer>> bfs(TreeNode root) {
    List<List<Integer>> levels = new ArrayList<>();
    Deque<TreeNode> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    if (root != null) q.offer(root);
    while (!q.isEmpty()) {
        List<Integer> level = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int size = q.size(); size > 0; size--) {
            TreeNode n = q.poll();
            level.add(n.val);
            if (n.left != null) q.offer(n.left);
            if (n.right != null) q.offer(n.right);
        }
        levels.add(level);
    }
    return levels;
}
// Top-down state (ancestors): pass it as a parameter, e.g. dfs(node, maxSoFar).

Backtracking

Aspect Detail
Use when Enumerating subsets, permutations, combinations, partitions, placements
Invariant path is exactly the current partial choice; it is restored after each recursive call
Cost (nodes in the decision tree) x (work per node), usually exponential
Mistakes Adding path without copying; forgetting to undo; wrong start index (i vs i + 1 vs 0)
Changes Goal test, duplicate skip, pruning, the recursion's next start
Java
static void backtrack(int[] items, int start, List<Integer> path, List<List<Integer>> out) {
    // CHANGE: if (goal reached) { out.add(new ArrayList<>(path)); return; }
    out.add(new ArrayList<>(path));                      // subsets: every node is an answer
    for (int i = start; i < items.length; i++) {
        // CHANGE: if (i > start && items[i] == items[i - 1]) continue;   // duplicates (sorted)
        // CHANGE: if (cannot lead to an answer) break or continue;       // pruning
        path.add(items[i]);                              // choose
        backtrack(items, i + 1, path, out);              // explore (i for reuse, 0 + used[] for permutations)
        path.remove(path.size() - 1);                    // un-choose
    }
}

Heap: top k

Aspect Detail
Use when k largest or smallest, kth element, streams
Invariant The heap holds the k best seen so far; its top is the worst of them
Cost O(n log k) time, O(k) space
Mistakes Max-heap for k largest (it should be a min-heap); expecting sorted iteration
Changes Heap direction, comparator, what is stored (value, pair, entry)
Java
// K largest: min-heap of size k. (K smallest: max-heap of size k.)
static List<Integer> kLargest(int[] nums, int k) {
    PriorityQueue<Integer> heap = new PriorityQueue<>();   // CHANGE: comparator for objects
    for (int x : nums) {
        heap.offer(x);
        if (heap.size() > k) heap.poll();
    }
    List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>(heap);
    Collections.sort(out, Collections.reverseOrder());
    return out;
}

Graph BFS and DFS

Aspect Detail
Use when Reachability, components, grid regions; BFS for fewest steps with equal costs
Invariant A node is marked when it is first discovered, so it is processed once; BFS processes distance d before d + 1
Cost O(V + E), or O(R x C) on a grid
Mistakes Marking on dequeue (duplicates in the queue); recursion depth on big grids; forgetting multi-source starts
Changes Sources, what blocks a move, what is recorded per node
Java
static final int[][] DIRS = {{1, 0}, {-1, 0}, {0, 1}, {0, -1}};

// Grid BFS shortest path from (sr, sc) to (tr, tc); -1 if unreachable.
static int gridShortestPath(int[][] grid, int sr, int sc, int tr, int tc) {
    int rows = grid.length, cols = grid[0].length;
    boolean[][] seen = new boolean[rows][cols];
    Deque<int[]> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    q.offer(new int[]{sr, sc});                          // CHANGE: multi-source = offer all sources
    seen[sr][sc] = true;
    for (int steps = 0; !q.isEmpty(); steps++) {
        for (int size = q.size(); size > 0; size--) {
            int[] cell = q.poll();
            if (cell[0] == tr && cell[1] == tc) return steps;
            for (int[] d : DIRS) {
                int r = cell[0] + d[0], c = cell[1] + d[1];
                if (r < 0 || c < 0 || r >= rows || c >= cols) continue;
                if (seen[r][c] || grid[r][c] == 1) continue;   // CHANGE: what blocks a move
                seen[r][c] = true;                             // mark on ENQUEUE
                q.offer(new int[]{r, c});
            }
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

// Adjacency-list DFS (recursive). Use an explicit stack if depth can exceed ~10^4.
static void dfs(List<List<Integer>> adj, int u, boolean[] seen) {
    seen[u] = true;
    for (int v : adj.get(u)) if (!seen[v]) dfs(adj, v, seen);
}

Topological sort (Kahn)

Aspect Detail
Use when Ordering with dependencies; detecting cycles in directed graphs
Invariant Every node in the queue has all its prerequisites already output
Cost O(V + E)
Mistakes Edge direction reversed; treating "fewer than V nodes output" as success
Changes Edge construction; what you do with each node as it is output (DP in topological order)
Java
// Kahn's algorithm. Returns an order, or an empty list if there is a cycle.
static List<Integer> topoSort(int n, int[][] edges) {          // edge u -> v
    List<List<Integer>> adj = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) adj.add(new ArrayList<>());
    int[] indeg = new int[n];
    for (int[] e : edges) { adj.get(e[0]).add(e[1]); indeg[e[1]]++; }
    Deque<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if (indeg[i] == 0) q.offer(i);
    List<Integer> order = new ArrayList<>();
    while (!q.isEmpty()) {
        int u = q.poll();
        order.add(u);
        for (int v : adj.get(u)) if (--indeg[v] == 0) q.offer(v);
    }
    return order.size() == n ? order : List.of();
}

Union-Find

Aspect Detail
Use when Dynamic connectivity, grouping by shared keys, redundant edges, Kruskal
Invariant Two nodes are in the same set exactly when find returns the same root
Cost Effectively O(1) amortized per operation with path compression and union by size
Mistakes Comparing parent[a] == parent[b] instead of find(a) == find(b); forgetting to initialize parents
Changes How items map to indices (use a HashMap for strings); what is counted on union
Java
static int[] parent;

static int find(int x) {
    while (parent[x] != x) { parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]; x = parent[x]; }
    return x;
}

static boolean union(int a, int b) {
    int ra = find(a), rb = find(b);
    if (ra == rb) return false;
    parent[ra] = rb;                 // add union by size/rank for guaranteed bounds
    return true;
}
// init: parent = new int[n]; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) parent[i] = i;

The full version with union by size and a component counter is in Module 12.

Dijkstra

Aspect Detail
Use when Single-source shortest paths with non-negative weights
Invariant When a node is popped with its current distance, that distance is final
Cost O((V + E) log V)
Mistakes Negative weights; not skipping stale entries; using int when sums can overflow
Changes How a path's cost combines (sum, max, product), the target, extra state in the node
Java
// adj.get(u) holds {v, w}. Non-negative weights only.
static long[] dijkstra(List<List<int[]>> adj, int src) {
    long[] dist = new long[adj.size()];
    Arrays.fill(dist, Long.MAX_VALUE);
    dist[src] = 0;
    PriorityQueue<long[]> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Long.compare(a[0], b[0]));
    pq.offer(new long[]{0, src});
    while (!pq.isEmpty()) {
        long[] top = pq.poll();
        int u = (int) top[1];
        if (top[0] > dist[u]) continue;                  // stale
        for (int[] e : adj.get(u)) {
            long nd = dist[u] + e[1];                    // CHANGE: max(dist, w) for bottleneck paths
            if (nd < dist[e[0]]) { dist[e[0]] = nd; pq.offer(new long[]{nd, e[0]}); }
        }
    }
    return dist;
}

Core DP patterns

Aspect Detail
Use when Counting, optimizing, or deciding with overlapping subproblems
Invariant Every state is computed only after the states it depends on
Cost (number of states) x (transitions per state)
Mistakes Incomplete state; wrong iteration order; wrong initialization for min problems; knapsack loop direction
Changes State definition, transition, base cases, answer cell
Java
// 1. Top-down: write the recurrence, cache it.
static long[] memo;
static long solve(int i, int[] a) {
    if (i >= a.length) return 0;                         // base case
    if (memo[i] != Long.MIN_VALUE) return memo[i];
    long take = a[i] + solve(i + 2, a), skip = solve(i + 1, a);   // CHANGE: the choices
    return memo[i] = Math.max(take, skip);
}

// 2. 0/1 knapsack (each item once): capacity loop goes DOWN.
static int knapsack01(int[] weight, int[] value, int cap) {
    int[] dp = new int[cap + 1];
    for (int i = 0; i < weight.length; i++)
        for (int c = cap; c >= weight[i]; c--)
            dp[c] = Math.max(dp[c], dp[c - weight[i]] + value[i]);
    return dp[cap];
}

// 3. Unbounded knapsack (items reusable): capacity loop goes UP.
static int knapsackUnbounded(int[] weight, int[] value, int cap) {
    int[] dp = new int[cap + 1];
    for (int i = 0; i < weight.length; i++)
        for (int c = weight[i]; c <= cap; c++)
            dp[c] = Math.max(dp[c], dp[c - weight[i]] + value[i]);
    return dp[cap];
}

// 4. Two sequences: dp[i][j] over prefixes a[0..i), b[0..j).
static int twoSequences(String a, String b) {
    int[][] dp = new int[a.length() + 1][b.length() + 1];   // CHANGE: base row/col
    for (int i = 1; i <= a.length(); i++)
        for (int j = 1; j <= b.length(); j++)
            dp[i][j] = a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1) ? dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1
                                                          : Math.max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1]);
    return dp[a.length()][b.length()];
}

Trie

Aspect Detail
Use when Prefix queries, autocomplete, wildcard search, many-word grid search, max XOR
Invariant The path from the root to a node spells a prefix; end marks complete words
Cost O(L) per insert or lookup
Mistakes Treating a prefix as a word; using arrays for large alphabets
Changes Child storage (array vs map) and what each node records
Java
static class TrieNode {
    TrieNode[] next = new TrieNode[26];   // CHANGE: Map<Character, TrieNode> for big alphabets
    boolean end;                          // CHANGE: count, word, or aggregated value
}

static void insert(TrieNode root, String w) {
    TrieNode n = root;
    for (char ch : w.toCharArray()) {
        if (n.next[ch - 'a'] == null) n.next[ch - 'a'] = new TrieNode();
        n = n.next[ch - 'a'];
    }
    n.end = true;
}

Interview framework

A repeatable 13-step process for an unfamiliar coding question, with the exact questions to ask yourself at each step, and a recovery playbook for when you get stuck.

On this page

  1. The 13 steps
  2. Questions to ask yourself at each stage
  3. Recovery playbook
  4. Communication checklist

The 13 steps

The decode method on its own page is how you think. This framework is how you think out loud, under time pressure, with someone watching. A typical 45-minute round leaves 35 to 40 minutes for one Medium problem or two shorter ones.

Phase Steps Rough budget (one Medium in 40 min)
Understand 1 to 3 5 minutes
Design 4 to 10 10 to 12 minutes
Implement 11 12 to 15 minutes
Verify 12 to 13 5 minutes
Details

1. Clarify the input, output, constraints, and edge cases

Ask, then write the answers in a comment at the top of the editor.

  • What are the sizes? (They set the complexity target; see Module 1.)
  • Can values be negative, zero, duplicated? Can the input be empty?
  • Is the input sorted? Can I modify it?
  • What should I return if there is no answer? Any answer, or a specific one (smallest index, lexicographically first)?
  • For strings: which characters? For graphs: directed? connected? self-loops?
Details

2. Translate the question into a simpler statement

Say it back in one sentence, without the story: "So I need the length of the shortest contiguous subarray whose sum is at least k, and values are positive." The interviewer will correct a misunderstanding now instead of in 20 minutes.

Details

3. Work through a small example by hand

Pick a 4 to 6 element example that is not the given one, and solve it out loud. Notice what you track in your head; that is usually the state of the final algorithm.

Details

4. Identify the input structure and the required operation

"Contiguous, positive values, minimize length." "Dependencies between items." "Many queries on a fixed array." Name the properties from the structure table.

Details

5. Formulate a straightforward correct approach

"The simplest correct approach is to try every start and extend until the sum reaches k." Say it even if you already see better; it shows you can always produce a correct answer and gives a baseline to improve.

Details

6. Analyze its time and space

"That is O(n^2) time and O(1) space. With n up to 10^5 that is 10^10 operations, too slow."

Details

7. Identify repeated work or useful properties

Ask the optimization questions one by one: What is recomputed? Can order discard candidates? Can a window be maintained? Is checking easier than computing?

Details

8. Derive the pattern and explain why it applies

"Because all values are positive, shrinking a valid window keeps the sum non-increasing, so once the window is valid I can move left without missing anything. That is a variable sliding window." State the required condition and why it holds.

Details

9. Visualize the algorithm and track its state

Draw the array with two pointers, the tree with return values, or the DP table, for your small example. Walk two or three steps. This is where many bugs are found before they exist.

The figures in this handbook use conventions you can reproduce in a shared editor or on a whiteboard in under a minute:

Structure How to draw it What to update as you step
Array, pointers, window Values in a row, indices underneath, pointer names above with an arrow, a bracket under the window Move the pointer labels; cross out discarded cells
Prefix sums A second row under the array, one cell longer, starting with 0 Circle the two cells you subtract
Linked list Boxes with arrows; write prev, curr, next above the nodes Erase one arrow and draw its replacement per step
Stack, queue, deque A vertical column (stack) or a horizontal row (queue); write indices, not only values Write each push and pop as its own line, with the reason for the pop
Recursion, backtracking A call tree: arguments in each node, return value next to it; mark pruned branches with an X Fill in return values bottom-up
Tree Nodes and edges; next to each node, what it returns to its parent Annotate on the way up
Graph BFS Nodes with distances written beside them; the queue as a row below Strike nodes off the queue as they are processed
DP A table with labeled rows and columns; an arrow from each cell to the cells it reads Fill cells in the loop order you will code
Details

10. State the invariant or reasoning that guarantees correctness

One sentence: "After the inner loop, the window is the shortest valid window ending at right." If you cannot say it, keep working on step 9.

Details

11. Implement clean Java

  • Write the function signature and the edge-case returns first.
  • Use descriptive names (left, windowSum, best), not i2, tmp.
  • Narrate briefly: "Now I shrink while the window is valid."
  • If a helper would make the main logic clearer (a feasibility check, a neighbor iterator), write it.
  • Do not optimize prematurely; finish a correct version first.
Details

12. Dry-run on a normal case and a boundary case

Trace the code, not your intention, line by line with your small example, writing variable values beside the code. Then run one boundary case: empty input, one element, all equal, no answer.

Details

13. State and justify the final complexity

"Time O(n): each index enters and leaves the window once. Space O(1)." Mention trade-offs and possible follow-ups ("If values could be negative, I would switch to prefix sums with a monotonic deque").

Questions to ask yourself at each stage

Stage Ask yourself
Before designing What would make this problem trivial? (Sorted input? Small n? Only positive values?) Which of those do I actually have?
Brute force What exactly does my brute force recompute? Can I name the inner loop's job in words?
Optimizing Which candidates can I prove irrelevant? What is monotonic here? What would I need to know in O(1) to skip the inner loop?
Choosing a pattern What is its required condition, and does my small example satisfy it? What would break it?
Before coding What are my variables and what does each mean exactly? What is the loop invariant? When do I update the answer?
After coding What happens on the first iteration and the last? What if the loop never runs? Where can an index go out of bounds? Where can an int overflow?

Recovery playbook

Details

"I cannot identify the pattern"

  1. Go back to the small example and solve it by hand, slowly. Write down what you track.
  2. Classify the task type (existence, counting, optimization, search, ordering, connectivity, construction) and look at the families for it in the task type table.
  3. Look at the constraints: n = 20 allows exponential search; n = 10^5 demands O(n log n); a value range of 10^9 hints at binary search on the answer.
  4. Say the brute force out loud and ask what it repeats. The optimization is almost always hiding there.
  5. Ask the interviewer: "I am considering X and Y; I am not sure X's condition holds because of Z. Does that seem like the right direction?" Asking well is a positive signal.
Details

"It looks like several patterns"

Write the required condition of each candidate and test it against your small example and one adversarial case. The one whose condition holds is the one. The decision tables list the deciding question for the common pairs.

Details

"My brute force is too slow"

  • Identify the innermost loop and name its job ("find the previous smaller element").
  • Ask what structure answers that job faster: hash map (lookup), sorted order (binary search), monotonic stack (nearest larger or smaller), heap (current extreme), prefix sum (range totals), memo table (repeated subproblem).
  • If the outer loop is the expensive part, ask whether order lets you skip candidates (two pointers, binary search on the answer).
Details

"I understand solutions when I read them but cannot derive them"

This is the most common plateau, and the fix is in how you review:

  • After reading a solution, close it and write down the one observation that made it work, in one sentence.
  • Re-derive the solution on a blank page the next day, starting from the brute force, without looking.
  • Mark the problem "Solved with hints" honestly and let the revision queue bring it back.
  • For each new problem, before searching for the solution, spend 20 minutes on the decode method and write down where you got stuck. That note is what to compare with the editorial.
Details

"My code passes the examples but fails hidden tests"

Check, in this order:

  1. Edge sizes: empty input, one element, two elements.
  2. Extreme values: negative numbers, zeros, Integer.MAX_VALUE and MIN_VALUE, overflow in sums and products.
  3. Duplicates: equal values in sorting, binary search, and backtracking.
  4. Boundaries in loops: < vs <=, n vs n - 1, the last window, the final flush of a stack.
  5. State reset: static or shared variables reused across test cases (LeetCode runs many cases on one instance).
  6. Misread requirements: subsequence vs subarray, strictly vs non-strictly increasing, 0-based vs 1-based.

Then write a brute-force checker and compare on small random inputs.

Details

"Time Limit Exceeded" or "Memory Limit Exceeded"

Symptom Likely cause Fix
TLE with an O(n^2) idea at n = 10^5 Wrong algorithm Return to step 7
TLE with the right algorithm Hidden O(n) operations inside loops: list.contains, list.remove(0), substring, string +, PriorityQueue.remove(Object) Use a set, ArrayDeque, indices, StringBuilder, lazy deletion
TLE in recursion Missing memoization, or memo keyed by an object that is rebuilt each call Memoize on primitive state; use arrays instead of maps where possible
TLE in BFS Nodes enqueued many times Mark visited when enqueuing
MLE A full 2D DP table where one row suffices; storing all paths; huge recursion Roll the table; store parents instead of paths; iterate
Stack overflow Deep recursion on 10^5 nodes or large grids Explicit stack or BFS
Details

"I am stuck in the interview and the clock is running"

  • Say where you are. "I have a correct O(n^2) approach. I believe there is an O(n) one because ..., but I have not found the key observation yet." Silence is the worst option.
  • Offer to code the brute force if 15 minutes or less remain. A working simpler solution beats an unfinished optimal one.
  • Simplify the problem: solve it for sorted input, for positive values only, or for k = 1, then generalize.
  • Use the hint well. When the interviewer gives a hint, repeat it in your own words and connect it to your example before changing code.
  • Keep the code clean even when rushed; it is easier to fix and easier to discuss.

Communication checklist

  • Restate the problem and confirm assumptions before designing.
  • Say the brute force and its complexity before optimizing.
  • Explain the key observation and the invariant before coding.
  • Narrate while coding at the level of intent, not syntax.
  • Test out loud with a small example and a boundary case.
  • State the final complexity and one realistic follow-up or trade-off.
