Roadmap and revision

The modules in prerequisite order, grouped into five phases, with a study loop that works at any pace, a revision system built into the problem statuses, and checkpoints that tell you when to move on.

On this page

  1. The five phases
  2. The study session loop
  3. The revision system
  4. Mixed practice and timed sets
  5. Mock interviews
  6. Revision checkpoints

The five phases

The phases follow the prerequisite map. Move to the next phase when you pass its checkpoint, not when a calendar says so. Faster is not better if the checkpoint is not honestly passed.

Phase Modules Focus Why here
1. Foundations 1, Decode, 2, 3, 4 Complexity, hashing, prefix sums, two pointers, windows, binary search Highest-frequency Medium patterns; everything later stores data in arrays and maps
2. Linear structures and recursion 5, 6, 7, 8 Intervals, pointers, stacks, monotonic structures, recursion, backtracking Pointer discipline and recursion are prerequisites for trees
3. Trees and priorities 9, 10, 11, 13 Tree recursion, BSTs, heaps, greedy proofs, tries Trees are the most common onsite topic; heaps and greedy reuse sorting
4. Graphs and DP 12, 14 Traversal, shortest paths, ordering, connectivity, the DP derivation process Both build on recursion and trees; they decide many Hard and late-round questions
5. Integration 15, 16, 17, mixed practice, mocks Bits, math, design, interleaved review, timed rounds Short modules plus the transfer from "I know the pattern" to "I can do it under time pressure"

Modules 15 and 16 are short and depend only on Module 2. If you want variety during a long phase, slot them in anywhere after Phase 1.

The study session loop

Every session, whatever its length, follows the same order:

  1. Revision queue first. Re-solve everything due (shown on the home page and in the tracker). Start from a blank editor. Update each status.
  2. One lesson, practice first. Attempt its "Try it first" problem, then read the short part, step through the figure, and work the guided solve. Tick "Studied" when you could teach it.
  3. New problems from the current bank, in order. Use the time limits below.
  4. Write one line per problem (in your own notes): the key observation, in one sentence.

Time limits per attempt

Difficulty Think before coding Total before a hint After the hint
Medium 10 to 15 minutes 30 minutes Read only the key idea, close it, implement yourself
Hard 15 to 20 minutes 45 minutes Read the approach, re-derive it the next day

Hint ladder. Do not jump to the full solution. In order: re-read the pattern card for the bank; look only at the problem's topic tags; read the first paragraph of an editorial; read the full approach; read code last, if at all.

The revision system

Problem statuses are the revision system. The five study categories map to statuses, and each status schedules the next review:

Category Status to set Review again in What the review should be
Not solved independently Not solved independently 2 days Re-derive from the brute force; do not look at the old code
Solved with hints Solved with hints 4 days Solve clean, then explain the observation out loud
Solved independently Solved independently 10 days Timed re-solve (Medium in 20 minutes)
Needs revision Needs revision 1 day A previously solved problem that went badly on review
Pattern mastered Pattern mastered 30 days Quick check that it is still automatic

Promotion rules. Move a problem up only after a clean re-solve at its review date: hints -> independently -> mastered (mastered requires two clean solves at least a week apart, plus being able to state the invariant). Move it to "Needs revision" whenever a review fails, regardless of its previous status.

Why spaced review works. Re-solving after a gap forces you to rebuild the reasoning instead of recognizing the code. The intervals grow because each successful retrieval makes the next forgetting slower.

Mixed practice and timed sets

Banks are grouped by pattern, which makes recognition easy: you already know the pattern when you open the bank. Interviews do not tell you. From Phase 3 onward, add interleaved practice:

  • Once a week, pick 3 to 4 problems from different earlier modules using the tracker (filter by priority High, any module, status "Solved independently" or "Not started"). Do not look at which module they came from before attempting.
  • Classify each problem before solving it: write the pattern and the required condition, then check.

Timed sets. From Phase 2 onward, once a week, do two Mediums in 45 minutes with the full 13-step interview framework, talking out loud. Record yourself or work with a partner.

Mock interviews

When How often Format
Phase 3 Once a week 45 minutes, one Medium, with a peer or a recording; review against the communication checklist
Phase 4 Once or twice a week Mix one Medium with one harder follow-up
Phase 5 Two or more a week Full loop practice: two coding rounds back to back

After each mock, write three lines: what slowed you down, which step of the framework you skipped, and one thing to practice. Feed missed problems into the tracker as "Not solved independently".

Practice tracker

All 407 problems in one place, Medium and Hard only. Filter by module, status, difficulty, or priority; choose "Due for revision" to see today's review list. Changing a status here updates it everywhere in the handbook.

Topic mastery overview

The module cards on the home page show solved problems, studied lessons, and mastery items per module. A module is ready for interviews when its lessons are studied, about 70% of its bank is solved independently (including at least one challenge problem), and all eight mastery items are ticked.

Backup and restore

Progress saves automatically. Use this to move progress between browsers when you are not signed in, or to keep a copy. Restoring merges: the newer entry wins for each problem and checkbox.
